{ "new_title": "Tidy your Git history with interactive rebase and squash", "new_heading": "A practical guide to squashing amending and safely pushing rewritten commits", "new_body": "

So you made a glorious mess of commits and now your branch looks like the aftermath of a coding snack attack. Relax, this is fixable. This guide walks through the sane way to combine commits using interactive rebase and a few command line rituals that keep teammates from staging an intervention.

Why clean commit history

Clean history helps reviewers understand intent and makes blame less embarrassing. Small, frequent commits are lovely during development but before merging you usually want fewer, clearer commits. Think of it as tidying your desk before guests arrive.

Make a backup before you rewrite history

Rewriting commits changes history. That can be powerful and terrifying at the same time. Create a snapshot so you can rollback if you get dramatic.

git log --oneline
git branch backup
# or
git checkout -b backup

Start an interactive rebase to squash or fixup

Pick a sensible range, for example the last three commits. Then open the interactive editor and mark commits to combine.

git rebase -i HEAD~3

In the editor change the word pick to s or squash to merge commit messages with a chance to edit, or use f or fixup to silently fold a commit into the one above. Save and close the editor to let Git do its thing.

Examples of what to write in the todo

  • pick keeps a commit as is
  • squash merges the commit and lets you edit the combined message
  • fixup merges and tosses the commit message

Resolve conflicts like a functioning adult

If a conflict shows up Git will pause and wait for you to clean it up. Use git status to find the angry files, stage the fixes, and continue the rebase.

git status
# fix files
git add 
git rebase --continue

Adjust the final commit message

If you want to polish the resulting commit message after the rebase you can amend it before pushing.

git commit --amend

Push without causing a meltdown

You rewrote history so you must force push. Use the safer option to reduce chances of overwriting other people's work. Also give your teammates a heads up so they do not hit a fantastical merge conflict party.

git push --force-with-lease

If you are working on a shared branch coordinate with the team instead of plunging ahead alone. If they are clever they will rebase their work onto the new branch head. If they are not clever then be kind and help them.

Recap and quick tips

  • Inspect history first with git log --oneline
  • Create a backup branch before rewriting
  • Use git rebase -i to squash or fixup small commits
  • Resolve conflicts with git add and git rebase --continue
  • Use git commit --amend to polish messages
  • Push with git push --force-with-lease and tell your team

Follow these steps and your branch will stop looking like a confessional. And remember to squash before merging to main when you want a tidy story rather than a season of tiny surprises.

" }

{"new_title":"Safely merge one Git branch into another and handle conflicts","new_heading":"Step by step Git merge workflow for branches and conflict fixes","new_body":"

If you want to merge one Git branch into another without starting a small fire you are in the right place. This guide walks through the command line workflow for merging branches testing the result and dealing with merge conflicts with the least amount of drama.

Prepare the repository

First do the boring but crucial stuff. Fetch the latest changes and make sure your working directory is tidy. This reduces the chance of surprises that will waste your time and mine.

git fetch origin
git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate

Use the log to inspect branch topology and see whether a fast forward is likely. If you enjoy mystery do not skip this.

Switch to the target branch

This is the branch that will receive the changes. Use the modern command or the classic one. Pick your favorite.

git switch target-branch
# or
git checkout target-branch

Make sure git status reports a clean working directory before you proceed. If it does not either stash or commit your work. Nobody likes accidental commits named fix later.

Merge the source branch

Time to bring the changes in. If you want to preserve an explicit merge commit for history clarity use the no fast forward option. If you prefer a tidy linear history then a fast forward is fine when available.

git merge source-branch
# preserve non linear history
git merge --no-ff source-branch

What happens when conflicts appear

Git will mark conflicting files with conflict markers. You will see things like <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= and >>>>>>> branch name. Open the files fix the code and remove the markers.

  • Edit the conflicting files to reconcile differences
  • Stage resolved files with git add
  • Finish the merge with git commit or use git merge --continue if you are in a rerere or interactive flow
git add path/to/resolved-file
# then
git commit
# or if using an interactive flow
git merge --continue

Verify and test the merged branch

Run unit tests build the project and do a quick manual check. The last thing you want is to push a broken merge and explain it in a meeting.

Push the merged branch to remote

Share your work with the rest of civilization. Push normally and if the remote rejects the push because of history changes discuss options with teammates. Forcing history is the nuclear option and should be coordinated.

git push origin target-branch
# if push is rejected discuss a pull request or coordinate before forcing history

When to use a pull request and code review

Pull requests and code review slow you down on purpose and that is a feature. They catch issues and document decisions. Use them for collaborative merges and for important branches like main or release.

Quick checklist

  • Fetch latest changes and inspect branch graph
  • Switch to the receiving branch and ensure a clean working tree
  • Merge the source branch with or without a merge commit depending on your policy
  • Resolve conflicts then test locally
  • Push and coordinate on any history rewriting

Tip Use git log --graph --oneline --decorate to visualize branch topology and consider git merge --no-ff when you want a clear merge commit to help future you debug the history. Merge responsibly and avoid force pushing unless you enjoy chaos.

"}

{ "new_title": "Force a merge commit in Git for clearer team history and audits", "new_heading": "When to choose no-ff merges in Git workflows for tidy audit trails", "new_body": "

What a no-ff merge does in Git

If you like clear crime scenes in your commit graph then the no-ff merge is your forensics kit. A Git no-ff merge always creates a merge commit even when Git could have taken the easy fast forward route. The command is simple and point blank

git merge --no-ff feature

That merge commit bundles the feature work as a single logical unit in the history. Instead of the main branch pointer sliding forward like nothing happened you get a named join point that says yes this work was merged and yes someone took responsibility for it.

Why teams pick no-ff merges

  • Clearer git history for reviewers and future you who has forgotten everything
  • Easier rollback of a whole feature because the merge commit isolates the change set
  • Useful with release branches and Git Flow so the merge commit names the feature and records when it joined main

The trade off is obvious. You get extra merge commits that can clutter history for tiny changes. For a one line typo fix you probably do not need a merge commit unless your team docs say otherwise.

How no-ff behaves after a rebase

Rebase rewrites the feature branch onto the tip of main so a normal merge might fast forward and avoid creating a merge commit. If you still want the feature grouped then use the no-ff flag after the rebase. The merge commit will be created regardless of whether a fast forward would be possible.

If you want to inspect or stage the merge before finishing use this trick

git merge --no-ff --no-commit feature

That lets you review the staged merge and edit the merge message to explain the rationale. Good commit messages save careers.

Commands that help you read and manage the graph

  • git log --graph --oneline --decorate to see the commit graph in an instant
  • git show <merge-commit-hash> to inspect what the merge actually did
  • Use branch protection and pull request checks to enforce whether merge commits are required

When to pick no-ff and when to let Git fast forward

  • Prefer no-ff for long lived branches or features that should be grouped for auditing or rollback
  • Prefer fast forward for tiny fixes and trivial refactors when you want a linear history
  • If your team likes a consistent narrative pick a policy and enforce it with your CI and PR settings

Quick checklist for a sane git workflow

  • Decide on merge commit policy and document it in your contribution guide
  • Use server side rules to enforce the policy so nostalgia does not wreck your history
  • Encourage useful merge messages that explain why a feature was added not what files changed

Bottom line do not treat no-ff as a magic cure all. It is a tool in the version control toolbox that makes history auditable and rollbacks less painful. Use it when the grouping of work matters and skip it when the change is so small that an extra commit would just be noise. Your future self will either thank you or file a restraining order depending on how consistent your team is.

" }

{ "new_title": "Make your Git history boring and neat with fast forward merges", "new_heading": "When to use fast forward merges in Git workflows for clean history", "new_body": "

Fast forward merges are the neat freak of version control. They move the target branch pointer forward to the feature branch tip when nothing happened on the target branch after you branched off. The result is a linear history with no merge commit and fewer existential questions from future you.

What a fast forward merge actually does

In plain terms a fast forward merge means Git does not create a new commit. If your feature branch is strictly ahead of the main branch then Git simply points main at the same commit as feature. No extra clutter in the log and no merge commit explaining what you already know.

How to run a normal fast forward merge

git checkout main
git merge feature

That is it. If there are no divergent commits on main Git will move main forward. If main has new commits then Git falls back to creating a merge commit and you will see the usual conflict negotiation drama.

How to force a merge commit even when a fast forward is possible

git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature

Use this when you want to preserve a visible grouping for the feature branch. The --no-ff flag tells Git to make a merge commit even though the history could be linear.

Pros and cons in real world speak

  • Pros Keep history tidy and linear. Easier to git log and bisect when you are trying to find the bug that ruined your Friday.
  • Cons You lose an explicit record that a branch existed. That grouping can be useful for audits, reverts, or telling your manager which commits were part of a single feature.

Workflow guidance for teams

Pick a convention and stick to it. If your team cares about clean readable history and most changes are small then allow fast forward merges. If you need traceability across a feature or you want a clear pull request record then require merge commits for PRs. Mixed practices lead to a history that looks like a hedge maze built by a drunk cartographer.

When to use fast forward merges

  • Trivial fixes or single commit updates
  • When your CI and review process do not require a visible branch boundary
  • When you prefer a linear history for easier debugging and bisecting

When to prefer merge commits or a no fast forward policy

  • Features that represent a unit of work you may want to revert together
  • When compliance or auditing requires clear grouping of changes
  • When PRs should remain visible in the timeline for reviewers or stakeholders

How to enforce your choice in pull request workflows

Most hosting platforms let you require a merge commit for pull requests. If branch context matters enable that policy in repository settings. If you want fast forward merges you can allow them but enforce branch protections to keep the main branch stable.

Quick cheat sheet

  • git merge feature Try a fast forward merge if possible
  • git merge --no-ff feature Force a merge commit and keep the branch visible
  • Pick team rules for git workflow and document them in your repo so new teammates do not invent chaos

Fast forward merges are not mystical. They are a choice about how tidy you want history to be versus how visible you want feature boundaries to remain. Use them thoughtfully and your git history will be a helpful ally instead of a horror story to be avoided at all costs.

" }

{"new_title":"Clean Up Uncommitted Git Messes Without Losing Your Mind","new_heading":"Practical git restore and clean tips for removing uncommitted files safely","new_body":"

If your working tree looks like a crime scene and you need to revert uncommitted changes without causing collateral damage this guide is your bleach and a prayer. Follow these safe commands to discard edits, unstage files, remove untracked junk and reset to the last commit. This is for developers who love version control but sometimes forget how tidy humans are supposed to be.

Discard edits to tracked files

When you made changes to tracked files and decide they are trash you can throw them away with git restore in modern Git. For older Git versions the old checkout form still works.

git restore path/to/file.txt
# older Git
git checkout -- path/to/file.txt

What happens here is simple. Your working tree file is replaced by the version in the index or HEAD depending on stage state. Any unsaved local edits are lost unless you stash or commit them first. This is irreversible by default so make sure it is what you want.

Unstage changes and keep your edits

If the staging area is too enthusiastic and you want to move files back to the working tree without losing edits use one of these.

git restore --staged path/to/file.txt
# or the classic approach
git reset HEAD path/to/file.txt

Both commands remove the file from the index so it will not be part of the next commit. Your working copy stays intact so you can edit more or run tests. This is a safe maneuver for developers who staged something prematurely.

Remove untracked files and directories the safe way

Untracked files are the junk build products and temp files you never meant to check in. Do a dry run first so you do not accidentally delete something you actually need.

git clean -n

This previews what will be removed. If the preview looks like actual trash run the real command.

git clean -f
# to remove untracked directories too
git clean -fd

Note that git clean will delete files from disk. If you ever want to protect certain generated files add them to .gitignore so you do not repeat cleanup chores forever.

Reset everything back to the last commit

If you want a nuclear option that makes your working tree match the last commit run this. It resets both index and working tree.

git reset --hard HEAD

This will discard staged changes and unstaged edits. Do not run this if you have uncommitted work you care about. Consider stashing first.

Safer alternatives and good habits

  • Stash changes if you want to save them for later with git stash or git stash push -m "wip"
  • Use git clean -n to preview deletions before you run git clean -f
  • Add recurring junk to .gitignore so you do not need to clean constantly
  • Commit small working snapshots instead of relying on destructive commands when possible

Quick stash examples

git stash push -m "WIP before clean"
# bring it back later
git stash pop

Stash is the polite way to save an in progress mess. Pop it when you are brave enough to deal with the chaos.

Final sanity check

When running destructive commands think twice and run a dry preview first. Use git clean -n before git clean -f and consider stashing or committing anything you might regret losing. Follow these steps to tame uncommitted changes and remove files without becoming the reason someone writes a blame driven postmortem.

"}

{ "new_title": "How to reset a Git repo and delete untracked files safely", "new_heading": "Quick steps to purge changes and clean untracked files in Git", "new_body": "

Why this matters

If your working tree looks like a crime scene and you just want to start over without crying into your keyboard this guide will get you back to a clean state fast. We cover inspecting the repo with git status, resetting tracked changes, and removing untracked files so your Git working tree is pristine again.

Check the repo status

Before doing anything dramatic run git status. It shows modified tracked files and the list of untracked files. This tiny step prevents the classic facepalm moment that follows losing something you actually needed.

git status

Reset tracked changes

If you are sure you want to throw away all modifications to tracked files use the hard reset. Yes it is destructive, and yes you should make sure you do not need those edits.

git reset --hard HEAD

This resets the index and working tree to the last commit. Tracked files are restored to committed contents and local modifications are removed.

Preview and remove untracked files

Untracked files are the loose socks of repositories. Preview what would be removed first to avoid accidental data loss.

  • Show candidates for deletion with git clean -n.
  • When satisfied delete those untracked files and directories with git clean -fd.
git clean -n    # preview
git clean -fd   # delete untracked files and directories

Remove ignored files when you mean it

Some projects generate build artifacts or caches that are ignored by Git. If you want to nuke those too preview first then run the more aggressive command.

git clean -nx    # preview including ignored files
git clean -fdx    # remove untracked and ignored files

Verify and use a safety net

After cleanup run git status again. It should report a clean working tree. If things do not look right do not panic. Check stashes or backups before escalating.

git status

If you are even a little unsure stash your work instead of deleting it. The stash is your safety net and can save your teeth from gnashing.

git stash push -m "wip"

Quick checklist

  • Inspect with git status.
  • Reset tracked files with git reset --hard HEAD.
  • Preview untracked deletions with git clean -n.
  • Remove untracked files with git clean -fd.
  • Optionally remove ignored files with git clean -fdx after preview.
  • Verify with git status and use git stash push -m "wip" if unsure.

Follow these steps and you will have a clean working tree without guessing. Use the preview commands, stash when in doubt, and remember that irreversible commands are like fireworks. Fun when intentional, not when they surprise you.

" }

{"new_title":"Master Java lambda expressions and streams with real examples","new_heading":"Practical Java 8 lambda syntax and functional programming tips","new_body":"

If you are still pretending anonymous classes are a feature then welcome to the modern age. This quick and slightly snarky guide walks through Java lambda expressions with clear examples and usable tips. You will learn what a functional interface is how lambda syntax works and how to use lambdas with collections and streams for cleaner programming.

Functional interfaces and why they matter

A functional interface is simply an interface with one abstract method that acts as a target type for a lambda expression. Annotating with @FunctionalInterface is polite and helps the compiler catch mistakes. Functional interfaces are the plumbing that makes functional programming in Java possible.

interface Adder { int add(int a, int b) }

That interface can be used anywhere a lambda of two ints to an int is expected. The lambda does the heavy lifting the interface just provides a type label.

Lambda syntax without the ancient rituals

Here are the common forms you will type until you stop making semicolon jokes. These are short and to the point.

(a, b) -> a + b
x -> x * x
(int a, int b) -> a + b

Use explicit types when the compiler is confused by overloaded methods or complex generics. Otherwise let Java infer types and enjoy the reduced boilerplate.

Using lambdas with collections and streams

Streams are where lambdas shine. They turn long loops into readable pipelines that you can actually reason about after coffee.

list.stream()
  .filter(x -> x % 2 == 0)
  .map(x -> x * 2)
  .forEach(x -> System.out.println(x))

This replaces a lot of anonymous class clutter and makes intent clearer. Use map when you transform data and filter when you remove items from the flow.

Method references and when not to overuse them

Method references are concise but not mandatory. If they make the code less clear stick with a tiny lambda. Clarity beats cleverness most of the time.

Type inference and common pitfalls

Java uses target typing to infer parameter types for a lambda. That is neat until overloaded methods or tricky generics make the compiler throw a tantrum. When that happens do one of these things.

  • Provide explicit parameter types like (int a, int b) -> a + b
  • Use a cast to the functional interface like (Adder) (a, b) -> a + b
  • Extract a named method if the lambda gets too long

These moves restore clarity and keep the compiler from guessing wrong.

Practice examples you can actually try

  • Compare strings by length with (s1, s2) -> Integer.compare(s1.length(), s2.length())
  • Create a Runnable with () -> System.out.println("Hello") and run it for instant gratification
  • Replace anonymous classes with lambdas in listeners and callbacks for shorter code and less scrolling

Final tips for real world use

Prefer short and clear lambda bodies. If a lambda grows beyond a single expression extract a private method with a clear name. This helps debugging and keeps stack traces readable.

Lambda expressions along with functional interfaces and streams are a central part of Java 8 functional programming. Use them to reduce ceremony write clearer stream pipelines and keep your codebase from becoming a museum of anonymous classes.

{"new_title":"Choose the Right Server for Java apps with Tomcat or Apache","new_heading":"When to use Apache HTTP Server as a reverse proxy and when to run Tomcat","new_body":"

Short version you need two different tools for two different kinds of problems. Apache HTTP Server is a general purpose web server that excels at serving static files and fronting traffic. Apache Tomcat is a Java servlet container that runs WAR files and executes servlets and JSP pages. One is the delivery truck, the other is the gourmet chef who uses Java to make you something fancy and occasionally slow.

Quick verdict

Use Apache HTTP Server when you want fast static content, TLS termination, caching and URL rewriting. Use Tomcat when your server side code is Java and you need servlet APIs or JSP support. If your infra is grown up and not stubborn, put Apache in front as a reverse proxy and let Tomcat do the Java work behind it.

What Apache HTTP Server does best

  • Fast and efficient static file serving for HTML, CSS, images and assets
  • TLS termination and certificate management with mature modules
  • Reverse proxy features via mod_proxy and mod_proxy_http
  • Advanced URL rewriting and request filtering with mod_rewrite
  • Edge friendly tasks like caching, rate limiting and basic auth

What Tomcat does best

  • Implements Java servlet specs and JSP to run Java web apps
  • Deploy WAR files and manage webapps with servlet containers
  • Exposes JVM level tuning, thread pools and garbage collection metrics
  • Handles session management and Java specific filters and listeners

Modules and connectors to know about

If you want a handshake between Apache and Tomcat use mod_proxy_http for HTTP proxying or mod_proxy_ajp or mod_jk if you must use AJP. mod_jk is older but still around for legacy setups. mod_proxy is simpler to configure for most modern setups and keeps things readable.

Common architecture patterns

Typical architecture places Apache HTTP Server in front as a reverse proxy, handling TLS and static assets, while Tomcat sits behind and serves dynamic Java responses. This separation gives a neat division of labor and keeps each component doing what it does best.

  • Frontend Apache, backend Tomcat for TLS, caching and static content
  • Tomcat alone for simpler deployments where everything is Java
  • Load balancer plus multiple Tomcats behind Apache for scale

Performance and tuning

Expect Apache HTTP Server to be more efficient at high volumes of small static requests. Tomcat requires JVM tuning, proper thread pool configuration and attention to garbage collection. Monitor thread counts and GC pause times, because a stalled JVM will ruin your day faster than a thousand 404 errors.

Key Tomcat tuning points include heap sizing, GC strategy, max threads in the connector and connection timeouts. For Apache focus on worker model, keepalive settings and caching rules.

Configuration and deployment differences

Apache HTTP Server uses text based configs and a module system. Tomcat uses XML based server.xml and web.xml descriptors and application specific deployment descriptors inside WARs. They speak different config languages so do not try to clone one config into the other and expect harmony.

Security and operational care

Use Apache for hardened frontends, request filtering and certificate management. Use Tomcat with secure manager settings, proper permissions and up to date JVM patches. Monitor both logs, because the first clue you have a problem is usually in the logs and not a sudden loss of faith.

How to choose

  • If your app uses Java servlets or JSP, pick Tomcat or run Tomcat behind a proxy
  • If you only serve static content or need TLS and caching, use Apache HTTP Server
  • If you want scale and separation of concerns, put Apache in front of Tomcat as a reverse proxy

In short, use the right tool for the job. Apache HTTP Server handles the internet traffic chores, Tomcat runs your Java logic. Together they make a pragmatic, battle hardened stack that will survive bad code and worse deadlines.

"}

{ "new_title": "Fix Git Stash Pop Conflicts and Rescue Changes Without Panic", "new_heading": "Step by step guide to resolving stash pop conflicts and recovering work", "new_body": "

When stash pop fights back

If you ran git stash pop and got hit with merge conflict drama, breathe and then laugh at Git for dramatic timing. Stash conflicts are annoying but solvable. This guide walks through resolving conflicted files, preserving stash contents when needed, and recovering work that wandered off into Git purgatory.

Quick sanity check before you charge in

  • Run git status to see what is staged and what is conflicted
  • Decide if you want to keep the stash or test it first with git stash apply
  • Create a branch if you want to tinker without wrecking mainline history

Step 1 Run git stash pop and inspect the scene

Execute git stash pop to apply the top stash and remove it from the stash stack. If Git complains and leaves conflict markers, run git status to get the list of files that need attention. This is not the apocalypse, it is just Git asking you to make decisions.

git stash pop
git status

Step 2 Choose the correct changes and resolve merge markers

Open each conflicted file and remove the conflict markers while choosing the right lines from your local work or the stashed changes. If you prefer a visual helper use git mergetool which will let you click around instead of suffering with raw markers.

Step 3 Stage and confirm

After you edit the files run git add on each resolved file. Then run git status to confirm the index is clean and there are no unresolved conflicts left.

git add path/to/file
git status

Step 4 Commit or keep the stash for later testing

If you want to record the resolution make a commit with git commit. If you wanted to test the stash without removing it use git stash apply instead of pop and only drop the stash later with git stash drop once you are sure.

git commit -m "Resolve stash conflict and keep changes"
# or test without removing stash
git stash apply
# once happy
git stash drop

Alternate approach Use a stash branch to isolate the mess

If you do not want to fight on your current branch create a branch from the stash with git stash branch and resolve there. This keeps the main branch neat while you untangle changes and gives you a safe place to merge or rebase.

git stash branch fix-stash
# now resolve conflicts on fix-stash then merge back

Recover work if stash pop seemed to erase things

If your changes seem to have vanished do not panic. Inspect git reflog to find recent states and use git fsck --lost-found to surface dangling objects. Recovery odds are often better than your blood pressure suggests.

git reflog
git fsck --lost-found

Practical tips that save grief

  • Label stashes so you remember what they were with git stash push -m "short description"
  • Use git stash apply to test before deleting the stash
  • Create a stash branch when the change is complex or when you want a safer workflow
  • Keep calm and resolve conflicts one file at a time

Final words

Stash pop conflicts are part of life when using version control. The winning strategy is to inspect status, resolve markers carefully, stage and commit, and use stash branch or reflog recovery when needed. Follow these steps and you will rescue your work without rewriting history with a flamethrower.

{ "new_title": "Choose between Tomcat and JBoss for Java deployments in Docker", "new_heading": "Pick Tomcat for microservices and JBoss for enterprise Java services", "new_body": "

Quick summary you can read between meetings

If you want the executive version with minimal IT grief here it is. Tomcat is a lightweight servlet container that handles HTTP requests and servlets with the efficiency of a trained courier. Feature comparison

Feature set

Tomcat focuses on servlets JSP and the servlet container APIs. You can bolt on session management security and other bits but by default it keeps things small and predictable. WildFly JBoss includes full Java EE features and admin tooling. If your app depends on EJB or integrated JMS it saves you from reinventing the wheel.

Footprint and memory

Tomcat usually eats far less RAM and boots faster. That makes it ideal for dense containerized deployments and microservices where startup time matters. JBoss runs many services by default which raises memory use and increases startup time. You can tune WildFly and disable subsystems but expect a larger baseline.

Operational complexity

Tomcat has fewer moving parts which means fewer ways for things to go wrong. Deploy a WAR or run a Spring Boot jar and carry on. JBoss gives you powerful enterprise capabilities but with more configuration and a steeper learning curve. If you enjoy XML or complex management consoles then great, otherwise plan for some ops work.

The only honest answer is to benchmark with representative workloads and not just one synthetic test.

Use case guide

  • Choose JBoss WildFly for legacy Java EE applications complex transactional systems or when built in enterprise APIs will speed development.

Use health checks and representative load tests. If your CI pipeline makes you cry try packaging a minimal runtime first and add features only when they are required.

{ "new_title": "Inspect Java class files with javap for debugging and learning", "new_heading": "Step by step bytecode inspection and javap flags explained", "new_body": "

Why you should pay attention to javap

If you ever wondered what the Java compiler actually does to your pretty source code this tool is your new best frienemy. Javap is the JDK class file inspector that shows method signatures bytecode and constant pool entries. Use it to debug surprising behavior verify compiler output or enjoy mild reverse engineering without the guilt.

Quick setup and first compile

Start with a compiled class file. No magic here just the standard compiler.

javac MyClass.java

This produces MyClass.class which is what javap reads. Yes the compiler is still a thing and no you do not need to reinstall Java to use javap.

Basic javap commands you will use a lot

  • javap MyClass shows public method and field signatures
  • javap -p MyClass includes private members when curiosity wins
  • javap -c MyClass shows disassembled bytecode for each method

Run those three until you stop being surprised by what the compiler generates. Examples of opcodes to look for include aload_0 invokespecial and return. Method descriptors describe parameter and return types and they help map source code to the generated instructions.

When you need more detail

Bring out the verbose output when you want to see the constant pool and attributes. Be warned it can be noisy but it is honest about what is in the class file.

javap -v MyClass

To see how bytecode lines map back to source lines use the line number table flag.

javap -l -c MyClass

Common flags and what they do

  • -c print disassembled code
  • -p include private members
  • -v verbose output including constant pool
  • -l include line number and local variable tables
  • -classpath point to jars or classes outside the current folder

Inspecting classes inside jars

If your target class lives in a library jar add it to the classpath argument. Use the fully qualified class name when calling javap.

javap -classpath lib.jar com.example.MyClass

Why this is useful in real debugging and reverse engineering

Javap is great for quick verification. Did the compiler inline that method Did the generated bytecode include a synthetic bridge method Is a lambda implemented as invokedynamic You will find answers here fast. It complements a debugger and catches things source level tools sometimes hide.

Pro tips and the least mysterious combo

  • When confused use a decompiler alongside javap. The decompiler offers readable source and javap shows exact bytecode and constant pool entries.
  • Use -l -c to correlate bytecode with source lines while stepping in a debugger.
  • Remember inner classes synthetic methods and compiler generated bridge methods can explain weird stack traces.

That is the practical bit. Inspect compile output with javap learn how the bytecode maps to source and then feel slightly wiser and more suspicious of the compiler. Repeat as needed.

" }

{"new_title":"Sign and verify Java JARs with jarsigner and keytool guide","new_heading":"Practical JAR signing workflow with keytool jarsigner and timestamps","new_body":"

If your Java app wants to wear a respectable coat of trust instead of a suspicious sticky note that says do not run this please, sign the JAR. This guide walks through creating a keystore and keypair, signing with jarsigner, verifying the result, and adding a timestamp so your signature does not expire like last week\'s latte.

Quick checklist

  • Create a keystore and keypair using keytool
  • Sign the JAR using jarsigner
  • Verify the signature on a clean system
  • Optionally add timestamping for long lived trust
  • Store keys securely and automate signing in CI

Create a keystore and keypair

Make a signing key so your keystore contains a private key and public certificate. Pick a secure password and treat it like a toothbrush. Never commit it to source control.

keytool -genkeypair -alias mykey -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -keystore mykeystore.jks -storepass changeit -keypass changeit -dname "CN=Dev"

Sign the JAR

Apply a digital signature that ties the code to your identity. This helps users and systems decide whether to trust the binary. Run jarsigner with your keystore and alias.

jarsigner -keystore mykeystore.jks -storepass changeit -keypass changeit myapp.jar mykey

Verify the signed JAR

Always verify after signing. Verification confirms the signature is intact and the certificate chain looks sane. Use verbose mode to see certificate details.

jarsigner -verify -verbose -certs myapp.jar

Timestamping and distribution

Add a timestamp so the signature remains valid after your key inevitably collects cobwebs. Use the -tsa option with a trusted timestamp server URL. If you do not want the signature to die with your key, timestamp it.

jarsigner -keystore mykeystore.jks -storepass changeit -keypass changeit -tsa <tsa server URL> myapp.jar mykey

Best practices

  • Use separate keys for development and release builds to avoid accidental chaos
  • Store signing keys in a hardware token or CI secret store to reduce risk
  • Automate signing in your build pipeline so humans do not accidentally forget or type passwords in public chats
  • Test verification on a clean machine to catch missing intermediate certificates

Common gotchas

  • Forgotten storepass or keypass will ruin your day so back up securely
  • Missing cert chain looks like a signed jar but verification fails keep the full chain handy
  • Timestamps from unreliable servers can be rejected use a reputable TSA and test it

Signing a JAR is not voodoo. It is a few commands that prove provenance and protect integrity. Follow the steps, lock up the private keys, and let your users install with only mild paranoia.

"}

{ "new_title": "When your Scrum is theater try fixing scrumbut habits", "new_heading": "Practical steps for fixing scrumbut and restoring real agile teamwork", "new_body": "

Practical steps for fixing scrumbut and restoring real agile teamwork

People say we do Scrum but no retros and we do Scrum but no timebox like they are announcing a quirky hobby. That attitude has a name and it is scrumbut. It means you claim the structure of Scrum while quietly removing the parts that actually make it useful. The result is less predictability, slower feedback loops, and team accountability that evaporates like a holiday pizza party.

How to spot scrumbut in the wild

  • We do Scrum but no retros. Retros happen only when someone remembers them.
  • We do Scrum but no timebox. Meetings are flexible in the way a black hole is flexible.
  • We do Scrum but no Product Owner. Priorities are decided by whoever shouted loudest.
  • Daily standup that became a status monologue. Also known as the yawntastic hour.

Why this matters for teams and stakeholders

Removing core practices from Scrum does not make you innovative. It makes planning vague and commitments meaningless. Stakeholders get fuzzy promises, the team loses focus, and the very benefits that made you try Scrum in the first place go missing. That is not transformation. That is passive resistance with a calendar invite.

Simple plan to stop the scrumbut nonsense

Fixing scrumbut does not require a manifesto or a trust fall. It needs a short, pointed experiment and a little accountability. Here is a small plan that actually works.

  1. Admit the current practice

    Have a frank conversation where the team names what is actually happening. No blame, just facts. When reality is in the room you can start to change it.

  2. Choose one ceremony to restore

    Pick the ceremony that will give the biggest return for your pain. Start with retrospectives if you want continuous improvement. Pick daily standup if communication is the problem. Try one sprint with the restored practice and measure.

  3. Give authority to the Product Owner

    Clear ownership beats committees. When the Product Owner owns scope and priorities teams can make trade offs with confidence. The Scrum Master supports that authority and protects the process.

  4. Enforce timeboxing

    Timeboxes are not punishment. They are a focus tool that forces decisions and reveals blockers. Short deadlines highlight what matters and expose what is just noise.

  5. Inspect and adapt real retrospectives

    Run retros that actually produce action items. Assign owners. Track the actions next sprint. Small measurable changes add up faster than motivational posters.

Metrics that do not lie

Run the experiment with a clear metric to judge success. Useful signals include sprint predictability, cycle time, number of closed action items from retrospectives, or stakeholder satisfaction. If the metric improves keep going. If nothing changes try a different practice and iterate.

Role of Scrum Master and Product Owner

The Scrum Master removes impediments and keeps timeboxes honest. The Product Owner prioritizes the work and makes trade offs visible. When both roles are empowered you get faster feedback and clearer commitments. It is not magic. It is process improvement with a policy check.

Final tip

Treat scrumbut like a science experiment. Change one variable at a time, measure outcomes, and celebrate the tiny wins. Small experiments beat grand declarations every time. If your next sprint feels like progress then keep it. If it still feels like theater then try something else and keep the popcorn for the retrospective.

" }

{ "new_title": "Share S3 files safely with presigned URLs and STS tokens", "new_heading": "Practical steps for temporary S3 access using presigned URLs and STS", "new_body": "

Quick summary

Want to share an S3 object without handing over permanent keys or causing a security incident that ruins your week? Use presigned URLs for one off uploads and downloads and use STS temporary credentials for broader but time limited programmatic access. This guide walks through bucket policy hardening presigned URL creation STS role assumption testing and cleanup with a little sarcasm and accurate steps.

Step 1 prepare the bucket and the policy

Minimal permissions are your friend. Create a bucket policy that allows only the actions you need and only from known principals. Do not leave public read or write enabled unless you are running a breach simulation lab. Keep the blast radius small and the audit logs quiet.

Checklist

  • Allow only s3 get object for downloads and s3 put object for uploads
  • Scope access to specific prefixes when possible
  • Limit principals to specific IAM roles or accounts
  • Enable server side encryption and bucket logging if useful

Step 2 use a presigned URL for single file share

Presigned URLs sign a single operation and expire. They are perfect when someone needs to upload or download one file and you do not want to hand them AWS keys. The simplest tool is the AWS CLI or any SDK that supports presigned links.

Example quick CLI command for a one time download link

aws s3 presign my-bucket/my-key --expires-in 3600

This hands you a time limited https link that the client can use without AWS credentials. If you need an upload link change the operation or use an SDK method for put objects.

Step 3 use STS for temporary credentials when you need more

If the client needs to list multiple objects or perform programmatic actions use STS to assume a role that has scoped permissions and a short expiry. This keeps long lived keys off the client and lets you control exactly what can be done and for how long.

High level steps

  • Create an IAM role that trusts the principal that will assume it
  • Attach a policy to that role with the minimum S3 actions and resource ARNs needed
  • Use STS to assume the role and return temporary access keys
  • Configure the AWS SDK or AWS CLI with the temporary keys and perform operations

Most SDKs make this easy. With boto3 for example you will call STS to get temporary credentials then create an S3 client with those credentials and proceed with uploads or downloads. No permanent keys leave your vault.

Step 4 test actual transfers

Do the boring but vital test with curl or your SDK. For presigned URLs see that a browser or curl can download or upload the object. For STS credentials configure the SDK to use the temporary keys and try the same operations you expect in production. Testing prevents the classic last minute panic when the automation runs for the first time.

Step 5 revoke or wait for expiry and clean up

If your environment allows manual revocation remove temporary roles or short lived sessions. Otherwise wait for automatic expiry and then rotate any long lived keys you touched during testing. Always remove test objects and unused policies so logs stay readable and security teams remain calm.

Tips and gotchas

  • Presigned URLs do not change bucket policies. Both must allow the intended action for the request to succeed
  • Clock skew matters. Make sure clients and servers have reasonably accurate time when using expiry windows
  • Shorter is better for expiry unless you enjoy incident response
  • Prefer role assumption for programmatic access and presigned URLs for user facing single file flows

Recap and parting thought

Use bucket policies to limit damage use presigned URLs for single file transfers and use STS temporary credentials for wider but time limited access. Test everything clean up when done and never trust someone who asks for permanent keys to play with your S3 bucket. Security is not glamorous but it keeps your data and your job intact.

{"new_title":"Set up a fast and secure Nginx web server on Ubuntu today","new_heading":"Step by step guide to installing Nginx and enabling HTTP on Ubuntu servers","new_body":"

Step by step guide to installing Nginx and enabling HTTP on Ubuntu servers

So you want a web server that does the job without drama. Nginx is fast, opinionated, and avoids the attention seeking of some alternatives. This guide will walk you through installing Nginx on Ubuntu updating packages letting traffic through the firewall and checking that the default page is served. It is practical and mildly smug when it works.

What we will do

  • Refresh the Ubuntu package index
  • Install the Nginx package
  • Start and enable the Nginx service on boot
  • Allow HTTP traffic with UFW if you use it
  • Verify the default web page and basic health checks

Update packages so apt does not sulk

First make sure your package list is current. This avoids surprises like old versions or missing dependencies.

sudo apt update

Install Nginx

Install the web server package. Apt will pull whatever dependencies Nginx needs without you holding its hand.

sudo apt install nginx -y

Start Nginx and make it survive reboots

Start the service now and enable it so it comes back after a reboot. That way your server behaves like a reliable co worker.

sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx

Open the firewall if you have one

If your Ubuntu setup uses UFW allow the built in HTTP profile so clients can actually reach your site. If you are in a cloud environment remember to check cloud firewalls too.

sudo ufw allow 'Nginx HTTP'

Verify the default page is served

Check locally with a quick request. Replace localhost with your server IP when testing remotely.

curl -I http //localhost

You should see a 200 OK response line and the Nginx server header. If not do not panic yet. Nginx will usually tell you what went wrong if you ask politely.

Quick health checks

  • Confirm service status
sudo systemctl status nginx
  • Test Nginx configuration before touching the service
sudo nginx -t
  • Scan recent error logs for clues
tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log

Troubleshooting common hiccups

If curl shows a non 200 status check these in order. Service not running check systemctl status. Config issues run the test command above and fix the file reported. Firewall blocking traffic check UFW and cloud firewall settings. Bad permissions or missing site files will show up in the error log.

Useful maintenance moves

  • After changing config run the syntax check and then reload without killing active connections
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

Final tip for the weary

Want to feel extra competent and avoid surprises? Keep your server packages up to date and test configs in a staging box before touching production. And remember that sudo nginx -t is the closest thing to a seatbelt in the server world.

{"new_title":"Secure file uploads with FileZilla and Nginx on Linux servers","new_heading":"Step by step SFTP and FTP setup with FileZilla and Nginx for deployment","new_body":"

Step by step SFTP and FTP setup with FileZilla and Nginx for deployment

If you want to shove files onto your Nginx webserver without invoking chaos or wild permission errors this guide gets you from zero to deployable with FileZilla. Yes this covers both FTP and the recommended SFTP route, and yes you should pick SFTP unless you like trouble.

Prepare the server

On a typical Linux box you either use OpenSSH for SFTP or a daemon like vsftpd for plain FTP. SFTP runs over SSH and avoids installing another legacy service that smells like the 90s. Install one of them with your package manager and keep calm.

sudo apt update && sudo apt install openssh-server

Or for old school FTP

sudo apt install vsftpd

Keep in mind SFTP uses sshd so you get encryption and key auth with almost no extra drama.

Configure Nginx document root and permissions

Point Nginx at the folder that will hold uploads and deployed files. Typical site root is under /var/www. Make the webserver user the owner so Nginx can read files and serve them. Aim for conservative permissions so nobody else can scribble on your site.

sudo mkdir -p /var/www/example.com/html/uploads
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/example.com/html
sudo find /var/www/example.com/html -type d -exec chmod 755 {} \;
sudo find /var/www/example.com/html -type f -exec chmod 644 {} \;

If a file appears to upload but you get a 403 or 404, check ownership and nginx error logs first.

Create a deploy user and set up chroot for SFTP

For SFTP you want jailed sessions so users cannot wander around the filesystem. The trickiest bit is that the chroot directory must be owned by root and not writable by the jailed user. Then you create a writable subfolder where the user can drop files.

sudo groupadd sftpusers
sudo useradd -m -g sftpusers -d /var/www/example.com html -s /usr/sbin/nologin deploy
sudo passwd deploy
sudo chown root:root /var/www/example.com
sudo mkdir /var/www/example.com/uploads
sudo chown deploy:www-data /var/www/example.com/uploads
sudo chmod 750 /var/www/example.com/uploads

Now tell sshd to use internal sftp for the group. Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config and add a block similar to this near the end of the file. Then restart sshd.

Subsystem sftp internal-sftp
Match Group sftpusers
    ChrootDirectory /var/www/example.com
    ForceCommand internal-sftp
    AllowTcpForwarding no
    X11Forwarding no

sudo systemctl restart sshd

Note that the ChrootDirectory must be owned by root and not writable by any other user for the jail to work. The upload folder then holds the files the deploy user can write.

FTP specifics if you must use FTP

If you choose vsftpd for plain FTP enable chroot for local users and disable anonymous logins. The config keys to look for are chroot_local_user and anonymous_enable. After changes restart vsftpd. Plain FTP should only be used behind a VPN or on internal networks.

Configure FileZilla

Open FileZilla Site Manager and create a new site. Use protocol SFTP for encrypted transfers. Put the server IP or hostname and the proper port, usually 22. For logon choose key file authentication if you can, or normal password if you are lazy but sensible.

  • Protocol choose SFTP
  • Host use your server IP or domain
  • Port 22 for SFTP or the port you configured for FTP
  • Logon type ask for key file when using SSH keys for better security

If you use a private key you might need to convert it to a format FileZilla accepts. Newer FileZilla supports OpenSSH keys but older versions prefer ppk from PuTTY. Use ssh key tools on your workstation to manage that.

Test upload and lock things down

Upload a tiny index.html to the uploads or html folder and then open your site in a browser to confirm Nginx serves the file. If Nginx cannot read the file fix ownership and chmod. If SFTP refuses the login check the chroot ownership rules and sshd logs.

echo 'ok' > /tmp/test.html
# upload the file with FileZilla into /var/www/example.com/html or uploads
# then open the site in a browser to verify

After you verify everything works tidy up the attack surface. Disable anonymous FTP. Turn off unused services. Enforce strong passwords or preferably use SSH keys. Consider installing fail2ban so repeated failed logins do not become a party.

Quick checklist

  • Install openssh-server for SFTP or vsftpd for FTP
  • Make sure Nginx document root is owned by www-data and has correct permissions
  • Use chroot and internal-sftp for jailed SFTP users
  • Prefer key based auth in FileZilla and save the Site Manager profile for repeat deploys
  • Upload a test file and verify in a browser
  • Disable anonymous access and tighten credentials

This fills the role of a compact tutorial for FileZilla, FTP and SFTP deployment to an Nginx webserver on Linux. It is practical, slightly sarcastic, and should keep your site from turning into a scenic drive through permissions hell.

{"new_title":"Make and run bash scripts on Ubuntu without losing your mind","new_heading":"Quick Ubuntu shell scripting guide for bash beginners and pros","new_body":"

Welcome to a short and slightly sarcastic tutorial on making a bash script in Ubuntu that actually runs. This is for humans who can open a terminal and who prefer things that work over mysteries and crying.

Create the file

Open a terminal and create a new file with your favorite editor. Example using nano.

nano hello.sh

Pick a filename that will not clash with system commands and save the file when done.

Add a shebang and the commands

Put a shebang on the first line so the kernel knows which interpreter to use. For portability use the env approach.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# a trivial script
echo "Hello World"

You can use #!/bin/bash on Ubuntu and most desktop distros but env makes life easier across different Linux systems.

Make the file executable and run it

Give the file execute permission so the kernel will let it run. This prevents the classic permission error that ruins afternoons.

chmod +x hello.sh

Run the script from the current directory with a relative path to avoid PATH confusion.

./hello.sh

If you want to force a particular interpreter for testing use that interpreter name directly.

bash hello.sh

Troubleshoot permissions and path problems

If the shell refuses to run the file check ownership and the execute bit with a quick listing.

ls -l hello.sh

If the wrong shell is running adjust the shebang or invoke the desired interpreter explicitly. If the script still misbehaves check for Windows line endings which cause weird syntax errors on Linux.

Make scripts available everywhere

Want to run your script without typing a path every time Use a personal bin folder and add it to your PATH.

mkdir -p ~/bin
mv hello.sh ~/bin
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"

Add that export line to your .profile or .bashrc to persist it across sessions and spare yourself the same rant tomorrow.

Quick practical tips

  • Use #!/usr/bin/env bash for better portability across Linux distributions
  • Do not name scripts after common system commands unless you enjoy chaos
  • Check file permissions and ownership if the script is stubborn

Follow these steps and you will have a working bash script in Ubuntu running from the terminal. Minimal fuss minimal drama and enough snark to keep things interesting while you learn shell scripting.

Generate a new SSH key

Generate an ed25519 key pair with ssh-keygen, start ssh-agent and add your private key with ssh-add, copy the public key and paste it into GitHub, test with ssh -T and update repository remotes to the SSH URL. {"new_title":"Set Up GitLab SSH Keys for Fast Passwordless Git Access","new_heading":"Step by step GitLab SSH key setup and local SSH config tips","new_body":"

Why use SSH keys with GitLab

If you enjoy typing passwords like it is the 1990s then this guide is not for you. For the rest of us SSH keys give secure, passwordless Git access and stop your workflow from being held hostage by credential prompts. It is easier, safer, and mildly satisfying.

Create a secure SSH key pair

Generate a modern key pair on the machine you use for development. ed25519 is the current go to for small keys and solid security.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"

Follow the prompts. Accept the default path unless you want to be fancy and store keys in a different location. Use a passphrase for safety or use an ssh agent if you want convenience without embarrassment.

Use an agent so you only enter the passphrase once

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Add the public key to your GitLab account

Copy the public key and paste it into GitLab. You can print it to the terminal then copy the output.

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

In GitLab open your profile settings and choose SSH Keys. Paste the entire key into the key field, give it a memorable title such as the machine name and save. No voodoo required just paste and save.

Configure the local SSH client for GitLab

Telling SSH which key to use keeps Git from asking you where the private key lives every time you run a command. Edit or create ~/.ssh/config and add a host entry for GitLab.

Host gitlab.com
  User git
  HostName gitlab.com
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  IdentitiesOnly yes

If you have multiple GitLab accounts create separate Host aliases and point each alias at a different IdentityFile. That way you avoid angry commits in the wrong repo.

Test the SSH connection

Make sure GitLab actually recognizes your key.

ssh -T git@gitlab.com

A typical successful reply mentions your username and confirms authentication. If SSH complains about permissions fix the private key permissions.

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Clone push and fetch using SSH

Use the SSH repo URL for passwordless operations. Example clone command.

git clone git@gitlab.com:group/project.git

Then push and fetch as usual. If you configured Host aliases in ~/.ssh/config you can use the alias in place of gitlab.com for multi account setups.

Troubleshooting quick hits

  • If ssh -T fails confirm the public key in GitLab matches ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
  • If permission denied ensure your private key is readable only by you with chmod 600
  • If the wrong key is used set IdentitiesOnly yes in your SSH config to force the chosen file
  • If you still see password prompts add the key to the ssh agent with ssh-add

Wrap up

You just created a secure key pair added the public key to GitLab configured your SSH client and verified a passwordless connection. The reward is fewer prompts and slightly more dignity when you push code. Go forth and commit responsibly.

Check for an existing SSH key

Before you start generating keys like a hacker in a movie montage take a deep breath and look in your home directory for an SSH folder. Typical files are ~/.ssh/id_rsa and ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. If one of those exists you can skip key generation and move on to adding the key to an agent and uploading the public part to GitHub.

Generate a modern SSH key

Use a modern algorithm so future you does not hate past you. Ed25519 is a solid choice unless your organization demands legacy keys. Run this in a terminal and follow the prompts.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

If you prefer RSA for some reason use a large size. Otherwise accept the default file name and set a passphrase if you want an extra layer of misery protection.

Add the private key to an SSH agent

The SSH agent stores your unlocked key so Git can use it without you typing the passphrase every five minutes. Start the agent and add your key.

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Check the agent has your key with ssh-add -l. If you see nothing then the agent is not running or the key was not added.

Upload the public key to GitHub

Copy the public key file such as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub and paste its contents into your GitHub profile under SSH and GPG keys. Give it a human readable name so the person who inherits your machine in ten years does not cry.

Verify your Git remote and file permissions

Make sure your repository remote is using SSH and not HTTPS. Run git remote -v and look for an SSH style entry described as git at github dot com followed by user slash repo dot git. If it shows HTTPS then change the remote to an SSH URL so publickey authentication is used.

chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Strict permissions matter because SSH will refuse to use keys that are world readable. Also be aware of multiple SSH agents or credential helpers that can interfere with which key is offered.

Test the SSH connection and run debug

Talk directly to GitHub to see what the server thinks of your key. The verbose flag spits out the useful garbage that tells you whether the key was offered or ignored.

ssh -T -v git@github.com

Read the debug output for lines that show which identities were tried and whether an agent supplied a key. Common failure causes include the wrong key being used missing the key on GitHub or file permission problems.

Troubleshooting tips

  • Confirm the public key on GitHub matches the file on your machine
  • Run ssh-add -l to see what the agent is offering
  • If you use multiple keys configure ~/.ssh/config with Host entries to force the right key for github dot com
  • On Windows use Git Bash or WSL and follow the same steps or use the native credential manager if you prefer a GUI trap

Recap and final thoughts

In short check for an existing SSH key generate a modern key if needed add it to an SSH agent upload the public key to GitHub ensure your Git remote uses SSH secure your file permissions and run an SSH debug session. Follow those steps and the permission denied publickey error should stop haunting your commits. If it does not then the problem is probably something silly like a mismatched key or an agent you forgot to start.

{"new_title":"Quick guide to get GitHub SSH URLs and clone repos securely","new_heading":"Use SSH keys to clone GitHub repositories from the command line","new_body":"

Find the SSH URL on the repo page

    Replace username and repo with your actual values before running commands.

Make or add an SSH key pair

If you do not already have an SSH key pair on your machine generate one. For modern security use ed25519 with a command like this

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"

That creates a public key file that usually ends with .pub. Copy the contents of that file and add it to your GitHub account under Settings then SSH and GPG keys. Paste the key into the web form and give it a name that will not embarrass you later.

Test the SSH connection

Make sure GitHub can see your key before any dramatic cloning attempts. Run this test and expect a friendly greeting if all is well

ssh -T git@github.com

If you see a message that welcomes you then congrats. If you see a permission denied message do not panic. Check that the public key is uploaded and that your ssh agent is offering the right key.

Clone the repo with SSH

Now for the main event. Use the SSH link you copied earlier. In plain text the command looks like this

git clone git at github dot com slash username slash repo dot git

That maps to the SSH URL format GitHub provides and will clone the repository to your machine without asking for your password on every network hiccup.

Troubleshooting tips and common fixes

  • No welcome message from the test command. Make sure your ssh agent has the key loaded and that the public key is correctly added to GitHub.
  • Host key prompt when connecting. Accept it if you trust the network you are on. Usually yes you do trust github com.
  • Permission denied. Verify you uploaded the right public key and that you are not using a different GitHub account by mistake.
  • Still stuck. Run ssh -v -T git@github.com for verbose output and read the logs like a mildly offended detective.

That is it. You found the SSH URL you copied the right link you generated or added an SSH key and you cloned the repo. Now go write code or at least fix one typo and call it progress.

"}

{ "new_title": "Make JDBC work in Java for secure fast database access today", "new_heading": "Practical JDBC guide for Connection pooling PreparedStatement and transactions", "new_body": "

If you are working with Java and a relational database you will meet JDBC whether you like it or not. It is the standard Java API for talking to SQL databases and it gives you a small set of reliable tools to open sessions run queries and wrangle results. Think of it as the plumbing behind higher level libraries and yes sometimes you will still need a wrench.

What JDBC actually gives you

At its heart JDBC is simple and stubbornly explicit. Key pieces are DriverManager or a DataSource implementation a Connection a Statement or PreparedStatement and a ResultSet. Those names are boring but they do the heavy lifting for database access in Java without drama.

Short and useful workflow

  • Load or obtain a driver or let modern Java detect it for you
  • Open a connection from DriverManager or a pooled DataSource
  • Create a Statement for one off SQL or prefer PreparedStatement for repeated or parameterized queries
  • Execute queries with executeQuery for select and executeUpdate for insert update and delete
  • Iterate the ResultSet and map columns to your domain types while handling nulls with respect
  • Close resources or use try with resources and manage transactions with commit and rollback

Load a driver and move on

In the past you had to explicitly load a vendor driver jar onto the classpath and register it. Modern Java versions and most app containers will auto detect JDBC drivers so manual loading is often unnecessary. Still include the correct driver on the classpath or rely on your container DataSource.

Open a connection and do not waste it

A Connection represents a session with the database and defines your transaction boundaries. Creating connections is expensive so use a connection pool or a DataSource provided by your container for production. Frequent session creation will kill your throughput and your developer morale.

PreparedStatement is your friend

For any SQL that accepts external input prefer PreparedStatement over Statement. Parameter binding prevents SQL injection and helps the database reuse query plans for better performance. It is not fancy but it works and it keeps you out of security audit meetings.

Executing SQL and handling ResultSet

Use executeQuery for select statements and executeUpdate for insert update and delete. Process the ResultSet row by row and map column values carefully. Watch out for null handling and JDBC type conversions when moving data into your domain objects.

Close resources and manage transactions

Always close ResultSet Statement and Connection to avoid leaks. Prefer try with resources so the JVM does the cleanup for you. Manage transactions explicitly by calling commit and rollback on Connection when you need atomic behavior. Leaving auto commit on can work for trivial tasks but it often surprises you at the worst possible time.

Production tips that save time and shame

  • Prefer PreparedStatement for any query that accepts external input
  • Use a connection pool to avoid the overhead of frequent session creation
  • Use a DataSource in containers for clean configuration and pooling
  • Set sensible fetch size and use batch updates for bulk operations
  • Keep your JDBC driver up to date and match it to your database version

JDBC is a bit verbose but it is reliable. It gives you clear control over connections transactions and result processing while pairing nicely with higher level tools when you want less boilerplate. Treat it like a classic tool that still gets the job done without drama.

Plan your lab topology

Choose your virtualization tools

Create devices and links

{ "new_title": "Make Your Site Feel Instant With Practical Web Performance", "new_heading": "Turn slow page complaints into measurable wins with profiling and caching", "new_body": "

Performance is not magic, it is measurement and small victories

Performance means how fast and reliably your site serves real humans under realistic load. When a page crawls like a sleepy sloth users leave, conversions drop and stakeholders invent dramatic metaphors. The solution is simple in concept and delightfully painful in practice. Measure what users actually experience, find the real bottlenecks, then apply surgical fixes that change behavior where it matters.

Measure both lab and field data

Want a baseline you can repeat in CI run synthetic tests with Lighthouse and similar tools. Want the truth about what users feel collect real user monitoring data. Both matter. Lab tests give you deterministic comparisons and CI enforcement. Field metrics show the chaos of networks, devices and actual behavior.

Key metrics to track

  • Time to first byte for server responsiveness
  • First contentful paint and largest contentful paint for perceived load
  • Total blocking time and long tasks for interactivity
  • First input delay for responsiveness to user actions

Profile instead of guessing

Profilers are your best friend when a page feels slow and your instincts are not. Use browser dev tools to capture performance traces and flame charts. Look for long tasks, CPU spikes and expensive paints. On the server run profilers and query logs to find slow database calls and blocking operations. The data points to the actual hotspot so you are not chasing the bandwidth boogeyman when the problem is CPU or vice versa.

Optimize the critical path and focus on what users see first

Make the first meaningful view cheap to render. Prioritize above the fold resources and defer anything that is not essential to the initial experience. Inline tiny critical CSS for the hero area. Defer or async nonessential scripts so they do not block rendering. Lazy load images and components that live below the fold to avoid shipping weight the user did not ask for.

Code splitting and lazy loading

Split bundles so initial payloads are small. Load feature code only when the user needs it. This reduces page speed impact on first load and improves perceived performance. It is not rocket science, it is just corridor level tidy up.

Cache smartly and compress everything that benefits

Use browser caching and CDNs to reduce latency for repeat visits. Enable HTTP compression such as gzip or Brotli for text payloads to save bytes and milliseconds. Cache where responses are stable and design a sane invalidation strategy for content that changes. Caching wrong is worse than no caching because wrong leads to stale surprises.

Monitor continuously and bake performance into your pipeline

Set up real user monitoring with alerts for regressions and run performance budgets in CI so a bad deploy cannot sneak in. Automate Lighthouse checks but treat them as signals not gospel. Track page speed and real user metrics over time and treat performance as something to maintain not a one time heroic sprint.

Practical monitoring checklist

  • Real user monitoring for field metrics
  • CI based synthetic tests for repeatable baselines
  • Performance budgets for size and timing
  • Alerts for regressions and dashboards for trends

Small wins beat heroic rewrites

Often a few targeted changes outperform a full rewrite. Remove a blocking script, compress images better, split a heavy bundle, or fix one slow database query. Focus on user facing metrics and measure every change under real conditions. Let the numbers guide priorities so you stop guessing and start winning.

Tip

When someone says the site is slow do not panic. Gather a flame chart and a field histogram first. Those two things usually point to the component causing the slowdown and prevent you from chasing the wrong problem. Then make a tiny change, measure the impact and repeat. Rinse and repeat until users stop complaining and your dashboard looks smug.

Keywords you can brag about in meetings include web performance, optimization, profiling, Lighthouse, page speed, caching, lazy loading, code splitting and monitoring. Use them wisely and carry a flame chart to every discussion.
