{ "new_title": "Master Java Comments That Make Code Clear and Helpful", "new_heading": "When to use single line block and Javadoc comments in Java projects", "new_body": "

Know the three comment types

If you write Java code and also like mercy for future you and your teammates then comments matter. Java has three comment styles and each one has a job. Use the right one and your code will look like it has its life together. Use the wrong one and your repo will be a crime scene.

Single line comments

Start with two slashes and keep it short. Single line comments are perfect for tiny notes right above a tricky expression or for flagging a temporary hack that needs cleanup.

// Validate user input before parsing
int parsed = Integer.parseInt(someString)

Block comments

Wrapped with slash star and star slash these are for multi line context. Use them to explain an algorithm rationale or to group several lines of commentary without repeating slashes.

/*
 This algorithm uses a simple heuristic that fails only on extremely rare cases
 Use when the why matters more than the what
*/

Javadoc

Javadoc comments start with slash star star and star slash and they fuel generated documentation. Put Javadoc on public classes and methods that other developers or tools will read.

/**
 * Add two numbers
 * @param a first number
 * @param b second number
 * @return sum
 */
public int add(int a, int b) { return a + b }

Best practices that do not make your code look desperate

  • Keep comments concise and accurate. If the code speaks clearly the comment can shut up
  • Do not restate the obvious. Saying that i equals i is not useful
  • Update comments during refactors so they do not lie and haunt future readers
  • Avoid big blocks of commented out code. They are tombstones for past intentions
  • Prefer expressive code over verbose comments. Well named methods beat an essay any day

Where to use each style in the wild

Single line comments for quick hints and warnings near complex logic. Block comments for context heavy explanations that need a few lines to breathe. Javadoc for public APIs method level behavior and expectations so tools and humans both get less confused.

Quick checklist for cleaner code documentation

  • Is the comment explaining why rather than what
  • Will a future reader thank you or curse you for this note
  • Does the Javadoc have clear tags like @param and @return for public methods
  • Can the code be made clearer instead of writing more comments

Summary

Remember the three comment types single line block and Javadoc Each one has a role Use them wisely and keep your codebase readable and maintainable. And if you ever feel like leaving a passive aggressive note in the code try a GIF in the team chat instead

{ "new_title": "Make clean console tables in Java with printf formatting tips", "new_heading": "Printf format specifiers and column alignment for readable Java tables", "new_body": "

If your console output looks like a sloppy grocery list then welcome. This short guide shows how to use Java printf and format specifiers to produce neat, readable tables that humans can scan without therapy. We keep the output aligned, the decimals respectful, and the code reusable.

Plan columns and widths

Start like a civilized person and decide on column labels and character widths. Think about the longest expected name and the largest number of digits you will get. Reserve a little slack so your table does not wrap mid drama.

Simple rules to follow

  • Give numbers a fixed width so decimals line up
  • Give text columns a bit more room and left align them when that makes sense
  • Print the header row with the exact same format string as the data rows

Choose the right format specifiers and flags

Match Java types to specifiers. Use %s for strings, %d for integers and %f for floating point numbers. Add a width to reserve space and add precision to control decimal places. A minus flag before the width left aligns text like %-20s, while a plain width right aligns numbers like %8.2f.

Build a reusable printf template

Make one format string and reuse it. This is the boring magic that keeps every row obedient to the same column rules.

String fmt = "%-15s %8.2f\n"
System.out.printf(fmt, name, price)

Loop rows and apply the template

Run a loop and feed each row into the template. Consistency wins here. One format string prevents one row from trying to steal the spotlight.

for (Product p : products) {
    System.out.printf(fmt, p.getName(), p.getPrice())
}

Tweaks that actually matter

If you want exactly two decimals use %8.2f. If a text column should hug the left edge use %-20s. If numbers should line up add sufficient width and right alignment. These are small changes that make big visual improvements.

Quick checklist

  • Plan column widths before typing anything
  • Pick the right specifiers for each type
  • Assemble one printf template and reuse it
  • Print headers with the same template as data rows
  • Adjust precision and alignment flags until your eyeballs approve

Follow these steps and your console tables will stop resembling modern art. Use width, precision and the minus flag together and you will have tables that are both readable and annoyingly professional. If you need help tuning a specific layout paste a sample and we will make it behave.

{"new_title":"Get single character input in Java Scanner the easy way","new_heading":"Practical Scanner examples to read a single char from console input","new_body":"

Reading a single char from the console with Java can feel like asking for a unicorn. Scanner has no nextChar method so we improvise using existing tools and a little common sense. This mini tutorial shows how to grab just one character from user input using Scanner next or nextLine and charAt while keeping the code simple and slightly smug.

Use next plus charAt for the quick route

Create a Scanner tied to System.in then read a token when space separated input is acceptable. The trick is to read the token then take token.charAt(0) to get the first character. It mimics a missing nextChar method without any dark magic.

Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in)
String token = sc.next()
if token.trim().length() == 0 {
  System.out.println("empty input try again")
} else {
  char ch = token.charAt(0)
  System.out.println("You entered " + ch)
}

Why this works

Scanner returns Strings for tokens so you borrow one of String s handy methods to extract a character. This keeps things explicit and avoids weird API hacks. Also you do not need a mythical nextChar method to get what you want.

Handle empty or multi character input

Users love to press Enter and walk away or paste entire sentences into a single character prompt. Validate input by checking length before calling charAt. Decide if you accept the first character or force the user to provide exactly one character.

  • Reject empty tokens with token.trim().length() == 0
  • Reject or warn on token.length() > 1 if you need strict single char input
  • Use sc.hasNext to avoid exceptions and to prompt again gracefully

When to use nextLine instead of next

Choose next when spaces are separators and you only need the first non space token. Choose nextLine when spaces matter or the user could enter a space as their response. With nextLine you read a whole line then trim and parse it for characters.

Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in)
while true {
  System.out.println("Enter a single character")
  String line = sc.nextLine()
  String trimmed = line.trim()
  if trimmed.length() == 0 {
    System.out.println("No input try again")
    continue
  }
  char ch = trimmed.charAt(0)
  // use ch as needed
  break
}

Quick checklist for robust console input

  • Prefer hasNext and checks like token.trim().length() > 0 before calling charAt
  • Decide policy for multi character input and document it for users
  • Use nextLine when you must capture spaces or when you want the whole line for parsing
  • Keep user prompts friendly and fail with guidance not rage

This approach keeps your code simple and avoids reinventing the wheel or expecting Scanner to have a nextChar method. It works in real Java programs and keeps your users from typing nonsense into the console while you pretend to be surprised.

"}

{"new_title":"Avoid the newline trap when reading input with Java Scanner","new_heading":"Read tokens and full lines from the console in Java without surprises","new_body":"

If you are new to Java input or you enjoy tiny punishments from the terminal then welcome. Scanner next and nextLine both read user input but they behave like two roommates who refuse to clean up after themselves. next grabs the next token while nextLine grabs the entire line. Mix them and you get the classic newline trap that makes beginner Java input handling feel like a prank.

Create a Scanner and grab a single token

Make a Scanner that reads from standard input and use next when you only want the next whitespace separated token. Great for a first name a one word command or any situation where spaces are a betrayal.

Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in)
String word = scanner.next()

Read a full line with nextLine

Use nextLine when you want everything the user typed up to the newline including spaces. This is what you want for addresses multiline comments or any sentence that refuses to be tokenized.

String line = scanner.nextLine()

Why mixing next and nextLine leads to an empty string

The annoying truth is that next does not consume the trailing newline. It leaves that newline sitting in the input buffer like a passive aggressive note. The very next call to nextLine will read that leftover newline and return an empty string. Not a bug a design choice that tests your patience.

String first = scanner.next()
scanner.nextLine()
String comment = scanner.nextLine()

Two simple fixes that do not involve crying

  • Call an extra nextLine right after next to consume the leftover newline then call nextLine to get the real input
  • Use nextLine for all console input then split or parse the returned String when you need tokens

Example using only nextLine then splitting for predictable String input handling

String line = scanner.nextLine()
String[] parts = line.split("\\s+")
String firstToken = parts[0]

Quick tips for beginner Java input handling

  • Prefer nextLine and parse when you want consistent behavior across mixed inputs
  • If you do use next remember that a newline remains until you consume it
  • Close the scanner when your program is done reading input but know that closing the scanner will also close System.in

If you follow these rules your console input will stop surprising you. If you do not the newline trap will continue to humiliate your program one empty string at a time.

"}

{ "new_title": "MVCC Tricks That Keep Databases Fast Under Concurrency Today", "new_heading": "Multiversion concurrency control for PostgreSQL and MySQL performance", "new_body": "

If your database could roll its eyes it would whenever someone says locking is easy. Multiversion concurrency control or MVCC is the grown up way databases let readers and writers share the same tables without staging a traffic jam. Think of it as a photo booth that stores old snapshots while new selfies are being taken. Readers get a polite, consistent picture and writers keep doing their thing in the background.

How MVCC actually works

MVC C stores multiple versions of rows so concurrent transactions do not block each other. The basic flow looks boringly reliable and mercifully useful.

  • Transaction begins and gets a snapshot timestamp or read view
  • Reads consult that snapshot and return the visible version for the timestamp
  • Writes create new row versions tagged with the writer transaction id
  • Commit makes the new versions visible to transactions that start afterwards
  • Garbage collection removes row versions that are no longer needed

In practice this means a long running read is not constantly bothered by writers. Readers see a stable snapshot, and writers do not usually block readers. Writer writer conflicts still happen when two transactions update the same row. The database will detect the conflict and apply its rule book, for example abort the second writer or force retries.

Snapshots and consistent reads

Snapshot timestamps or read views are the secret sauce. When a transaction starts it gets a view of the world as of that moment. Every select consults that view so you do not get statement level surprises when you wanted transaction level stability. This is core to isolation levels and why MVCC is a performance win for many workloads with lots of reads.

Isolation levels and the weird things they let happen

Not all isolation levels are created equal and MVCC does different jobs depending on your setting. Read committed commonly returns the latest committed row for each statement. Repeatable read gives one snapshot for the whole transaction so you avoid some phantom surprises. Serializable aims to behave like transactions ran one after another but may add overhead or require conflict detection. Different engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL implement these modes with their own details so read the docs when you hunt for edge cases.

Tradeoffs and practical tips for performance

More versions means less blocking but more history to manage. If you are not careful your database will keep old row versions like a hoarder with too many photos.

  • Monitor version chain length and vacuum activity for PostgreSQL or undo log cleanup for InnoDB in MySQL
  • Keep transactions short especially under heavy write loads to avoid version bloat
  • Tune autovacuum and related cleanup parameters so garbage collection runs before things go slow
  • For write heavy workloads consider batching updates or partitioning hot tables to reduce contention

Tuning is mostly boring monitoring plus small tweaks. Watch the metrics, find long running transactions, and make sure your cleanup processes are not asleep at the wheel.

When MVCC saves you and when it nags you

MVCC is a great fit when you have lots of reads and concurrent writers, because readers get consistent snapshots and writers do not block reads. It gets annoying when transactions live forever or when cleanup fails. Then you get version chain bloat and performance becomes a nostalgia act for speed that used to be.

Final rule of thumb. Treat MVCC like a helpful but needy roommate. Give it short transactions, regular cleanup, and a few monitoring alerts. It will repay you with better concurrency and fewer deadlocks. And it will not steal your leftovers.

" }

{"new_title":"Forward proxy vs reverse proxy explained for engineers quickly","new_heading":"How to choose a forward proxy or a reverse proxy for your servers","new_body":"

If you like middlemen and mild chaos then welcome to the world of proxy servers. In plain terms a proxy is a gatekeeper that sits between two parties and manipulates traffic for fun and profit. The practical difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy comes down to placement and representation. One stands with the clients the other stands with the servers. That split decides why you would pick one or the other.

Where each proxy lives and who it speaks for

Keep it simple. A forward proxy represents the client. It sits closer to users and acts on behalf of outgoing requests. A reverse proxy represents the server. It sits at the edge of your backend and handles incoming requests before they ever touch origin servers.

  • Forward proxy role: act for users and control what they can access.
  • Reverse proxy role: present a single public face for multiple backend services.

Common use cases and features

Forward proxy scenarios

Forward proxies are the office bouncer for outbound traffic. Typical uses include privacy for end users filtering or blocking sites for policy compliance and caching to save outbound bandwidth. In many shops an HTTP proxy like Squid runs this role and enforces network security rules and content filters.

Reverse proxy scenarios

Reverse proxies are the concierge for incoming traffic. They do load balancing SSL termination caching and hide internal topology from the internet. Nginx and HAProxy are popular reverse proxy choices and are often deployed as edge servers for production web fleets.

Caching and performance

Both proxy types can cache but they solve different problems. A forward proxy cache reduces repeated downloads from the internet and saves precious outbound bandwidth. A reverse proxy cache speeds up delivery to many clients and lowers load on your origin servers. If you want to be fancy you can combine reverse proxy caching with a CDN or edge server to make things even faster for users around the world.

Security and visibility

Forward proxies enforce client side policy. They log what users request and can block or redirect connections for compliance. Reverse proxies centralize server side defenses. They are where you terminate TLS inspect traffic insert web application firewalls and hide backend IPs from random scanners.

Tools and deployment notes

Many tools can play both roles but configuration matters. Squid is a classic forward proxy and excels at HTTP proxy features. Nginx and HAProxy are common reverse proxy options that do load balancing SSL termination and caching at scale. Some platforms support both roles meaning you can run a single binary to do everything but that is a tempting shortcut that often makes troubleshooting miserable.

How to decide which proxy you need

  • Manage user outbound requests and enforce policies choose a forward proxy.
  • Protect backends handle TLS or balance traffic choose a reverse proxy.
  • Need caching for internal users save bandwidth with a forward cache.
  • Need caching for many clients speed up responses with a reverse cache or CDN.

Quick practical tips

  • Use a reverse proxy for SSL termination and load balancing to simplify certificates and scale services.
  • Use Squid for classic forward proxy features and Nginx or HAProxy for reverse proxy and edge server duties.
  • Do not try to be clever and jam both roles into one config unless you enjoy playing detective during outages.

If you remember only one thing make it this The side that needs control is the side you protect. Put the proxy on that side and then enjoy slightly fewer surprises and slightly more predictable traffic.

"}

{"new_title":"Fix Java Class Chaos with SRP for Cleaner Safer Code Today","new_heading":"Practical SRP for Java developers to simplify classes and reduce bugs","new_body":"

Make Java classes less dramatic with SRP

The Single Responsibility Principle or SRP is the mildly tyrannical rule that says each class should have one reason to change. In Java this means your classes should focus on a single role so maintenance does not feel like archaeology mixed with guessing games. Follow SRP and your code will be easier to read test and refactor which is the adult thing to do.

What a responsibility really means

A responsibility answers a single why for change. If you cannot name a class with a single clear verb or role then it probably does more than one job. Pick names that tell the truth like OrderRepository PaymentValidator or CsvExporter. If the name sounds like a shopping list then split it up.

How to spot a class that is trying to be everything

  • Mixed concerns such as business logic mixed with file access or UI rendering
  • Huge classes with dozens of methods that do unrelated things
  • Methods that touch persistence validation and formatting in one go
  • Unit tests that require massive setup to exercise a single behavior

Refactor moves that do the heavy lifting

When you find a class with multiple reasons to change move related methods into a new class. For example pull CSV export logic out of a service and into a CsvExporter. That makes the service easier to read and the exporter easier to test. Keep method signatures small and avoid passing an armful of parameters around because nobody enjoys that.

Small practical steps

  • Extract a class for one cohesive responsibility
  • Move helper methods out when they belong to a different role
  • Prefer composition over stuffing unrelated methods into one class
  • Run tests after each small refactor so you do not unleash surprises

Design minimal interfaces for each role

Expose only what the consumer needs. An interface named Notifier should offer methods for sending messages not database hooks. Clear focused interfaces make swapping implementations painless and reduce coupling across the system. This is how you get clean abstractions that do not leak implementation details like shame.

Write tests that reflect single responsibility

Unit tests should target one behavior per test. If your tests need complex setup touching persistence formatting and external calls then the class under test is probably doing too many jobs. Focused classes lead to focused tests and faster refactoring with less fear.

Quick rename exercise

If you are unsure about a class try renaming it. If you cannot pick a single clear name that fits then the class likely needs to be split. If the name is a paragraph then refactor.

Applying SRP in Java is not a magic spell but it is one of the highest value habits in SOLID clean code and software architecture. Expect fewer ripple effects when requirements change and fewer surprise bugs that show up at 2 AM. Your future team will thank you and your present self will stop apologizing to the code base.

"}

{ "new_title": "Master Git fetch and pull to avoid merge chaos and surprises", "new_heading": "See what changed with git fetch then decide or pull to apply updates", "new_body": "

Short version for the impatient

git fetch grabs updates from the remote and politely leaves your working tree untouched. git pull grabs the same updates and then immediately merges or rebases them into your current branch. One is a reporter with manners. The other is a friend who shows up and rearranges your furniture. Both are useful when used at the right time.

What git fetch does and why you should care

git fetch updates your remote tracking branches like origin/main without touching your local branches. This gives you a chance to look at incoming commits before you decide to integrate them. Think of it as reading the spoilers without changing your Netflix queue.

How to run it

git fetch origin

After that you can inspect the changes with commands such as

  • git log HEAD..origin/main to see new commits
  • git diff HEAD..origin/main to view code changes
  • git branch -r to list remote branches

Use fetch when you want to be cautious or when multiple people push to the same branch. Fetch first then evaluate. That simple habit saves you from surprise merge conflicts and baffling history.

What git pull does and when it helps

git pull runs a fetch and then integrates the remote changes into your current branch. Integration can be a merge or a rebase depending on your configuration or flags. It is a time saver when you trust the remote branch or when your workflow expects you to stay in sync quickly.

Typical usage

git pull origin main

git pull --rebase origin main

The plain pull will create a merge commit when histories have diverged. If you prefer a linear history use pull with the rebase option. That keeps the log tidy and reduces the number of merge commits that look like tiny black holes in your project history.

Rebase or merge which one for history

If your team likes a straight line of commits choose rebase. It applies your local commits on top of the new upstream commits so the history looks clean. If your team likes to preserve explicit merge commits and record the fact that two lines of work were combined then use merge. Neither choice is morally superior. They just have different aesthetics and maintenance trade offs.

  • Linear history fans use git pull --rebase
  • Merge fans use plain git pull

Practical workflow suggestions

Here are a few concrete rules to stop blame and start shipping.

  • Run git fetch frequently so you know what others pushed
  • Inspect with git log and git diff before merging
  • Use git pull --rebase when you want a linear history
  • Use plain git pull when merge commits are useful for context
  • If a pull causes conflicts stash or commit your work first with git stash or a local commit

Conflict handling and reducing drama

Conflicts are just disagreements between commits that you must resolve. They do not mean you are a bad developer. When a pull creates conflicts step through them, run tests, and make sure the resolved code works. If things get messy you can abort a rebase with git rebase --abort or recover from a botched merge with git reset --hard HEAD if you are absolutely sure about it.

For GitHub workflow push small focused branches, open pull requests, and prefer feature branches over working directly on main. That reduces churn on the shared branch and keeps both fetch and pull less terrifying.

Final sanity check

If you want to be safe fetch then inspect and merge or rebase only after you are comfortable. If you want speed and your team agrees use pull so your branch stays up to date. Either way learning these commands will save you time and needless apologetic commit messages later.

Use these tips and your future self will thank you or at least stop yelling at the terminal so often.

" }

{"new_title":"Run Java 21 Early Access JDK on Windows Mac and Linux Today","new_heading":"Step by step setup for Java 21 EA JDK on Windows Mac and Linux systems","new_body":"

Why you might install an early access JDK

So you want to try Java 21 before everyone else brags about it at the coffee machine. Early access builds are perfect for testing new features and finding bugs before they find you. This guide walks through downloading the JDK21 early access build, verifying the package, installing or extracting the files, setting environment variables, and confirming the JDK works on Windows macOS and Linux.

Download the right package and do the sanity checks

Go to the official OpenJDK early access page or a trusted vendor build page and pick the package that matches your OS and preferred format. If you like living dangerously skip verification. If you prefer fewer surprises do this first.

Verify checksum and signature

Always compare the checksum to the one published on the vendor site. Use sha256 tools on all platforms and a GPG tool if a signature is provided. This stops corrupted downloads and third party tampering from ruining your day.

# Linux or macOS
shasum -a 256 path/to/openjdk-21.tar.gz
# or
sha256sum path/to/openjdk-21.tar.gz

# Verify a signature if provided
gpg --verify openjdk-21.tar.gz.sig openjdk-21.tar.gz

Install or extract the JDK

Pick installer if you want a simple wizard. Choose archive if you enjoy manual labor and exact control. On Windows run the installer and follow the prompts. On macOS run the .pkg if available. For archive formats just extract to a folder you control. Avoid overwriting system managed JDKs unless you have a rollback plan and a safe backup.

Example extraction

# Linux and macOS
mkdir -p $HOME/jdks
tar -xzf openjdk-21.tar.gz -C $HOME/jdks

Set JAVA_HOME and update PATH so you actually use the JDK

Tools look for JAVA_HOME and the java command on PATH. Set JAVA_HOME to the new JDK folder and prepend its bin to PATH so java and javac come from this installation. Keep early access builds isolated in a dedicated folder or use a version manager to switch cleanly.

Windows

Open System Properties and edit environment variables. Create or update JAVA_HOME with the full path to the JDK and add the JDK bin folder to Path entries via the UI.

macOS and Linux

Add lines to your preferred shell profile file like .zshrc .bashrc or .profile. Then reload the shell or open a new terminal.

# Example for macOS or Linux
export JAVA_HOME="$HOME/jdks/jdk-21"
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"

Verify installation

Open a terminal or command prompt and run these commands. If they report the expected build and version you are done. If not adjust environment settings or remove older JDK entries from PATH.

java -version
javac -version

Troubleshooting quick hits

  • If java -version shows a different JDK then echo PATH and check for older java binaries earlier in the path.
  • On Linux consider update-alternatives to manage multiple JDKs when you need a system wide switch.
  • If a tool still picks the system JDK check IDE settings because some IDEs ship their own JDK pointers.

Safety tips for early access builds

Keep EA builds out of production and install them in distinct folders. Use a version manager or update-alternatives to switch between JDKs. Backups save you from the self inflicted pain of accidental production upgrades.

Summary

Download the Java 21 JDK early access build from a trusted source verify the checksum and signature extract or run the installer set JAVA_HOME and PATH and confirm with java -version and javac -version. That is the whole ritual. Now go test the shiny new features and report bugs like a responsible chaos agent.

"}

{"new_title":"Practical JPA 3 CRUD with Hibernate in Java made simple","new_heading":"EntityManager patterns and transaction best practices for JPA 3 CRUD in Java","new_body":"

{"new_title":"Stop Breaking Code Learn Open Closed Principle for Extensibility","new_heading":"Practical OCP techniques for polymorphism interfaces and clean design","new_body":"

Why OCP matters in the real world

If your codebase looks like a set of landmines that explode when a product manager sneezes you need the Open Closed Principle from SOLID. The idea is simple and magical. Keep modules closed for modification so bugs do not proliferate. Keep them open for extension so new features arrive without scalpel surgery on working code. This matters for architecture quality, clean code and long term maintainability.

Step 1 Spot the fragile code

Hunt down long switch statements and nested if trees that change when business rules shift. Those are the spots that will cause regressions. If you find code that requires edits every time a new variant shows up you found technical debt in its natural habitat.

Step 2 Extract an abstraction

Create an interface or an abstract class that captures the behavior that varies. That abstraction becomes the stable contract the rest of the system relies on. Think of it as a parking space for behavior. The rest of the code cares about the contract not the implementation.

Step 3 Provide concrete implementations

For each variant implement the interface. Each class handles one responsibility so adding another behavior is a matter of adding a file not editing ten of them. This is where polymorphism shows up and does the heavy lifting for extensibility.

Step 4 Wire with factories or dependency injection

Use a factory or dependency injection so calling code depends on the abstraction not a concrete class. That turns behavior swaps into configuration work rather than surgery on production code. This is plain good architecture and a lifesaver during refactoring.

Step 5 Add new behavior by extending

Need a new rule or product variant Add a new class that implements the abstraction and register it with your wiring. No changes to existing classes means fewer regressions and calmer code reviews. Tests that target the abstraction will tell you quickly if the new implementation keeps the contract.

Practical tips that sound like common sense because they are

  • Prefer small focused interfaces. Large god interfaces scream refactor later.
  • Write tests against the abstraction so every implementation proves it behaves like a citizen.
  • Keep single responsibility in mind. Classes that do one thing are easier to extend and reason about.
  • Use polymorphism for behavior changes instead of conditionals for simpler refactoring.

Recap and final snark

To apply OCP in your software design spot fragile code extract a clear abstraction provide concrete implementations wire dependencies via factories or DI and then add behavior by adding classes. Follow these steps and your codebase will be more extensible and easier to maintain. Your future self and your teammates will send you grateful but slightly suspicious messages because they do not trust miracles yet.

"}

{ "new_title": "Deploy serverless Python on AWS Lambda the practical way", "new_heading": "Step by step guide to building and packaging Python Lambda functions for AWS", "new_body": "

Step by step guide to building and packaging Python Lambda functions for AWS

If you want reliable serverless Python that does not explode on launch day this guide will help. You will learn how to write a handler that AWS can actually find package dependencies cleanly deploy with either the console or the AWS CLI and verify behavior using CloudWatch. There is mild sarcasm and a strong preference for least privilege policies.

Write a clear Python handler

Your function needs a clear entry point so AWS does not play hide and seek. Use a simple signature like

def handler(event, context)

Name the file and the handler so the runtime can find it without drama. Keep the handler focused on orchestration rather than heavy lifting. Parse the event validate inputs and hand off real work to helper modules or out of process workers when necessary.

Package dependencies and use layers

For most projects create a virtual environment then pip install the libraries you need into it. Bundle the site packages with your handler file for small to medium dependencies. For larger packages use a deployment package or a container image to avoid runtime surprises.

  • Create venv and install with pip install -r requirements.txt
  • Zip the handler plus site packages for the deployment package
  • Use Lambda layers for common libraries to reduce upload size and speed up deployments

Pin dependency versions in requirements files to avoid a random library update breaking production when your coffee is cold.

Create the Lambda with the Console or AWS CLI

You can click your way through the Console or automate with the AWS CLI. Choose the correct Python runtime version and upload your deployment package or reference a container image in an image registry like ECR. If you automate choose a repeatable script so future you does not curse past you.

Assign an IAM role that grants only the permissions required. Least privilege is not optional. Attach resource based policies if your function needs to be called by other AWS services.

Configure environment variables and settings

Use environment variables for configuration so code does not get littered with magic values. Set sensible timeout and memory values based on observed performance rather than intuition. Enable X Ray or other tracing if you like digging into behavior at 2am.

Deploy and test

Deploy using the Console the AWS CLI or a CI pipeline. Test with the Console test harness or by invoking the function with the CLI. Automate tests in CI so you catch regressions before production users do.

Check logs in CloudWatch to verify invocations errors and cold start behavior. Add basic metrics and alarms to monitor performance and error rates so you get paged before the outage tweet goes viral.

Quick checklist

  • Handler defined and discoverable by the runtime
  • Dependencies packaged or moved to layers
  • Correct Python runtime selected
  • Least privilege IAM role assigned
  • Environment variables used for config
  • Logging enabled and CloudWatch reviewed
  • Tests automated in CI pipelines

Following these steps will get you dependable serverless functions that behave as expected and do not surprise you on a Monday morning. If something still breaks blame cache or dependency drift and then fix it by pinning versions using a requirements file and using layers where it makes sense.

{"new_title":"Clone a GitHub Gradle repo and get it building in Android Studio","new_heading":"Hands on guide to import and build Gradle projects from GitHub","new_body":"

So you found a Gradle project on GitHub and want to run it in Android Studio or IntelliJ without summoning ancient build demons. This guide walks you through cloning the repo, opening it in the IDE, relying on the Gradle wrapper, syncing dependencies, setting the JDK and Android SDK, and handling the usual build grief with a minimum of existential dread.

Clone the repository to local disk

Open a terminal or use your IDEs VCS clone action and fetch the repository to a local folder. If you do not care about history use a shallow clone to save time on huge repos.

  • From a terminal run git clone --depth 1 <repo-url> for a quick download
  • Or use Android Studio or IntelliJs VCS clone feature if you like pretty dialogs

Open the project in the IDE

From the welcome screen pick Open or Import Project and point the IDE at the folder that contains build.gradle or settings.gradle. The IDE will detect Gradle and offer to import. Say yes unless you enjoy manual configuration therapy.

Use the Gradle wrapper for consistency

The project should include a Gradle wrapper script. Prefer running the wrapper over a system Gradle install. It guarantees the same Gradle version across machines which prevents many of the lovely failing surprises caused by version drift.

  • Unix and macOS run ./gradlew tasks or ./gradlew assembleDebug
  • Windows run gradlew tasks or gradlew assembleDebug

Why the wrapper matters

  • Reproducible builds across developers and CI servers
  • No guessing which Gradle version the build actually needs
  • Less time spent on Stack Overflow rituals

Sync and download dependencies

Let Android Studio perform a Gradle sync when prompted. If dependencies are missing check network access and proxy settings. On flaky networks use a local cache or a company proxy if your infrastructure provides one.

Command line lovers can refresh dependencies with ./gradlew build --refresh-dependencies to force downloads without opening the IDE.

Configure JDK and Android SDK

Open Project Structure or Settings and make sure the project JDK matches the version expected by the build. Modern Android projects often require Java 11 but check the project docs or the Gradle toolchain settings.

Also verify the Android SDK location and install missing build tools from the SDK Manager. A mismatch here produces dramatic looking errors that are usually just configuration oversights.

Build and run

Use the IDEs Build menu or the run action to assemble or launch the app. If you prefer the command line run ./gradlew assembleDebug or ./gradlew installDebug from the repository root to build artifacts without opening the IDE.

Quick troubleshooting tips

  • Missing dependencies or failed downloads check proxy, firewall, or corrupt cache
  • No wrapper present ask the maintainer to include it or create one locally with a system Gradle by running gradle wrapper
  • JDK mismatch set Project SDK to the version required by the project
  • Android build tools missing open SDK Manager and install the required packages
  • Gradle version mismatch prefer using the wrapper so this does not happen

Recap

Clone the repo, open it in Android Studio or IntelliJ, use the Gradle wrapper, sync dependencies, set the JDK and Android SDK, then build. If things fail follow the troubleshooting list and remember that most problems are configuration drama not code tragedy.

{ "new_title": "Avoid Disaster with git reset --hard and git log Tricks", "new_heading": "Safely reset HEAD then inspect commits and recover history with git reflog", "new_body": "

If you ever typed git reset --hard and felt the sudden urge to apologize to your repository you are in the right place. This short, slightly sarcastic git tutorial shows how to prepare the working tree before a hard reset then use git log and git reflog to inspect and recover git history when things get dramatic.

Prepare the working tree the boring but useful way

Think of this as the safety net you should have raised before doing something destructive. Use git status to see what is staged and what is untracked. If you have uncommitted work that you care about stash it or commit it.

  • Check status with git status
  • Stash uncommitted changes with git stash if you want to preserve work without committing
  • Or commit to a quick local branch if you prefer an explicit record

Pro tip for the boldly lazy: create a throwaway branch before doing risky things. Branch management is the duct tape of version control.

Perform the hard reset and know what it does

When you run git reset --hard <commit> you move HEAD to that commit and force the index and working tree to match. That is efficient and merciless. Expect uncommitted changes to vanish unless they were stashed or committed first.

git reset --hard <commit-hash-or-ref>

This is great when you want to undo a messy experiment and get back to a known state. This is terrible when you ran it without looking. That is also why branches exist.

Inspect history with git log like a curious detective

git log is the flashlight for your commit history. Use a compact view to see relationships between branches and commits without scrolling for an hour.

  • Graphical compact view: git log --graph --oneline --decorate
  • Limit output when history is long: git log -n 20
  • Search messages or authors with git log --grep="text" if you remember something about the commit

Make git log actually fun by experimenting with formats and aliases. You will spend less time guessing which branch did what and more time pretending you always planned it that way.

Recover a commit with git reflog when you forgot you were a hero

The reflog records where HEAD has been. If you accidentally nuked something with a hard reset it often holds the key to redemption.

git reflog
git reset --hard <reflog-hash>
# or create a branch at the hash
git branch rescue <reflog-hash>

Browse the reflog to find the pointer you need. Then either reset back to it or create a branch to preserve that state. The reflog is like the repository memory after a night you do not fully remember.

Quick recap and developer tips

  • Check git status and stash or commit before running git reset --hard
  • Use git log --graph --oneline --decorate to inspect git history quickly
  • Search the reflog with git reflog to recover lost HEAD positions
  • Create a branch for risky experiments and practice branch management

Final note for the brave and exhausted: git reset --hard is powerful and irreversible on uncommitted changes. Use it with the respect it demands and a backup if you can stomach the extra steps. Follow these developer tips and you will avoid most small tragedies and enjoy fewer frantic searches for lost commits.

{"new_title":"Log into DockerHub with tokens for safer automated builds","new_heading":"Step by step Docker login using a personal access token in CI","new_body":"

Want to push images without handing your password to the internet like a trusting pigeon? Use a DockerHub personal access token instead. It behaves like a one use friendly bouncer for your registry access and keeps your real password off party logs and process tables.

Generate a DockerHub access token

Sign in to DockerHub and open your account settings under Security or Access Tokens. Create a named token with the smallest scope that still lets your build breathe. Copy the token now because DockerHub will not show it again. If you lose it you will need to revoke and create a new one which is also a healthy opportunity to clean up old tokens.

Login with the Docker CLI the safe way

Do not paste tokens into your shell where history will hoard them forever. Use the password stdin option so the secret never appears in your shell history and does not show up in the process list.

Commands to use

echo TOKEN | docker login --username USERNAME --password-stdin

# interactive alternative
docker login --username USERNAME
# paste the access token when prompted for the password

# remove stored credentials
docker logout

Replace TOKEN and USERNAME with your token and DockerHub username. On interactive logins paste the token when asked for the password. When you are done use docker logout to remove credentials from the Docker config file.

Use tokens safely in CI and automation

CI systems are where tokens earn their keep. Store the token as a secret in your CI provider and never commit it to source. Most CI systems let you inject secrets as environment variables which you can pipe into docker login. This keeps the secret out of logs and prevents accidental exposure.

CI example

# in a CI job
echo $DOCKER_TOKEN | docker login --username $DOCKER_USERNAME --password-stdin

Use the CI secret store provided by your runner for GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, or whatever mysterious cloud you use. If a build needs only pull access grant only that scope to the token.

Best practices and hygiene

  • Give each token a name so you know what to revoke when something goes wrong
  • Grant least privilege and pick minimal scopes
  • Rotate tokens on a schedule or after incidents
  • Revoke tokens you are not actively using
  • Consider a Docker credential helper to avoid plaintext tokens on disk

Summary in plain honesty. Create a named access token in DockerHub. Use echo TOKEN pipe docker login with the password stdin option to avoid shell history and process leaks. Store tokens in CI secrets not in repo files. Rotate and revoke like a responsible adult.

Now go push your images with the smug satisfaction of someone who just did security correctly and still has time for coffee.

"}

{"new_title":"Build a Spring Boot Docker image and publish to Docker Hub","new_heading":"Containerize a Spring Boot app with Maven and push to Docker Hub","new_body":"

So you have a Spring Boot app that runs locally and you want to ship it into the wild world of containers and CI pipelines. This guide walks you through packaging the app with Maven building a Docker image and publishing it to Docker Hub with minimal drama and maximum repeatability.

Quick overview of the steps

We will follow a simple flow that you can put into a CI job or run on your laptop

  • Create a Dockerfile in the project root
  • Build the Spring Boot jar with Maven
  • Build a Docker image that contains the jar
  • Tag and push the image to Docker Hub
  • Pull and run the image on another host to verify

Prepare a Dockerfile

Create a Dockerfile next to your pom.xml. Keep it simple and deterministic. A common pattern uses a small runtime image and copies in the packaged jar.

FROM openjdk:17-jdk-slim
ARG JAR_FILE=target/*.jar
COPY ${JAR_FILE} app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app.jar"]

Tip for smaller images: consider a multi stage build that compiles and then copies only the jar into a runtime image. That reduces attack surface and build churn.

Build the application jar

Use the Maven wrapper so CI and local builds behave the same. From the project root run

./mvnw package -DskipTests

The artifact will be in the target folder and the Dockerfile will copy it into the image.

Build the Docker image

From the project root run a docker build and give the image a repo name that maps to Docker Hub. That saves you a separate tagging step in many workflows.

docker build -t myusername/myapp:1.0.0 .

Using semantic version tags makes rollbacks and deploys far less miserable.

Tagging and pushing

If you forgot the repository name during build you can tag the local image

docker tag localname myusername/myapp:1.0.0

Then authenticate and push. For interactive use run

docker login
docker push myusername/myapp:1.0.0

For automated pipelines create a Docker Hub access token and use it instead of a password. Storing tokens in your CI secret manager makes you look responsible.

Pull and run on another host

On a remote machine or a fresh CI agent validate the image

docker pull myusername/myapp:1.0.0
docker run -p 8080:8080 myusername/myapp:1.0.0

Then hit your app at http://localhost:8080 and pretend you did not spend three hours hunting down a stray dependency.

Common gotchas and best practices

  • Use deterministic builds. Avoid timestamps and local paths in your jar when possible.
  • Tag images with both a version and latest when appropriate so CI can do controlled rollouts.
  • Use a Docker Hub access token for CI instead of your password to limit blast radius.
  • Consider scanning your image with a security tool before publishing to a public repo.
  • If you use multi stage builds keep the final image as small as you can. Smaller images are faster to push and pull.

That is all you need to turn a Spring Boot project into a Docker image and get it onto Docker Hub for distribution. Follow these steps in CI and you will have a repeatable pipeline for builds image creation and deployment that makes rollbacks and debugging less soul crushing.

"}

{"new_title":"Shrink Spring Boot Docker Images and Speed Up Startup Times","new_heading":"Practical steps to Dockerize Spring Boot apps for CI and Kubernetes","new_body":"

Overview

So you built a Spring Boot app and now want to wrap it in a container so it can live a glamorous life on Kubernetes or in CI. This guide walks through the sensible steps to containerize a Spring Boot service, keep the image small, and make startup faster. No magic tricks, just proven techniques that your future self will thank you for.

Build the application artifact

Start by producing a runnable jar. Use Maven or Gradle as you already do and let the build tool assemble a single executable artifact with dependencies. Typical commands are:

./mvnw clean package -DskipTests
# or
./gradlew bootJar -x test

Skipping tests is fine for local image builds when you are iterating. In CI you should run tests earlier in the pipeline before the image step though, unless you enjoy surprises in prod.

Create a multi stage Dockerfile

Multi stage builds are your friend. They let you run a full build with the JDK then copy only the runtime artifact into a much smaller image. That keeps layer count down and avoids shipping your build tools to production.

FROM openjdk:17-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY mvnw .
COPY .mvn .mvn
COPY pom.xml .
COPY src src
RUN ./mvnw -B package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /workspace/target/*.jar app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app/app.jar"]

Notes on the example

  • Use a build image with the full JDK to compile and assemble the jar.
  • Use a smaller runtime image for production such as a JRE or an OpenJDK slim variant.
  • Copy only the jar into the runtime stage to keep the final image tiny.

Order your Dockerfile for cache friendliness

Docker uses layer caching. Put stable files like pom.xml and dependency declarations earlier so they change less often. Copying the whole source too early forces full rebuilds and makes CI slow and sad.

Optimize image size and startup

Smaller images and faster startup are separate but related goals. Some practical tactics that actually work:

  • Use a slim runtime image or a distroless base for the final stage.
  • Consider jlink or a native image with GraalVM if startup time is critical and your app can handle the complexity.
  • Trim dependencies and avoid fat jars if you can, or use layered jars so that small changes do not bust the entire layer.
  • Set JVM flags for container environments such as -XX:+UseContainerSupport and sensible memory limits.

Build the Docker image and test locally

Build with a descriptive tag so your CI and humans can understand what they are looking at. Example:

docker build -t myorg/myapp:feature-branch-123 .

Run locally and verify health endpoints and logs. Expose only the port the app needs and prefer binding to localhost while developing. Check readiness and liveness endpoints if you plan to deploy to Kubernetes.

Publish to a registry and integrate with CI

In CI you should build the artifact, run tests, then build the image, scan it and push to your registry. Typical steps:

  1. Run unit and integration tests in CI
  2. Build the jar artifact
  3. Build the Docker image using the artifact
  4. Run a quick security scan and static checks
  5. Tag the image and push to the registry used by your deployment platform

Automate versioning with semantic tags or commit SHAs so rollbacks are not guesswork.

Checklist before you push to production

  • Artifact built and reproducible
  • Multi stage Dockerfile in use
  • Layer order optimized for cache
  • Runtime image minimized
  • Health endpoints and resource limits configured
  • CI builds, scans, and registry pushes automated

Conclusion

Containerizing Spring Boot apps is boring but rewarding. Follow these steps to get smaller images, faster startups, and less grief in CI. If you like surprises in production then by all means skip the checklist. For everyone else this approach will make deployments smoother and debugging less of a weekend hobby.

"}

{ "new_title": "Designing REST responses for a successful HTTP PUT that users like", "new_heading": "Choosing between 200 OK 204 No Content and 201 Created for PUT", "new_body": "

Quick primer with a small side of sarcasm

PUT is idempotent. That means if a client repeats the exact same request nothing spooky should happen like duplicate resources or existential dread. What you return after a successful PUT depends on two facts that matter more than your API designer ego. First, did you return a representation of the updated resource in the response body. Second, did the server create a brand new resource as a result of the request.

The short rules that save time and arguments

  • 200 OK when you send the updated resource back in the body. Nice for user facing flows and for clients that hate extra fetches.
  • 204 No Content when the server prefers to return no body. Ideal for background jobs or bandwidth sensitive devices that want less noise.
  • 201 Created when the PUT created a new resource on the server. Include a Location header that points to the new URI so clients do not go wandering in the dark.

Why each choice matters

Return a representation with 200 OK when the client expects to see the fresh state immediately. It avoids an extra GET and keeps developers from grumbling. Send 204 No Content when the result is trivial or when the client already knows the new state. Use 201 Created only if the server actually made a new resource that did not exist before the PUT. Consistency beats cleverness every time.

Headers you should not skip

Do not be stingy with headers. They are the plumbing that keeps things from blowing up in production.

  • Location set it to the new resource URI when you return 201 Created. For example in plain text form show the value as Location space slash items slash 123
  • ETag provide an entity tag when possible. Example syntax looks like ETag space "abc123"
  • Last-Modified use this when ETag is not available and you rely on timestamps for caching

Concurrency control and conditional updates

PUT is great until two clients decide to play update roulette at the same time. Prevent accidental overwrites by honoring conditional requests. Require the client to send an If-Match header with the ETag the client saw. If the ETag no longer matches return 412 Precondition Failed and let the client choose to reconcile changes.

Practical tips for real world APIs

  • Prefer 200 OK with a representation for user facing endpoints so clients get an immediate view of the new state.
  • Prefer 204 No Content for background or bandwidth sensitive flows where the client does not need a body.
  • If your PUT created the resource return 201 Created and include Location with the resource URI so clients have a single source of truth.
  • Always provide ETag when possible and honor If-Match to avoid surprise overwrites.
  • Keep responses predictable. Send plain status lines like HTTP slash 1.1 space 200 OK or HTTP slash 1.1 space 204 No Content. Predictability reduces bug reports and passive aggressive emails.

Example responses that do not require a fortune teller

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type application JSON
ETag "abc123"

{ "id": 123, "name": "widget", "status": "updated" }

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
ETag "abc123"

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location /items/123
ETag "abc123"

Final word for busy humans

Be consistent. Pick rules that match your client workflows and document them like you mean it. Returning the updated representation is usually the least annoying choice for developers. Returning no content is the least annoying choice for bandwidth. And if you ever find yourself guessing which status to use stop, ask whether a new resource was created and whether the client needs a body. That will lead you to the right status more often than heroic intuition.

" }

{"new_title":"How to use git reset soft or hard and not lose your work","new_heading":"Understand HEAD index and working tree when using git reset soft or hard","new_body":"

Welcome to the thrilling world of undoing your mistakes with style. If you ever typed git reset and felt your stomach drop you are not alone. The real question is whether you want to rewind history but keep your edits or wipe the slate clean and pretend that pesky work never happened.

Quick summary for people who hate long explanations

git reset --soft moves the HEAD pointer only and leaves the index and working tree alone. That means your files and staged changes stay where they are. git reset --hard moves HEAD and also replaces the index and the working tree to match the target commit. Unstaged local edits vanish. Use soft to rework or split commits and use hard when you want a pristine working tree and you accept that some edits will die forever.

What each part refers to

  • HEAD is the current commit pointer that tells git where you are in history
  • The index is the staging area where git keeps the next commit snapshot
  • The working tree is your local files that you edit with reckless abandon

Commands you will actually use

Want to uncommit but keep your changes staged for a quick amend or split

git reset --soft HEAD~1

Want to roll back to a previous commit and toss all local edits into the void

git reset --hard HEAD~1

Rescue mission with reflog when you go full disaster mode

If you blinked and lost a commit git reflog is your emergency contact. It records where HEAD has been so you can find the lost state and reset back to it.

git reflog
# find the entry you want then
git reset --hard HEAD@{3}

Yes this can bring things back but do it quickly and do not expect miracles if you overwrote the reflog or garbage collected unreachable objects.

When to use which reset in version control workflows

  • Use git reset --soft when you want to rewrite history locally but keep all changes ready for a new commit
  • Use git reset --hard when you want a clean working tree and you do not need to keep local edits
  • If you are collaborating and already pushed that history consider avoiding reset and use a revert based workflow instead

Safer alternatives and small survival tips

  • Create a safety branch before you reset with git branch backup-before-reset
  • git reset without flags defaults to mixed which rewinds HEAD and resets the index but leaves the working tree alone
  • Use git restore to target specific files if you only want to discard certain edits
  • Pushing after a reset may require git push --force and that will probably annoy teammates so communicate first

Checklist before you press enter

  • Do you need the changes elsewhere If yes make a branch or stash first
  • Is this branch shared If yes prefer revert or coordinate with your team
  • Can the reflog save you If yes you might still survive a bad reset

Knowing what moves and what dies when you use git reset soft or git reset hard gives you actual control over undo changes in git. Play fast but keep a safety net and spare your future self the regret.

"}

{ "new_title": "Master idempotent pronunciation and stop sounding unsure", "new_heading": "A quick guide to saying idempotent correctly in code reviews", "new_body": "

Want to say idempotent with confidence and not like you just pulled a word out of a hat? Good news. This short guide breaks the word down into chewable bits so you sound like someone who knows math and programming but is still allowed to be human.

Quick breakdown of the word

The word splits into four parts for most speakers. Think of it as eye dem po tent. That structure makes the pronunciation predictable and a lot less scary than it looks on paper.

Standard IPA for the common General American pronunciation is /ˌaɪdɛmˈpoʊtənt/. A common British variant is /ˌaɪdɛmˈpəʊtənt/. Either one is fine as long as you make the stressed syllable clear.

Syllables and stress

Count the beats and put the emphasis on the third syllable. The strong syllable sounds like POH in many accents or a lighter puh depending on your dialect. So practice eye dem POH tent instead of trying to smash the stress into the first part like a grammar gremlin.

Finish with a crisp tent sound. Do not swallow the final t unless you are auditioning for background noise in a mystery podcast.

Practice steps to nail it

  • Say the parts slowly: eye dem po tent
  • Say it at normal speed once you can do the slow version without tripping
  • Record a short clip and compare to native speakers on pronunciation sites
  • Use it in a sentence during a code review so it becomes muscle memory
  • Try both pronunciations and pick the one that fits your accent and audience

Common mistakes and why they happen

  • Misplacing stress by saying eye DEM po tent which makes the word sound off
  • Dropping the POH sound and compressing the middle so it becomes unintelligible
  • Making the final t muffled which turns tent into something suspiciously like mush
  • Overthinking it during a meeting and then never saying it again out of embarrassment

Quick phrases to practice out loud

Try these aloud until you stop wincing. First slow then normal.

  • eye dem POH tent
  • eye dem puh tent
  • IPA form slash aɪ d e m emphasis poʊ tent slash spelled out as a fun exercise
  • Use it in a sentence like this The API is idempotent so you can retry safely

Final note The point is clarity not imitation. Accent variation is normal and acceptable. If you get one nod of recognition in a code review you win. If you get applause that is extra and slightly suspicious.

" }

{ "new_title": "When to Use PUT or POST in REST APIs and Why It Matters", "new_heading": "How idempotence shapes PUT and POST behavior in real world REST APIs", "new_body": "

Welcome to the thrilling world of HTTP verbs where tiny differences ruin your day or save you from bugs. If you have ever wondered whether to use PUT or POST when designing an API the short answer is idempotence and who owns the URL. The long answer is funnier and slightly more useful.

What idempotence means for your API

Idempotence sounds like a math lecture but it is just a promise. If a method is idempotent then repeating the same request does not change the result after the first time. In HTTP land PUT is idempotent POST usually is not. That affects retries caching and developer expectations.

PUT versus POST in plain English

Think of PUT as telling the server to set a resource at a known address. You pick the URL and you send the full representation. Repeat the same PUT over and over and you get the same end state. Use case example

PUT /users/123

With POST you are asking the server to do something for you. Create a new child resource process some data or trigger a command. The server often assigns the id and may return 201 Created with a Location header that points to the new URL. POST is not guaranteed to be idempotent so repeated requests can create multiple resources or repeated side effects.

POST /users

What the server usually does

  • PUT stores the supplied representation at the given URL and is expected to be idempotent.
  • POST accepts the entity and then creates or processes one or more resources at server chosen URLs.
  • For partial updates use PATCH instead of trying to abuse PUT.

Status codes and responses

Status codes matter because they set expectations. A successful POST that creates a resource typically returns 201 Created and a Location header with the new URL. PUT can return 200 OK 201 Created or 204 No Content depending on whether the server returns a body. Use 409 Conflict or conditional headers like If-Match for concurrency control when you care about lost updates.

Practical guidance for web development

  • Use PUT when the client controls the resource URL and needs an idempotent replace operation. This is great for CRUD update flows where the id is known.
  • Use POST when the client asks the server to create or process and duplicate side effects are acceptable or expected. This is common for create endpoints where the server picks the id.
  • When in doubt choose POST for creation and PUT for updating a known URL.
  • For partial changes prefer PATCH. Document whether your endpoints are idempotent so other developers do not cry into their logs.

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

  • Sending partial data with PUT and pretending it is a full replace. That breaks the idempotence contract.
  • Relying on idempotence to solve race conditions. Use ETag based conditional requests to be safe.
  • Assuming POST never returns 201. It frequently does when a new resource was created.

In short pick PUT if the client owns the URL and requires predictable retries. Pick POST when the server should own the creation process and side effects are fine. Keep your status codes consistent document idempotence and avoid surprise behavior. Now go forth and design APIs that do not haunt your future self.

" }

{"new_title":"Pick the Right HTTP Method for Your API Without Tears","new_heading":"Use GET POST PUT PATCH and DELETE to make REST APIs behave predictably","new_body":"

HTTP verbs are the tiny commands that stop your API from becoming a lawless wasteland. They tell the server what you want done with a resource, and picking the wrong one can lead to mysterious duplicates, accidental data loss, or a support ticket that smells like panic. Here is a clear and slightly sarcastic guide to the common methods and how to use them without summoning chaos.

Quick cheat sheet

  • GET Safe, read only, cache friendly, do not change server state
  • POST Create or trigger server side processing, not idempotent by default
  • PUT Replace a full resource, idempotent so retries are safe
  • PATCH Partial update, efficient for small changes, idempotence depends on implementation
  • DELETE Remove a resource, ideally idempotent so multiple deletes are harmless
  • HEAD Like GET without the body, good for existence checks and freshness
  • OPTIONS Ask what the server supports, useful for discovery and preflight checks

Method by method without the fluff

GET

Use GET when you just want to fetch data and nothing else. It should not change state, so clients and caches can be optimistic. If your GET starts mutating things then explain yourself in a very long email to your future self.

POST

POST is your go to for creating resources and for operations that require server side logic like starting a job or accepting file uploads. POST is not idempotent, which means repeating the call may create duplicates. If you need retry safety add a client generated id or use idempotency keys.

PUT

PUT replaces the entire resource with the payload the client sends. It is idempotent, so sending the same PUT over and over should end up with the same server state. Prefer PUT when the client owns the full resource representation.

PATCH

PATCH is for partial updates when sending the whole object is wasteful. It is more efficient and reduces accidental overwrites. Note that idempotence for PATCH depends on how you implement the patch semantics, so document the behavior.

DELETE

DELETE removes a resource. Aim for idempotence so repeated deletes do not produce errors. Soft delete is a common pattern, but be explicit about what delete means in your API.

HEAD and OPTIONS

HEAD is a skinny GET without the response body, handy for existence and freshness checks. OPTIONS tells you which methods are allowed on a resource and is often used in CORS preflight requests. Use them, they keep cross origin drama to a minimum.

Design rules that do not require a ritual sacrifice

  • Prefer idempotent methods for automated retries. PUT and DELETE buy you safer retry behavior.
  • Use POST when the server performs processing that creates side effects or when a resource id is assigned by the server.
  • Document how PATCH behaves and whether it is idempotent for your API so clients do not guess.
  • Think about caching rules for GET. Proper cache headers can save bandwidth and developer tears.

Status codes and error handling that do not confuse humans

Tell consumers what happened with reasonable status codes and useful error payloads. Examples that work well in practice include 200 for OK responses, 201 for created resources, 204 for successful requests with no body, 400 for bad requests, 404 when a resource is missing, and 409 for conflict when a resource cannot be created due to a duplicate. If you use retries, document which codes are safe to retry on and which are not.

When in doubt pick the clearest option

If you cannot decide between PUT and PATCH ask whether the client is managing the entire representation or just a few fields. Use PATCH for small updates to avoid accidental overwrite. If the action is mainly server driven or creates new state then choose POST. And if you still cannot decide, choose the verb that makes the least impressive of your future self.

Following these rules will reduce accidental data loss and confusing bugs. Your API users will thank you and the support inbox will cry less. That is a win for everyone.

"}
