{"new_title":"Create AWS access keys and secrets for CLI and S3 access","new_heading":"Step by step guide to IAM keys and CLI setup for secure S3 workflows","new_body":"

Quick warning before we start

This is the friendly tutorial that helps you create an AWS access key and secret for CLI access to S3 without setting your account on fire. You will learn where to make keys in IAM how to configure the AWS CLI and how to test that your new credentials actually work.

What you will need

  • An AWS account with permission to manage IAM users or your friendly admin on speed dial
  • A user account to attach programmatic access to
  • A password manager or secrets vault so you do not paste secrets into a gist or a public repo

Step by step

  1. Open the AWS Console and go to IAM

    Find IAM in the services list and click in. That is where identities and credentials live. You can create a brand new user or pick an existing one to grant programmatic access.

  2. Enable programmatic access for the user

    When you create or edit the user enable programmatic access so API and CLI calls will be allowed. This is required for S3 command line operations.

  3. Attach least privilege policies

    Do not hand out AdministratorAccess like candy. For S3 tasks attach a scoped policy or use AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess when read only is enough. If you need write access craft a policy that limits buckets and actions to the smallest scope that still gets the job done.

  4. Create the access key and save the secret

    From the user security credentials tab create a new access key. The secret access key is shown only once. Save it to your password manager or download the key file. If you lose the secret you cannot recover it and must make a new key pair.

  5. Configure the AWS CLI

    Run aws configure and paste in the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key when prompted. You can also set credentials using environment variables if you prefer shell scripting.

    export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=YOURACCESSKEY
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=YOURSECRETKEY
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1

    The CLI stores credentials in the .aws folder under your user profile so commands can authenticate without you typing the key every minute like a caffeine powered robot.

  6. Verify S3 access

    Test the new credentials with a simple command. If you have at least list permission try running

    aws s3 ls

    If you get a permission error go back and check the policies you attached. Do not create more keys as an emotional reaction to permissions errors.

Best practices that keep you out of trouble

  • Rotate keys regularly and delete any keys that are not in use
  • Never commit keys to source control or paste them into issue trackers
  • Use scoped policies to follow least privilege principles
  • Store secrets in a secure vault or use AWS Secrets Manager when appropriate
  • Enable MFA and monitor usage with CloudTrail so you spot suspicious access fast

Troubleshooting and tips

If aws s3 ls fails with access denied inspect the attached policy and the resource ARNs involved. If the policy looks fine check for deny policies at the account level or SCPs in AWS Organizations that might be blocking access.

If you need temporary credentials consider using roles and assume role flows rather than long lived keys. Roles are the grown up way to do things and they reduce the chance of accidental exposure.

Final words of wisdom

Creating keys is boring but necessary. Treat the secret like a toothbrush and not like a sticky note. Rotate keys often and remove unused credentials. Follow least privilege and you will sleep better at night. If you ever need to explain why a credential leaked at least make it a good story.

"}

{"new_title":"Remove old AWS secret keys from IAM without breaking production","new_heading":"Step by step credential rotation for IAM access keys and cleanup","new_body":"

Step by step credential rotation for IAM access keys and cleanup

So you found an AWS Secret Access Key that needs to go. Good call. This guide shows how to remove a secret access key from an IAM user using the AWS Management Console and the AWS CLI while keeping your services online and your oncall person from crying into their coffee.

What to check before you start

  • Sign in with an account that can manage IAM users. Root works but do not make a habit of it unless you want to scare the rest of the team.
  • Identify which services use the key. S3, EC2, EKS workloads, CI systems and environment variables are usual suspects.
  • Plan a rotation. Deleting first without a replacement is a fast track to broken jobs.

Delete a secret access key in the AWS Management Console

  1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console.
  2. Open IAM and choose the user that owns the key.
  3. Open the Manage Security Credentials tab and find the Access Keys section.
  4. Identify the Access Key ID you want to remove and confirm no production job depends on it.
  5. Choose the Delete action for that access key and confirm the deletion.

Console clicks are satisfying but final. The delete action permanently revokes the credential so do the rotation first if you need continuity.

Delete a secret access key with the AWS CLI

If you prefer keyboards and short temper you can use the CLI. First list keys if you need to confirm the IDs.

aws iam list-access-keys --user-name USERNAME

Then remove the key you want gone for good.

aws iam delete-access-key --user-name USERNAME --access-key-id ACCESSKEYID

This command revokes the key permanently. If you run it by accident you will be doing a lively troubleshooting session.

Rotate credentials like a responsible human

  1. Create a new access key for the IAM user using the console or
  2. Use the CLI to create a new key with aws iam create-access-key --user-name USERNAME
  3. Update application configuration and environment variables to use the new key and secret.
  4. Test the apps with the new credentials until you are certain everything works.
  5. Remove the old access key to avoid credential sprawl and future surprises.

How to verify the old key no longer works

Do a harmless read against a resource that relied on the old credentials. For example try an S3 list with the old profile or run a small API call. If that request fails you have proof the key was revoked. You can also check CloudTrail for requests that used the deleted key to see failed attempts.

Common gotchas

  • Hard coded credentials in EC2 user data, container images, Lambda environment variables and EKS secrets are common leak points. Search and replace them.
  • CI systems and scheduled jobs often run with access keys stored in variables or secret stores. Update those first.
  • Prefer IAM roles and instance profiles when possible to avoid manual keys entirely.

Quick checklist before you hit delete

  • New key created and tested
  • Applications updated to use new credentials
  • Verification performed with API calls or CloudTrail
  • Old key deleted and audit noted

That is all. You have rotated credentials, removed the old AWS Secret Access Key and hopefully avoided an outage. If something breaks go blame the last person who checked in a hard coded key and then rotate their coffee too.

"}

{ "new_title": "How to Store Encrypted Secrets in SSM Parameter Store Using KMS", "new_heading": "Best practices for SecureString in Parameter Store with KMS and IAM", "new_body": "

Best practices for SecureString in Parameter Store with KMS and IAM

Quick recap for people who skipped the meeting

SSM Parameter Store can hold plain text values if you are brave, or SecureString values if you prefer your secrets to stay secret. Use a customer managed KMS key to control rotation and access, grant only the roles that need to decrypt, and use CloudTrail to catch the suspicious stuff. This guide shows practical steps with the AWS CLI and sensible defaults so you do not end up explaining how a password leaked to the interns.

Step 1 Create or select a KMS key for encryption

Customer managed KMS keys give you control over rotation and key policy. Create a key and give it a friendly alias so your commands do not look like computer gibberish.

aws kms create-key --description 'SSM parameter key'
aws kms create-alias --alias-name alias/ssm-params --target-key-id example-key-id

Use an alias for day to day commands and enable automatic rotation when appropriate. If you like drama you can rotate manually, but most teams prefer slightly less chaos.

Step 2 Store a SecureString parameter with the AWS CLI

Encrypt at rest by telling SSM which KMS key to use. Use the alias or the key id. Keep values out of terminal history if you are serious about security.

aws ssm put-parameter --name '/prod/db/password' --value 'SuperSecret123' --type SecureString --key-id alias/ssm-params

If you are automating this from CI avoid plain text values in logs and use parameter store put calls from ephemeral runners.

Step 3 Grant least privilege access via IAM and key policy

Two places control decrypt access. The KMS key policy and the IAM permissions of the role or principal. Grant the KMS decrypt permission to only the application roles that need it. Also allow the SSM service principal to use the key if needed by SSM actions.

  • Attach KMS decrypt to your application role.
  • Limit the key policy to the SSM service and specific IAM roles.
  • Avoid wildcards that invite mischief and accidental access.

Step 4 Retrieve the parameter decrypted when the app needs it

When your process runs, request the parameter with decryption enabled. This requires the role to have both ssm get permission and KMS decrypt permission at the right time.

aws ssm get-parameter --name '/prod/db/password' --with-decryption

Do not persist decrypted secrets to disk unless you have a good reason and an audit trail. Memory is ephemeral and your logs are permanent.

Step 5 Audit and rotate so your security team smiles

Use CloudTrail to log parameter and KMS calls. Enable KMS automatic rotation when it fits your compliance rules. Regular rotation and audits reduce the blast radius when things inevitably go wrong.

Practical tips and common pitfalls

  • Use aliases for friendly CLI usage and easier key swaps.
  • Do not grant decrypt to broad principals. Least privilege is not negotiable.
  • Monitor CloudTrail for unusual get requests and configure alerts.
  • Keep parameter names consistent and environment specific to avoid accidental reads.
  • Use IAM roles for compute resources rather than embedding credentials in code.

Wrap up

Parameter Store with SecureString and KMS gives you encrypted secrets with an audit trail and controlled access. Combine AWS CLI commands for setup, tight IAM and key policies for access control, and CloudTrail plus rotation for ongoing hygiene. Follow these steps and your secrets will be safer, your ops team will be less nervous, and you will avoid awkward all hands meetings where someone explains how a password ended up in a pastebin.

" }

{ "new_title": "Create an AWS IAM User for EC2 and EKS Access With MFA Safely", "new_heading": "Step by step IAM user setup in the AWS console for EC2 EKS and roles", "new_body": "

If you need an AWS IAM user for EC2 or EKS work and you want to do it without breaking anything or starting a security incident, this guide is for you. You will get a user, sensible permissions, and multi factor authentication so your keys do not end up in a pastebin of shame. This covers the AWS Management Console flow and practical checks for EC2 and EKS access.

Sign in and open the IAM service

Log in to the AWS Management Console with administrator credentials and navigate to Identity and Access Management. No drama required just clicks. If you lack permissions you will need an admin to do this for you or a ticket with a convincing amount of teamwork language.

Create the user

Click Create user and follow the prompts. The main choices are programmatic access for API calls and console access for a web password. Pick only what the person or automation actually needs. Picking both because you are feeling generous leads to confusion later.

  1. Choose a clear username so audit logs do not read like a riddle.
  2. Select access type. Programmatic access gives access keys for CLI and SDK usage. Console access provides a password for the web console.
  3. Decide whether to require the user to reset their password at first sign in.

Attach permissions using groups policies or role delegation

Do not attach broad permissions directly to the user. Prefer adding the user to a group with managed policies for consistent and maintainable permissions. When temporary elevated privileges are required use a role and issue temporary credentials. Roles are the polite way to do escalation without permanent risk.

  • Use AWS managed policies when they match your need.
  • Create custom policies for least privilege when managed policies are too broad.
  • For EC2 tasks grant only the actions needed to launch or manage instances.
  • For EKS remember that cluster access often involves mapping IAM entities to Kubernetes RBAC and using the aws eks update kubeconfig flow for kubectl access.

Add tags and review the configuration

Tags help with billing, ownership, and audits. Add an Owner tag and an Environment tag if you enjoy good governance. Review the policies attached to the group or user and make sure least privilege is respected. Excess permissions cause trouble faster than you can type sudo.

Save credentials and enable MFA

When creation finishes download the CSV with access keys or copy the console password. Store these credentials securely and treat access keys like radioactive materials. Enable multi factor authentication for the account as soon as you can. Use a virtual MFA app or a hardware token for higher assurance.

Test access and validate workflows

Do not assume permissions are correct. Test the actual workflows the user needs. For EC2 verify that the user can launch, tag, and stop instances if that is required. For EKS test that the user can authenticate to the cluster and run the kubectl commands they need after updating kubeconfig.

  1. Try the intended task such as launching an instance or listing nodes in the EKS cluster.
  2. If a permission is missing tweak the policy rather than granting wide permissions.
  3. Use the IAM policy simulator to validate changes before applying them in production.

Troubleshooting tips

If something fails check the policy simulator and CloudTrail logs to see what API call was denied. Remember that EKS cluster RBAC is separate from IAM and may need a mapping in the aws auth config map. If you see AccessDenied then narrow down the missing action and fix the policy rather than granting full admin status.

That is the whole song and dance. Create the user, give the minimum needed permissions, enable MFA, test with real tasks and log everything. Congratulations you now have an IAM user that behaves for EC2 and EKS and does not cause unnecessary panic during the next audit.

{"new_title":"Set up an AWS IAM admin user the safe and sane way today","new_heading":"Step by step guide for IAM admin users in the AWS Management Console","new_body":"

Why bother creating an admin user instead of living dangerously

If you enjoy heart palpitations and dramatic password resets then keep using the root account for daily tasks. If you prefer not to cry into your keyboard at 3 a m make an IAM admin user and treat the root account like a rare artifact. Creating a dedicated admin user improves security and lets you delegate tasks without handing over the nuclear keys.

Sign in and find the IAM dashboard

Sign in as the root user only when you absolutely must or use an existing administrator account for regular setup. From the AWS Management Console search for IAM and open the dashboard where users, groups, roles and policies live together in mild chaos.

Create the user and choose access type

  1. Click Create user and pick console access for humans or programmatic access for code and automation.
  2. Name the user clearly like admin billing or admin infra so future you does not guess who had the keys.

Attach policies and prefer least privilege

You can attach the AWS managed policy named AdministratorAccess to give everything to a user in one click. That is convenient and dangerous in equal measure. Better practice is to assign scoped permissions or put the user in a group that grants only the required permissions. Think of AdministratorAccess as a blunt instrument and least privilege as a scalpel. For example if this admin only needs to manage S3 then give S3 permissions rather than everything.

Using groups

Groups make life easier. Create an administrators group and attach the necessary policies there. Add users to the group so permissions are consistent and auditable.

Enable MFA and strong password rules

Multifactor authentication stops credential theft from turning into a full blown disaster. Enable MFA for the new admin user and enforce a strong password policy in the IAM password settings. Hardware tokens or authenticator apps work well and do not require you to whisper secret codes into Slack.

Verify the new admin account

  1. Log out and sign in with the new admin credentials.
  2. Confirm access to IAM and to any other required services such as S3.
  3. Test tasks you expect this admin to perform so you do not discover missing permissions during a fire drill.

Lock up the root account

After verification stop using the root account for daily tasks and store root credentials securely. Consider storing them offline and enable MFA for the root user too. Less frequent use means fewer opportunities for mistakes and fewer opportunities for attackers.

Quick best practices checklist

  • Create named admin users rather than sharing credentials
  • Use groups to manage permissions at scale
  • Prefer least privilege over AdministratorAccess when possible
  • Require MFA for all admin users and for the root account
  • Test access to services like IAM and S3 before calling it done
  • Audit and rotate credentials regularly

Wrap up

Creating an AWS IAM admin user in the Management Console is simple and worth the two minutes it takes. Follow these steps for better security and fewer 2 a m panics. You keep your root account under lock and keep the rest of your team doing actual work without playing admin roulette.

"}

{ "new_title": "Master AWS Batch with Fargate EC2 and EKS for Production Jobs", "new_heading": "Set up job definitions job queues and compute environments for AWS Batch", "new_body": "

If you need to run batch jobs at scale and you do not enjoy babysitting servers then AWS Batch is your new best frenemy. This guide walks through the practical steps to build job definitions, provision compute environments with Fargate EC2 or EKS, create job queues, submit work and monitor results. No fluff, just the parts that keep your costs down and your deadlines alive.

Why use AWS Batch

AWS Batch handles scheduling containerized batch jobs across suitable compute resources so you can focus on the workload and not on which EC2 flavor to cry over. Use it for parallel data processing scientific workloads or any batch job where automation matters more than hand tuning.

Core concepts explained without the corporate jargon

Job definition

This is the container spec and runtime rules. It tells Batch which image to run what command to execute and how much vCPU and memory to reserve. Add retries and timeouts in the job definition to stop runaway bills and ghost processes.

Compute environment

This is where the work actually runs. Choose one of three options based on how much control you crave.

  • Fargate You get serverless containers and no host management. Great for simple tasks and predictable scaling.
  • EC2 Use a managed compute environment to let AWS handle instance lifecycle or unmanaged if you want full control over AMIs and instance types.
  • EKS Connect an existing Kubernetes cluster and run batch pods if you already live in the K8s ecosystem.

Job queue

Queues route jobs to compute environments. Attach multiple compute environments and set priorities. Put fast responsive capacity at higher priority and cheap spot capacity with fallback at lower priority to save money without sacrificing completion.

Step by step setup without the drama

Follow these steps in order and you will have a working pipeline that does not require daily pep talks.

  1. Create a job definition by packaging your container image and declaring command and resource needs. Match vCPU and memory to your workload profile.
  2. Provision a compute environment and choose Fargate EC2 or EKS based on your needs. For managed EC2 let AWS handle instances. For unmanaged EC2 pick the AMI and instance types that fit your workload.

Example CLI command

That enqueues your job and AWS Batch schedules it according to queue rules and compute availability. It is thrilling in a very boring way.

Monitoring and troubleshooting like a pro

Use the Console CloudWatch logs and describe job CLI calls to monitor status. Capture container logs for debugging and add retries and timeouts in the job definition to prevent runaway costs. If something fails check IAM roles network settings and container exit codes first before blaming AWS.

Tips to save money and time

Follow these steps and you will move from setup to running batch workflows without unnecessary pain. AWS Batch gives you a way to run containers at scale whether you prefer serverless Fargate managed EC2 or integrating with EKS. Now go submit jobs and pretend you planned this all along.

If you want frontend developers to stop sending passive aggressive Slack messages about backend delays try mocking your API first. API Gateway mock integration gives you predictable mock responses without touching Lambda or ECS. That means faster contract design and fewer meetings with people who like to argue about JSON shapes.

What a mock integration actually does

Mock integration returns a response straight from API Gateway instead of calling a backend service. Use it to emulate success, errors, headers and different payload shapes while the real REST backend is still under construction. It is perfect for integration testing and frontend development where you need stable responses fast.

Quick setup steps for the impatient

  1. Create a new REST API in the API Gateway console and add a resource path like /users or whatever your frontend cries for.
  2. Add a method such as GET or POST on that resource.
  3. For Method Integration choose Mock integration. No Lambda is invoked and no ECS task gets woken up.
  4. Under Integration Request add mapping templates to transform incoming requests if your mock needs to echo or validate inputs.
  5. Under Integration Response add mapping templates to produce the outbound JSON and to shape headers.
  6. Configure Method Response status codes and make sure each Integration Response maps to the correct Method Response.
  7. Test with the API Gateway Method Test tool or send an HTTP request with curl or Postman to verify the contract matches frontend expectations.

Example mapping templates to get you started

Mapping templates use Velocity Template Language to build predictable JSON payloads. Keep them small and explicit so the frontend can rely on stable fields.

Integration Request example

#set($inputRoot = $input.path('$'))
{
  "query": "$input.params('query')",
  "body": $input.json('$.body')
}

Use that to normalize incoming data when your mock needs to echo something back or simulate validation errors.

Integration Response example for a 200 response

{
  "id": "123",
  "status": "ok",
  "message": "Mocked response for testing",
  "requestEcho": $input.json('$')
}

Save this template under Integration Response for the application/json content type. Then map headers in the Integration Response mapping area so the method response includes header keys your frontend expects.

Simulating errors and multiple status codes

Create multiple Integration Responses and give each one a different status code mapping. For example provide a 200 happy path template and a 400 or 500 template for error simulations. You can switch between them manually in the console or configure selection patterns so tests can exercise realistic error shapes.

Testing tips for the cautious

  • Start with one small example response and expand fields incrementally.
  • Map headers like Content Type and any custom headers explicitly so clients do not get surprised.
  • Cover different error shapes so frontend error handling gets real life practice.
  • Use curl or Postman to automate calls and verify your mocked contract in CI.

Why this saves time

Mock integration plus mapping templates decouples contract design from implementation. Frontend teams can iterate on UX and validation while backend engineers build Lambda functions or ECS services. When the real backend lands there is less guesswork and fewer Git revert parties.

If you want more advanced mocks consider pairing this with API Gateway stage variables or a simple feature flag so you can flip from mock to real backend without redeploying client code. That keeps everyone happy and reduces the number of passive aggressive Slack messages you have to answer.

Now go mock something useful and enjoy the brief bliss of zero 500 responses.

{ "new_title": "Build DynamoDB Tables That Play Nice With EC2 EKS and APIs", "new_heading": "Practical DynamoDB table design for NoSQL storage and AWS integrations", "new_body": "

This guide walks through creating tables and wiring them to EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS and SQS so your data lives somewhere safe and your services can actually talk to each other.

Pick keys like you mean it

Your partition key decides whether your table will scale or become a hot mess. Choose a partition key that spreads traffic across partitions. Add a sort key when you need ordered queries. Only add a global secondary index when your query patterns actually demand a different key. Example field names are userId and orderId and those names are boring for a reason.

Quick rules for keys and indexes

  • Prefer a high cardinality partition key to avoid hot keys.
  • Add a sort key when you need range queries or time ordered items.
  • Use GSIs for alternate query patterns and pay attention to their capacity cost.
  • Keep attribute names consistent across apps so no one spends the afternoon debugging misspelled attributes.

Create tables with the console or CLI

Want shiny visuals and click therapy Use the AWS Console. Want repeatable automation and the ability to cry into version control Use the AWS CLI with CloudFormation or Terraform templates. When scripting include attribute definitions and key schema in JSON so your infra lives in code and not in someone s memory.

Example approach

Create a CloudFormation or Terraform template that defines your table name attributes key schema and any GSIs. Then deploy it as part of your pipeline. This avoids the classic manual setup problem where prod and staging disagree about whether orderId is a number or a string.

Choose capacity mode and autoscaling

If your traffic is predictable choose provisioned capacity with autoscaling. If traffic is spiky or full of surprises choose on demand to avoid unexpected throttling and billing soap operas. Set IAM roles and resource policies the right way

Integrate with EC2 and EKS

Integrate with API Gateway SNS and SQS

For SNS and SQS use Lambdas that consume messages and write to DynamoDB for durable state. This way your notifications and queues become sources of truth instead of flaky messengers.

Integration tips

  • Use Lambda error handling and dead letter queues to avoid data loss when writes fail.

If you see throttles investigate partition distribution and consider adaptive capacity tuning or key redesign. Add alarms for throttles and high consumed capacity so you know before your users start shouting.

Optimization checklist

  • Look for uneven partition usage and fix hot keys by redesigning keys or adding random suffixes when appropriate.
  • Use Query not Scan when possible to reduce billing and improve performance.
  • Consider time to live for expiring items to avoid storage bloat.
  • Monitor GSI usage and provision capacity or switch to on demand if needed.

If you want to be extra responsible add automated tests to your pipeline that deploy a table copy run read and write checks and tear it down. Your future self will send you a thank you note and maybe a coffee if you do it right.

Keywords for your nerdy search engine queries include DynamoDB NoSQL AWS EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS SQS and database. Go build something resilient and try not to break production.

Review settings and create the bucket

Scan your configuration checklist for name, region, versioning, encryption and access controls. Create the bucket and watch for the success notification. Confirm the new entry shows up in the console so you can stop worrying and start uploading.

Exam friendly checklist and quick tips

  • Enable versioning for accidental delete protection.
  • Turn on server side encryption for data at rest.
  • Use tags for environment and owner to help cost allocation and troubleshooting.
  • Test permissions with a nonadmin user to verify least privilege.

Follow these steps and you will have an S3 bucket that survives both exam questions and the real world. {"new_title":"Host blazing fast static sites on AWS S3 with CDN and DNS","new_heading":"Step by step S3 static site guide for CloudFront and Route 53 users","new_body":"

Step by step S3 static site guide for CloudFront and Route 53 users

If you want a cheap reliable home for a static site and you like the idea of serverless hosting without the drama of servers, welcome to S3 hosting. This guide gets you from bucket name panic to a CDN backed site that actually loads fast and uses HTTPS like a grown up. Expect a few useful tricks and a little sarcasm along the way.

Quick checklist

  • Create an S3 bucket with a memorable name
  • Upload site files and set correct content type metadata
  • Choose index and error documents for friendly navigation
  • Enable static website hosting in the bucket settings for quick testing
  • Optionally add CloudFront for TLS and global caching
  • Configure DNS with Route 53 or your DNS provider
  • Test the site and set up logging and monitoring

Step 1 Create a bucket

Pick a globally unique bucket name and a region near your users. The name becomes part of the S3 endpoint so make it memorable and mildly professional. If your goal is a public static site turn off block public access for the bucket or use CloudFront with origin access so the bucket can stay private. Apply a bucket policy that grants public read only to objects or the equivalent permission for your chosen setup.

Step 2 Upload site files

Upload HTML CSS JS and assets from your build output. Set correct content type metadata on objects so browsers do not try to reinterpret your files. Point the index document to index.html and set an error document with a friendly 404 page so curious users do not meet an ugly XML error from S3.

Use versioned filenames for assets so you can mute caching problems without yelling at customers. Fingerprinted file names work wonders for long cache TTLs.

Step 3 Enable static website hosting

Flip the static website hosting switch in the bucket properties and copy the provided endpoint to sanity check the site in a browser. The console endpoint is perfect for quick testing. If you want better security and HTTPS use CloudFront in front of S3 instead of relying on the S3 website endpoint.

Step 4 Add CDN and DNS

For production traffic add a CDN such as CloudFront for global cache performance and TLS. Create a distribution with your S3 bucket as origin. If you need the bucket to remain private configure the origin access control or the appropriate origin access method so only CloudFront can fetch objects.

Use AWS Certificate Manager to provision an HTTPS certificate and remember that CloudFront certificates must live in the us east 1 region. Point your custom domain to the CloudFront distribution. If you use Route 53 create an alias record for the distribution, otherwise add the appropriate record at your DNS provider.

Step 5 Test and monitor

Open the S3 endpoint and your custom domain to make sure everything resolves and loads. Check the browser console for mixed content warnings and missing assets. Verify that caching behaves as expected by testing updated assets with new filenames.

Enable access logging for the bucket or for CloudFront and wire up CloudWatch metrics and alarms for unusual traffic patterns or errors. Logs are boring until you need them, then they are the hero you did not deserve.

Extra production tips

  • Set cache control headers for immutable assets and shorter TTLs for HTML
  • Minify and compress assets in your build step to save bandwidth and patience
  • Use redirects or a single page app routing strategy if you rely on client side navigation
  • Automate uploads with your CI pipeline so deployments do not require manual suffering

That covers the essentials for hosting a static site on S3 with production level polish. Create the bucket upload files choose hosting or a CDN configure DNS and then monitor. In other words follow the steps and enjoy fast pages with fewer server tantrums.

{"new_title":"Secure an S3 Website with ACM and CloudFront in Minutes","new_heading":"DNS validated ACM TLS for S3 hosted sites with CloudFront and Route53","new_body":"

If you want HTTPS for a static S3 site without turning into a cloud wizard this guide walks you through the real life steps. You will request a public ACM certificate, validate it with DNS in Route53, and let CloudFront terminate TLS so your visitors do not see the dreaded mixed content warnings or a broken padlock.

Quick overview

High level plan that actually works in production. Request a public ACM certificate for your apex domain and any subdomains such as www. Use DNS validation because Route53 can insert records automatically. Create a CloudFront distribution that uses the issued ACM certificate. Point your Route53 records to the CloudFront distribution so traffic arrives over HTTPS.

What you need before starting

  • An AWS account with permissions for ACM Route53 S3 and CloudFront
  • An S3 bucket served as a static website or as a plain S3 origin
  • A Route53 hosted zone for the domain and name servers configured at your registrar

Step 1 Request the ACM certificate

Request a public certificate for the apex domain and any SANs like www. You can use the console or the AWS CLI. If you use the CLI the command looks like this

aws acm request-certificate --domain-name example.com --validation-method DNS --subject-alternative-names www.example.com

ACM reserves the certificate and generates DNS validation records for each name. Keep an eye on the console or the CLI output so you can grab the CNAME values.

Step 2 Use DNS validation with Route53

DNS validation is automation friendly and avoids email hoops. If your hosted zone is in Route53 you can choose the automatic option in the console and let ACM add the records for you. Otherwise copy the CNAME entries into the hosted zone manually.

Step 3 Confirm Route53 hosted zone and registrar settings

Make sure a hosted zone exists in Route53 for your domain. If you create one you must also update the registrar so the domain points to the zone name servers. If the registrar still points elsewhere ACM validation will not see the records and issuance will stall.

Step 4 Wait for certificate issuance

Once the DNS records are visible to public resolvers ACM will change the certificate status to issued. This can take a few minutes up to an hour depending on DNS propagation. If it does not issue check that the CNAME entries match exactly and that they are in the right hosted zone.

Step 5 Create a CloudFront distribution

S3 website endpoints do not speak HTTPS directly. Use CloudFront to terminate TLS and forward requests to your S3 bucket origin. When selecting the certificate pick the one issued by ACM in the region required by CloudFront which is us east 1. Configure an alternate domain name that matches your domain and set the origin to the S3 bucket or the S3 website endpoint depending on your needs.

  • Use an alternate domain name that matches your certificate
  • Pick the ACM certificate in us east 1
  • Choose the caching and behavior settings that match your app

Step 6 Update Route53 to point to CloudFront

Create an alias record in Route53 that points your domain to the CloudFront distribution domain name. For the apex domain use an A alias. For www you can use a CNAME or another alias. This ensures TLS termination happens at CloudFront and your site serves HTTPS to visitors.

Troubleshooting tips

  • If issuance is stuck check the hosted zone and the exact CNAME values
  • Remember CloudFront uses cached name records so SSL changes may take a few minutes to appear
  • If you need to automate use the AWS CLI or IaC tools but validate in the console the first time to see the flow

That is it. You now have a secure S3 hosted site with TLS provided by ACM and CloudFront and DNS managed in Route53. If anything goes wrong blame DNS propagation and then check the CNAMEs.

"}

{"new_title":"Host and Deploy a Static Website on GitHub Pages for Free","new_heading":"Step by step guide to publish HTML CSS and JavaScript sites on GitHub Pages","new_body":"

Want to put a small static site online without renting a server or learning a new curse word? GitHub Pages will do it for free and with minimal drama. This guide walks through making a repo adding your HTML CSS and JavaScript files pushing code enabling Pages and optionally wiring up a custom domain that looks way more professional than a raw username dot github dot io address.

Quick checklist before you start

Keep this short list in your head like it is a shopping list for success

  • Create a public repository on GitHub
  • Put an index.html file at the repo root or use a docs folder
  • Commit and push your code to main or to a gh-pages branch
  • Enable GitHub Pages in the repository settings

Create the repository

Create a new public repository on GitHub or reuse an existing one. Public repos get the free hosting feature so do not make it private unless you enjoy paying or hiding your work.

Add your site files

Put your static assets in the repo. The simplest setup is an index.html at the project root plus a css folder and a js folder. If you prefer to keep many projects together use a docs folder and tell Pages to publish from there.

Recommended structure

/index.html
/assets/css/styles.css
/assets/js/app.js

Commit and push

From your local machine initialize git add your files commit and push. If you are pushing the first time follow the instructions on GitHub to add the remote. Typical commands look like this

git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
# follow GitHub instructions to add the remote
# then push to main or push to gh-pages when using a generator
git push -u origin main

Enable GitHub Pages in settings

Open the repository settings find Pages and choose the source branch and folder. After a short build your site will appear at username.github.io slash repository name or at the root username.github.io for repositories named username.github.io.

Custom domain setup

If you have a custom domain add a CNAME file with the full domain name or enter the domain in the custom domain field in settings. Then update DNS at your registrar. For root domains add A records that point to GitHub Pages IPs and for subdomains use a CNAME that points to your GitHub Pages address. Check the official GitHub Pages documentation if your DNS provider uses special record types.

Enable HTTPS and other tips

  • Enable the enforce HTTPS checkbox in Pages settings to avoid mixed content warnings
  • If you host multiple projects in one repo use the docs folder to keep things tidy
  • Use a gh-pages branch when a static site generator needs a separate build branch
  • Include a CNAME file at the repo root that contains your custom domain name exactly once
  • Clear browser cache or use an incognito window when testing changes to avoid false negatives

Troubleshooting quick hits

  • No site yet Wait a couple minutes and then refresh the Pages settings page to see any build errors
  • 404 on assets Check that your paths are correct and that files live where you expect
  • Custom domain not secure Make sure DNS changes have propagated and that the enforce HTTPS option is enabled
  • Using a generator and builds fail Check build logs and push the generated output to the branch that Pages is serving

There you go. Your static HTML CSS and JavaScript site is now hosted with no server maintenance and minimal drama. If anything breaks enjoy the tiny existential crisis and then fix the bug with a calm commit and an apologetic commit message.

{"new_title":"Point a GoDaddy domain to GitHub Pages and enable SSL fast","new_heading":"Step by step DNS setup at GoDaddy for a GitHub Pages custom domain","new_body":"

Why bother mapping a domain to GitHub Pages

Because username.github.io is fine for hobby projects but not great for looking professional or less like a student who learned HTML yesterday. Pointing your GoDaddy domain to GitHub Pages gets you free hosting, automatic SSL, and less explaining to clients who ask if your site is safe to visit.

What you need before you start

  • A GoDaddy account with the domain in your control
  • A GitHub repository serving a Pages site that works at username.github.io
  • Access to the repository settings or the ability to add a CNAME file
  • Patience because DNS can be slow and petty

Prepare the GitHub Pages repo

Pick the repo and branch that will serve the site from the Pages settings, or create a CNAME file at the repo root with your full domain, for example example.com. The CNAME tells GitHub which repo owns the domain. Confirm your site is live at the default username.github.io address before touching DNS.

Choose the right DNS records for your domain

If you want the root domain, also called the apex domain, you will create A records. For a www subdomain you will create a CNAME record that points www to username.github.io.

Apex domain A records

Add these four A records in GoDaddy DNS for the root domain. Use one record per IP with the host set to @

185.199.108.153
185.199.109.153
185.199.110.153
185.199.111.153

www subdomain CNAME

If you prefer www, add a CNAME for host www and point it to username.github.io where username is your GitHub account or organization name. That keeps the www traffic routed to GitHub Pages correctly.

Update DNS in GoDaddy

Log into GoDaddy and open the domain manager, then edit DNS records. Remove or replace any conflicting A or CNAME records for the same host to avoid DNS drama. While testing set a low TTL so changes show up faster, then raise it back to normal after everything is stable.

  • Replace old A records for the root if they point to something else
  • Remove any duplicate records that will cause unexpected behavior
  • Save changes and do a small victory dance

Wait for DNS propagation and enable HTTPS

DNS propagation can take minutes or a few hours depending on caches. Once your domain resolves to GitHub Pages open the repository settings and enable HTTPS. GitHub will request and install a certificate automatically when DNS is correct.

After the certificate appears turn on enforce HTTPS in the Pages settings so visitors always land on the secure version.

Troubleshooting tips that actually help

  • If the site shows an error, double check that the CNAME file has exactly the domain and no extra whitespace
  • Use dig or nslookup to verify DNS records from different locations, for example dig example.com or dig www.example.com
  • If the certificate does not provision, wait and then verify DNS is correct. GitHub needs to see the right records publicly before it will issue SSL
  • Make sure you do not have an A record and a CNAME for the same host, that is an instant conflict

Final checklist

  • Repo serves site at username.github.io
  • CNAME file or custom domain set in repo settings with your domain
  • A records for apex domain pointing to GitHub Pages IPs or CNAME for www to username.github.io
  • DNS changes saved in GoDaddy and propagated
  • HTTPS enabled and enforce HTTPS turned on

Follow these steps and your GoDaddy domain should be mapped to GitHub Pages with a shiny SSL certificate applied. If something breaks, blame DNS caching and then check the records again.

"}

{"new_title":"How to ace EC2 cluster placement on the AWS architect exam","new_heading":"Choosing EC2 placement groups for low latency and fault tolerance in exams","new_body":"

If you are staring at an AWS Solution Architect question about EC2 placement groups and feeling nostalgic for simpler times, this guide will save you from picking the wrong toy in the AWS sandbox. Cluster placement groups pack EC2 instances close together in a single Availability Zone so your nodes can gossip fast and furious. That makes cluster placement groups the usual answer for high performance computing and tightly coupled workloads that care about network latency and throughput.

What a cluster placement group actually does

Cluster placement groups try to place instances on the same rack or in very close network proximity inside a single Availability Zone. The payoff is low node to node latency and high inter instance throughput. That is why they are recommended for HPC, distributed compute, MPI jobs, and other workloads that act like small armies and need to coordinate quickly.

Key constraints to memorize

  • Single Availability Zone only. Cluster groups do not span AZs.
  • Compatible instance types matter. Some families do not behave the same and enhanced networking drivers may be required.
  • Capacity can be limited at launch, so you might hit placement errors during provisioning.

Spread and partition placement groups explained

Not every exam prompt wants the lowest latency. Sometimes the goal is fault isolation or scale. Here are the other choices and when they matter.

  • Spread placement group places instances on distinct underlying hardware to reduce correlated failures. Use this when you need the lowest blast radius for critical single instances.
  • Partition placement group divides instances across logical racks which helps large clusters tolerate rack level failure and still scale across multiple Availability Zones.

Exam strategy and common traps

Exam questions love to hide one simple requirement inside a sea of noise. Develop a checklist you run through fast under pressure. That will help you avoid classic distractors that mention multi AZ setups when the correct answer is a single AZ cluster placement group.

  • Identify the primary requirement first. If the prompt screams low latency and high throughput, favor cluster placement group.
  • Confirm the question allows same Availability Zone and compatible instance types. If not, cluster placement group is likely wrong.
  • Watch for capacity constraints during launch. If the scenario mentions immediate large scale launches, consider partition placement or rethinking instance choices.
  • Remember enhanced networking. Some instance families require drivers for the best results and exam scenarios may call that out.

Operational gotchas that can decide the answer

Placement groups are best chosen at instance launch if you want predictable placement. Moving running instances into a placement group is not magical. You may need to stop and start the instance or recreate it from an AMI depending on instance type and storage configuration. That detail often flips multiple choice questions.

  • If an instance uses instance store volumes you might need to recreate from an image to preserve data when changing placement.
  • EBS backed instances usually allow stop and start to re attach in the new placement scenario but check the prompt for caveats.
  • When the prompt mentions resilience across AZs, think spread or partition not cluster.

Quick checklist for exam answers under pressure

  • Primary need is network performance, and single AZ is allowed, and instance family is compatible, choose cluster placement group.
  • If the focus is fault isolation for critical instances pick spread placement group.
  • If you need large scale with reduced blast radius across racks and AZs pick partition placement group.
  • Always verify instance type compatibility and mention stop start or AMI recreation if the question covers migration.

Wrap up, breathe, and read the question like it owes you money. If the exam wants the fastest possible node communication pick cluster placement group but only after you confirm same Availability Zone and compatible instance types. If the problem cares about resilience choose spread or partition depending on scale. Now go pick the right answer and pretend it was obvious all along.

"}

{"new_title":"Blue green deployments with AMIs on AWS for solution architects","new_heading":"Immutable EC2 blue green strategy with AMIs ALB and Route53 for exams","new_body":"

Immutable EC2 blue green strategy with AMIs ALB and Route53 for exams

Short version for humans and exam takers who like coffee and worry. Blue green deployment with AMIs and EC2 gives you predictable, immutable releases. You build a golden AMI, spin up a fresh Auto Scaling group, attach it to the load balancer for staging, shift traffic gradually and then retire the old group when the metrics stop yelling at you.

Build the golden AMI

Start with a validated instance. Run your tests, apply security patches, and then bake an AMI so your servers are identical little soldiers. Using a prebaked AMI enforces immutability and prevents surprise configuration drift that will ruin your afternoon.

aws ec2 create-image --instance-id i-12345678 --name app-v2 --no-reboot

Or use EC2 Image Builder for repeatable pipelines that do the heavy lifting for you. Tag AMIs with semantic versions and put build metadata in the AMI description so rollback is not an archaeological dig.

Provision a new Auto Scaling group

Launch a new Auto Scaling group that uses the new AMI. Use launch templates and keep versions so rollback is a simple switch back to a previous template version instead of a tragic reinstallation ritual.

  • Set proper health checks
  • Keep cooldowns and scaling policies sane
  • Make sure instance role and security groups are correct

Attach to ALB and test like a paranoid engineer

Attach the new group to an Application Load Balancer target group for staging. Run smoke tests and synthetic checks against the new target group before moving production traffic. If you do not have automated tests here then I assume you like living dangerously.

Shift traffic and cleanup

Move traffic gradually while watching health checks, latency, and error rates. Use weighted target groups in the ALB or Route53 weighted records to split traffic. Increase weight slowly and monitor logs and metrics. If something breaks route traffic back to the old target group and troubleshoot.

Once the new fleet is healthy reduce the old Auto Scaling group size and then decommission it to save money. Remember to deregister instances from the target group and remove stale resources that quietly bill you every month.

Rollback and exam prep tips

If rollback is needed switch the ALB or Route53 weights back to the old target group or old DNS record. Because you used versioned launch templates the rollback should be quick. If you find yourself rebuilding from scratch you forgot to bake the AMI properly.

  • Tag AMIs and use semantic versioning to make rollbacks fast
  • Keep health checks strict so bad nodes do not get traffic
  • Automate smoke tests against the staging target group
  • Use CloudWatch alarms and dashboards for quick triage

Why this pattern matters for the Solution Architect exam and real life

Blue green with AMIs shows immutability, safe traffic shifting, rollback capability, and use of ALB Auto Scaling and Route53. Those are the keywords your brain and the exam committee both like. And in real life this pattern limits blast radius and keeps your managers marginally happier.

{"new_title":"Master API Gateway and Lambda for the AWS DevOps Certification","new_heading":"Practical API Gateway Lambda integration tips with VTL mapping examples","new_body":"

Quick reality check

If you are studying for the AWS DevOps certification and you see API Gateway and Lambda appear in the exam you will be fine as long as you stop treating mapping templates like ancient dark magic. This guide gives clear notes on proxy versus non proxy integration mapping templates VTL and error mapping with a few sarcastic asides to keep your brain awake.

Integration types and when to pick which

There are two main ways to hook API Gateway to Lambda. One is the lazy efficient option where the whole HTTP request is shoved into your Lambda and you decide what to do. The other is the control freak option where API Gateway transforms the request and response with mapping templates.

  • Lambda proxy integration sends the entire HTTP request payload to Lambda including headers body path and context. Minimal mapping work in API Gateway and more logic inside your function. Great when you want a single place to own behavior.
  • Non proxy integration requires explicit mapping templates written in VTL to shape the request and response. Use this when API Gateway must present a specific contract or when you want to translate legacy backend formats.

Mapping templates with VTL explained without hand waving

Mapping templates use Velocity Template Language which is simple once you stop panicking. You will see $input.path to read JSON paths and $input.params to pull query string path or header parameters. These are exam favorites because they test you on syntax and intent not on drama.

{
  "message" -> "$input.path('$.message')",
  "userId" -> "$input.params('userId')"
}

That example shows extracting a JSON field and grabbing a path or query param. In real life you will often wrap things into a new payload that the downstream service or Lambda expects.

Error handling and status mapping that actually matters

On exams you will be asked how to map backend errors to HTTP status codes. Integration responses let you match backend error messages using selection patterns and then transform or replace the response body so clients get a clean status and friendly payload.

  • Define selection patterns that match known error strings returned by your backend.
  • Create a default integration response with an empty selection pattern to catch everything else.
  • If you skip a default mapping the resulting behavior depends on the integration type and may return unexpected output or an error so do not skip the default unless you enjoy guessing games.

Practical tip on selection patterns

Match the exact text or use simple regex like Error or Exception to route to a 4xx or 5xx method response. Then use mapping templates to craft the client facing body. This is where non proxy integration shines because API Gateway does the translation work for you.

Hands on practice that saves exam points

Create two APIs in the console and compare them side by side. One API should use proxy integration and the other should use non proxy with a couple of mapping templates. Trigger simple flows and check CloudWatch logs to see the raw event Lambda receives and the transformed payload API Gateway sends upstream.

  1. Create a REST API with Lambda proxy integration and record the event payload your function receives.
  2. Create a REST API with non proxy integration and add a request mapping template plus an integration response that maps an error to 400.
  3. Compare logs and responses so the difference stops feeling like a riddle and starts feeling like a useful tool.

Final exam friendly checklist

  • Know when to pick proxy or non proxy integration based on where you want control
  • Practice $input.path and $input.params until you can type them without blinking
  • Always add a default integration response to avoid surprise failures
  • Test in the console and check CloudWatch logs for the raw event and headers

Master those items and the API Gateway Lambda questions will feel less like a pop quiz and more like a polite formality. Now go break stuff in a sandbox and fix it before the exam.

Elastic Beanstalk deploys your app to a managed fleet of EC2 instances. That means Beanstalk often handles scaling and deployment concerns while the EC2 instance owns the instance attached storage. Encryption at rest made boring and clear

Quick rules to remember

{ "new_title": "Move your domain to AWS Route 53 from GoDaddy without the drama", "new_heading": "Complete guide to domain transfer and DNS migration to Route 53 on AWS", "new_body": "

Ready to stop letting GoDaddy babysit your DNS and hand everything over to AWS Route 53 Instead of a boring checklist this guide will walk you through the real steps with enough sass to make the registrar blush

Why move your domain to Route 53

AWS Route 53 centralizes DNS and registrar management under one roof. That means easier hosted zone edits, tighter control of TTL and record versions, and fewer places to blame when something breaks. You will still pay the registrar fee, but you get streamlined DNS management in return. Also you can mock your old registrar in peace.

Before you start

  • Unlock the domain at GoDaddy. Domains are locked by default to prevent unauthorized moves. Unlocking is the key step that stops the registrar drama.
  • Disable WHOIS privacy so approval emails can reach the registrant contact. If you leave privacy on you may never see the transfer approval message.
  • Get the EPP or authorization code from GoDaddy. AWS will require this to validate the transfer.
  • Confirm the admin and registrant email addresses. If the contact email is stale the approval will stall.

Prepare DNS for migration

DNS migration and domain transfer are related but not identical. If you want zero outage do the DNS move first then the registrar move. Basic prep steps are simple and boring, and that is their strength.

  • Lower the TTL on critical records at least 24 to 48 hours before changes. A shorter TTL speeds propagation when you switch nameservers.
  • Export or copy your existing DNS records. Use zone file export if available or manually copy records into a text file. Backups are boring until they are heroic.
  • Create a hosted zone in Route 53 and prepopulate it with your records. This avoids surprises after the domain transfer completes.

Transfer steps in Route 53

  1. Open the Route 53 console and choose transfer domain. Enter the domain name you want to move.
  2. Provide the EPP or authorization code you got from GoDaddy. Route 53 uses this to request the transfer from the old registrar.
  3. Review contact details for registrant and admin. Confirm nameserver settings and the hosted zone you prepared in Route 53.
  4. Complete the payment for the transfer fee. This typically renews the domain for one additional year.
  5. Watch for approval requests in the GoDaddy account or via the registrant email. Approve quickly to avoid delays.

Approval tips that save time

  • Check the GoDaddy domain transfer section first. The approval may be waiting there rather than in email.
  • Search spam folders and archived mail. Approval emails are small and easily misfiled.
  • If the registrant contact is a personal address update it before starting the transfer. You do not want the approval going to an unattended inbox.

After the transfer completes

Once AWS becomes the registrar your hosted zone in Route 53 should be authoritative. Confirm the following to avoid a support ticket or an existential crisis.

  • Verify that the hosted zone has the correct records and that nameserver assignments match the hosted zone entries.
  • If you precreated the hosted zone and matched the records there should be no downtime. If you did not, update nameservers promptly.
  • Check TTLs and adjust back to normal values after propagation is complete.

Troubleshooting and timing

Most transfers finish in a few days. Some complete in hours if both registrars agree quickly. The official worst case is usually up to 5 or 7 days depending on the registrars involved. If the transfer is stuck check for pending approvals, locked status, or WHOIS privacy blocking messages.

If DNS looks wrong first confirm the hosted zone records then validate which nameservers the parent registry lists for your domain. Mismatched nameservers are the usual culprit when traffic goes sideways.

Quick checklist you can actually follow

  • Unlock domain at GoDaddy
  • Disable WHOIS privacy
  • Get EPP or authorization code
  • Lower TTL 24 to 48 hours before switch
  • Back up all DNS records
  • Create a hosted zone in Route 53 and import records
  • Start transfer in Route 53 and pay the fee
  • Approve the transfer in GoDaddy or via registrant email
  • Verify hosted zone and nameservers after transfer

There you go. You moved the domain, migrated DNS, and now have fewer vendor accounts to curse at. If anything goes wrong the registrar support team will provide a roundabout explanation. You will prevail with patience and a backup zone file.

{"new_title":"Move a domain into AWS Route 53 and avoid DNS downtime safely","new_heading":"Step by step DNS migration to AWS Route 53 with low downtime risk","new_body":"

If you are about to transfer a domain to AWS Route 53 do this guide first unless you enjoy mysterious outages and frantic support tickets. This is a clear practical walkthrough for a smooth domain transfer that preserves DNS continuity and keeps services online.

Quick overview of the plan

The goal is simple transfer domain ownership while keeping DNS working. The basic stages are unlock the domain at your current registrar get the authorization code export DNS records lower TTL values start the transfer in Route 53 approve and monitor the transfer then verify everything after it lands in AWS.

Before you start at the domain registrar

Do not skip this. A lot of transfers stall because one checkbox was ignored or privacy shield blocked an email. You want these items handled before initiating the move.

  • Confirm the domain is unlocked and eligible for transfer. Some registrars lock or impose a 60 day block after recent changes. Check the domain age and lock status in the registrar dashboard.
  • Request the authorization code also known as the EPP code from the current registrar. You will need it to submit the transfer at AWS.
  • Update WHOIS contact emails to valid addresses. Transfer approvals are sent by email so fake addresses and cloaked contacts will slow you down.
  • Disable privacy or proxy services when the transfer requires visible contacts. Those services sometimes swallow approval messages.

Prepare DNS to avoid downtime

DNS is the fragile part. You can make the move painless by thinking like a paranoid network admin.

Lower TTL values

Reduce TTL values at your current DNS provider to something short like 300 seconds at least a day before transfer. That helps DNS changes propagate faster if you need to switch name servers.

Export DNS records

Export or copy every DNS record including A, AAAA, MX, TXT, CNAME and SRV. Route 53 will not magically know about custom records, so bring a clean copy to recreate them in AWS Route 53.

Kick off the transfer in AWS Route 53

In the AWS console go to Domains then Transfer Domain and follow the prompts. When asked paste the authorization code and confirm the contact details and payment. AWS will try to import name server settings but always verify manually.

At this point AWS will contact the current registrar and the transfer approval flow will start. Some registrars require an email click and others let you approve in a dashboard.

Approval and monitoring

Watch your inbox like it contains your dog. Approve any confirmation emails from the current registrar. Transfers can complete in a few hours or take a few days depending on the registrar policies and their mood.

  • If an email approval is missed use the registrars portal to approve the transfer.
  • Keep an eye on the transfer status in the Route 53 console. It will show progress and helpful error messages when something goes wrong.

After the domain lands in Route 53

Once the domain appears in your AWS account you must recreate or import the DNS records and confirm the name servers match. If you lowered TTLs earlier DNS changes will propagate quickly and you can raise TTLs back to normal later.

Test your website email and any APIs that rely on the domain. Check mail delivery DNS TXT records such as SPF DKIM and DMARC and confirm they are intact. If a service is missing trace the request to the name server and the specific record.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

  • Privacy services blocking approvals. Disable them temporarily and reenable after transfer.
  • Missing records that break services. Export everything and check MX and TXT records for mail.
  • Assuming AWS will copy everything automatically. Always verify imported records and the name servers.
  • Recent domain changes that trigger a 60 day transfer lock. Plan for that and do not expect magic.

Final checklist before you declare victory

  • Domain shows in Route 53 and is not in pending transfer state
  • All DNS records recreated or imported accurately
  • Name servers are set to the Route 53 hosted zone if you moved DNS
  • Web mail and APIs tested and confirmed working
  • Raise TTL values back to normal after everything looks stable

Follow these steps and you will move a domain to AWS Route 53 with minimal drama. If something still breaks you will at least have logs screenshots and an obviously prepared support ticket to send to the registrar and AWS.

"}

{"new_title":"Launch a fast static site with GitHub Pages and a custom domain","new_heading":"Step by step deploy for static sites using GitHub Pages and Actions","new_body":"

Step 1 Create the repo and add site files

Make a repository on GitHub and decide if you want it public for free hosting or private if you have a paid plan that supports Pages. Add an index.html and any static files. If you use a static site generator build the site locally and include the generated output in the branch you will publish.

Step 2 Choose the publishing source

Open repository settings and pick one of the supported publishing sources. Common options are the main branch the gh-pages branch or the docs folder. The docs folder is handy if you want your source and site together. The gh-pages branch keeps the site output separate from your content and source history.

Step 3 Push changes and check status

Use the usual git commands to push your content. For a basic start try this in your local repo

git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git push -u origin main

Then go to repository settings and check Pages publishing status. If there are build errors the page will show a hint or log to help you troubleshoot.

Step 4 Configure a custom domain and enable HTTPS

If you bought a domain register a DNS record with your registrar that points to GitHub Pages. For simple sites a CNAME record pointing to username.github.io works well. Set the custom domain value in Pages settings. Once DNS has propagated enable the HTTPS toggle to get a secure connection. Wait a bit and then verify your site loads with HTTPS.

Step 5 Automate deployments with GitHub Actions

If your site needs a build step like a static site generator you can add a GitHub Actions workflow to build the site and push the generated output to the publishing branch. The workflow typically runs on push builds the site and then commits the output to the docs folder or gh-pages branch. Keep your secrets safe and test the workflow on a feature branch before you rely on it.

What to check when builds fail

  • Read the build logs in the Actions tab for the failing job
  • Confirm the publishing source has the expected files
  • Ensure DNS has finished propagating for custom domains
  • Test locally with a static server before pushing

Recap and final swagger

You created a repository added site files chose a publishing source pushed your content configured a custom domain and enabled HTTPS and optionally automated builds with GitHub Actions. The result is a fast static site served from GitHub Pages that you can update by pushing commits. It is efficient it is free and it will make your README slightly more impressive.

Pro tips keep branch names descriptive test locally with a static server and check the build logs when things go sideways. Now go deploy something pretty or at least functional.

{ "new_title": "Sign up for AWS Free Tier the easy way and avoid surprise bills", "new_heading": "Beginner friendly AWS signup guide with MFA IAM and billing alerts", "new_body": "

Quick truth for the AWS beginner

If you are new to cloud computing and need to create an AWS account without triggering a financial tragedy this guide walks you through the signup process step by step. What you need before you start

  • A password manager so you do not invent predictable passwords

Step by step AWS signup without drama

Open the official AWS registration page

Use a trusted browser and navigate to the AWS signup page. Bookmark it so you do not end up on a phishing site later. If a site asks for your Social Security number then you are in the wrong place and also see a therapist.

Create account credentials and verify contact

Enter a valid email and pick a strong password. Store that password in your password manager immediately. Provide your full contact details and complete phone verification when prompted. AWS will send a short code by SMS or voice call to confirm your identity. Have your phone handy and do not use a message in a bottle.

Add payment details and expect a small authorization

AWS requires a credit or debit card to verify identity and to bill anything that exceeds the Free Tier. A small temporary authorization may appear on your statement. That is normal, and it will disappear after verification. Do not use a prepaid card unless you want an error message to cheer you up.

Select the Free Tier and basic support

During signup choose the Free Tier offerings and basic support if you want to avoid paid support charges while experimenting. Pay attention to monthly limits and free usage windows to avoid accidental overages. Services like EC2, S3 and RDS have separate Free Tier quotas so keep track of them.

Make the account secure from day one

Security is not optional even for hobby projects. The root account is powerful and fragile. Treat it like a live grenade that also stores your birthday.

Enable multi factor authentication MFA

  • Turn on MFA for the root account using an authenticator app or hardware key
  • Do not rely on SMS alone if you can avoid it

Create an administrative IAM user

Never use the root account for daily tasks. Create an IAM user with administrator access for routine work and then apply least privilege policies to reduce risk. Use groups and roles when possible and rotate credentials with a plan.

Set up billing alerts and budgets

Go to the billing console and set a free budget with email alerts. You can configure thresholds to get notified before charges become a surprise. This is the part where you act like a responsible adult and the cloud behaves itself sometimes.

  • Rejected card. Use a mainstream bank card and avoid prepaid cards
  • Phone verification fails. Try voice call instead of SMS or use a different number
  • Accidental paid services. Check Free Tier quotas and enable billing alerts

Final notes for the newly minted AWS user

Creating an AWS account and staying in the Free Tier is simple if you prepare a real email and a supported payment method and if you enable MFA and an IAM admin user right away.   • Choose Free Tier and basic support

{ "new_title": "How a Viper GTS spin on QEW nearly became a total loss and why", "new_heading": "High speed Viper GTS spin on QEW and practical safety takeaways for owners", "new_body": "

A high speed near miss on QEW 427 almost turned a Dodge Viper GTS into an expensive paperweight. The dash cam shows a rear end breakaway followed by a spin into the guardrail. Speed plus a sudden steering correction caused oversteer that quickly became uncontrollable. A tiny road imperfection or a bit of debris likely amplified the loss of traction while nearby traffic removed any margin for error. The driver avoided other vehicles which was part luck and part practiced reflexes.

What went wrong

Here is the short version without the doom music. The rear end stepped out, a reactive steering input made the slide worse, and the car found the guardrail before it found traction again. Contributing factors were all too familiar to owners of high performance cars on highways like the QEW and Highway 427.

  • Rear end breakaway after loss of traction at speed.
  • Sudden steering correction that turned a recoverable slide into oversteer.
  • Road surface issues such as a pothole or debris amplified the instability.
  • Busy traffic reduced space and time to correct the skid which increased risk of a single car crash.

Why the Viper reacts this way

Performance cars like the Viper GTS carry a lot of power and tend to be unforgiving when grip is thin. Weight distribution, tire choice and pressure, and suspension setup all change how a car behaves once traction is compromised. A sudden input at speed is the automotive equivalent of poking a hornet nest while wearing flip flops.

Practical driving safety tips for performance cars

You do not need to live in fear of your sports car, but accept that public highways are for commuting not for teaching physics. Use these tips to stay out of repair shop photo albums.

  • Respect speed. Maintain legal speed and back off when traffic is dense or the pavement looks like a lunar landscape.
  • Smooth inputs. Sudden steering or throttle changes can provoke a spin when traction is thin.
  • Watch the surface. Potholes, ruts and debris can turn confident handling into chaos fast.
  • Setup matters. Tire choice, pressure and suspension tuning change how a sports car reacts under sudden loads.
  • Practice recovery at a closed facility. Threshold braking and countersteer drills at a track build reflexes you can actually use on the road.
  • Reduce speed on uneven pavement. Even modest speed gives much more time to correct a skid.

After the near miss

Damage to body panels, suspension and alignment can happen in an instant. Safety cages and restraint systems do their job, but repairs are often costly and time consuming. A prompt tow to a specialist shop and a careful insurance claim process will reduce surprises and keep the rebuild from becoming a saga.

If you own a high performance car treat public highways like shared space. Small mistakes become expensive lessons. Drive like someone who wants to keep the car on all four wheels and not the subject of a parts swap thread.

Final thought

Cars like the Dodge Viper reward respect. Practice in the right place, keep your setup sensible, and remember that surviving a near miss is a good story only if you plan to keep telling it.

Missing context is the killer. A single camera angle that cuts at the wrong moment or an overworked sound effect can make a rehearsed bump read as real injury. Viral sharing compresses nuance into a scream clip and social feeds prefer drama over footnotes.

Ethics and archival concerns for creators and fans

Posting this kind of footage without clear labeling invites misinformation and can harm a performer reputation. When a clip goes viral the court of public opinion runs wild so tagging clips with kayfabe or storyline status helps protect performers and preserves audience trust.

Checklist for posting and sharing

  • Add a brief note about whether this is part of a storyline or a real incident
  • Include timestamps for full context when possible
  • Avoid sensational captions that imply real harm if it was worked

Pro tips for staging dramatic angles

If you are a practitioner trying to create a big moment safely then rehearse timing camera placement and sound cues until they are boring. A single misplaced lens or a late sound hit will change audience perception from 'wow' to 'oh no'.

  • Run a short prebrief with camera operators and sound crew before the show
  • Use a sync cue that matches the physical action with a specific camera move
  • Agree a safety stop word to pause the sequence if anything feels off

At the end of the day this is match analysis and ring safety wrapped in showbiz. Superkickd and Doctor Giggles gave fans a powerful moment of drama while also reminding everyone how fragile perception can be when editing and sound design get to work. Share responsibly and keep the performers safe while you enjoy the ride.
