{"new_title":"Fix Jenkins TLS trust errors by adding the cert to Java keystore","new_heading":"Import server certificate into Java cacerts to stop SSL failures in Jenkins","new_body":"

If Jenkins is whining about an unable to find valid certification path error you are in the right place. This guide walks you through finding the bad certificate chain exporting the server certificate importing it into the Java cacerts keystore and verifying that Jenkins can talk TLS again. Expect a little command line work a touch of mild panic and the sweet satisfaction of a job that does not fail on first contact.

Why Java refuses to trust the server

Java maintains its own trust store in a cacerts keystore. If a server presents a certificate chain that is incomplete self signed or anchored to a CA that Java does not know about then the TLS handshake fails and Jenkins throws that certification path error. This is a common devops headache when internal CAs corporate proxies or new certificates appear out of nowhere.

What you will do

  • Inspect the certificate chain to find the missing or self signed link
  • Export the server certificate from the TLS endpoint
  • Import the certificate into the Java cacerts keystore with keytool
  • Restart Jenkins and verify the connection from the Jenkins host

Step one Find the problematic certificate chain

Use a browser certificate viewer to inspect the chain from the problem host. If you see an incomplete chain or a self signed cert then Java will reject it. You can also use openssl s_client or similar tools to dump the chain and show which certificates are being sent by the server. Look for missing intermediate certificates or a chain that ends in a self signed entry that your JVM does not trust.

Step two Export the server certificate

Browsers make this easy. Click the padlock view the certificate and export the server certificate as PEM or CRT. If you prefer the command line use openssl to fetch the cert chain and write the leaf cert to a file. Save the result as server.crt or server.pem so the next step is straightforward.

Step three Import the certificate into Java cacerts

Use the keytool that ships with your Java runtime. Point to the cacerts keystore used by the JVM that runs Jenkins. Typical Linux paths vary by distribution and Java version so check the actual java process before editing the file.

sudo keytool -importcert -file server.crt -keystore /usr/lib/jvm/java-8-openjdk/jre/lib/security/cacerts -alias myserver.example.com -storepass changeit -noprompt

Adjust the keystore path and alias to match your environment. Use a distinct alias per host to avoid stomping on other entries. The default keystore password is often changeit but verify your organization policy before using defaults in production. Always take a backup of the original cacerts file before making changes.

Step four Restart Jenkins and verify

Restart the Jenkins service so the JVM reloads the updated trust store. Then trigger the failing job or curl the endpoint from the Jenkins host to confirm the handshake succeeds. From the Jenkins host you can run a quick check with curl verbose output to see the TLS result or rerun the previously failing build.

Troubleshooting tips

  • If you still see trust errors check that Jenkins is using the JVM you modified and not an alternate runtime or container image
  • If a corporate proxy or custom trust store sits between Jenkins and the target import the cert into that trust store instead or set JVM options to point Jenkins to the correct trust store path
  • Use unique aliases and keep a versioned backup of the cacerts file so you can rollback if needed

Recap and best practices

In short find the bad chain export the server certificate import it with keytool into the Java cacerts restart Jenkins and verify. Keep an inventory of trusted internal CAs and periodically review your JVM trust stores to avoid surprises. Now go enjoy the rare feeling of having fixed a TLS problem with your own two hands and a little carefully targeted stubbornness.

"}

{"new_title":"Pull a single Git commit into another branch and keep history tidy","new_heading":"Step by step git cherry pick guide for backports bug fixes and conflicts","new_body":"

Step by step git cherry pick guide for backports bug fixes and conflicts

If you need to bring one bug fix from branch A into branch B without dragging the whole feature branch along then cherry pick is your friend and your mild curse. This guide walks the command line workflow for git cherry pick while keeping history readable and handling conflict resolution like a grownup.

Quick idea of what cherry pick does

Cherry pick copies a commit from one branch and reapplies it on another branch as a new commit. That is perfect for backporting fixes or picking an isolated change. Abuse it and you will create duplicate commits across git branches and make future merges awkward for your future self.

Steps to cherry pick a commit

  1. Find the commit

    Use git log --oneline or your favorite GUI to locate the commit hash. Copy the short or full COMMIT_HASH for the next step.

  2. Switch to the target branch

    Make sure you are on the branch where the change should land. You can use either git switch target-branch or the older git checkout target-branch. Update first with git fetch if you need to stay current with origin.

  3. Apply the commit

    Apply a single commit with

    git cherry-pick COMMIT_HASH

    To apply a contiguous range use either git cherry-pick A..B or git cherry-pick A^..B depending on which commits you want.

  4. Handle conflicts

    If Git finds conflicts it will stop and tell you. Check git status to see the files. Resolve each file, then stage with git add path/to/file. Finish the operation with git cherry-pick --continue. If you decide the pick was a bad idea use git cherry-pick --abort to roll back cleanly.

  5. Push and verify

    Once the pick is committed locally push with git push origin target-branch. Inspect the log with git log --oneline to confirm the commit arrived as expected.

Troubleshooting and common gotchas

  • Duplicate commits If the same change exists on both branches you may get an empty commit or conflicts while rebasing later. Use cherry pick sparingly for backports and isolated fixes.
  • Signed commits Cherry pick creates a new commit id. If you need the original signature you will not keep it unless you manually set GPG signing options.
  • Partial changes If you only want some hunks use git cherry-pick -n COMMIT_HASH to apply changes without committing and then edit the index before committing.

Handy tip

Use git cherry-pick -x COMMIT_HASH to add a tiny reference to the original commit in the new commit message. Future you will thank present you for that breadcrumb trail when playing detective.

Cherry pick is a neat tool in the developer workflow toolbelt for one off fixes, backports, and surgical changes across git branches. Use it with care and keep the conflict resolution tools ready. Now go fix that bug and try not to anger your repo history.

"}

{"new_title":"How to Use git reset --hard Without Losing Your Mind or History","new_heading":"Step by step guide for git reset --hard with stash and reflog tips","new_body":"

Welcome to the nuclear option of version control. git reset --hard will move your branch pointer and replace your working tree with whatever commit you point it at. That is powerful, convenient and mildly terrifying when you forget to breathe first. This guide shows how to run the command safely, update a remote if needed and recover if you panic and hit enter too soon.

Check your working tree and stash anything you care about

Before you do anything destructive use git status to see what is uncommitted. If you like your work better than chaos then stash it. If you enjoy drama skip this step and accept the consequences.

git status
git stash save "wip before reset" or git stash push -m "wip before reset"

Pick the commit you actually want

Use a short log view to find the commit hash for the state you want to return to. Copy the 7 to 40 character hash for the reset step.

git log --oneline --decorate --graph

Run git reset --hard to move the branch and working tree

When you run this command the branch pointer moves and tracked files in the working tree are replaced with the chosen commit. Staged changes and unstaged edits are discarded. This is not a suggestion, this is an actual deletion of local state.

git reset --hard 
# or to reset to the previous commit
git reset --hard HEAD~1

What happened

  • Your current branch now points at the chosen commit
  • Tracked files were overwritten to match that commit
  • Staged and unstaged changes were removed from the working tree

Update a remote if the branch is shared

If the branch also exists on a remote and you want the remote to match your local rewrite push with force. This rewrites history for anyone else on that branch so be polite or at least warn them.

git push --force origin your-branch-name

Recover with reflog when things go sideways

If you did reset the wrong thing git reflog records previous HEAD positions locally. Use it to find the prior HEAD and then reset back to it. Reflog is the safety net when haste meets human error.

git reflog
# find the entry you want then
git reset --hard

Quick recovery checklist

  1. Run git reflog to find the lost HEAD
  2. Run git reset --hard with the reflog entry
  3. If you had stashed work run git stash list and git stash pop to restore it

Safety tips that will save you grief

  • Use topic branches so force pushing only hurts the branch owner
  • Stash or commit changes before destructive commands
  • Prefer git reset --soft if you want to keep staged changes
  • Tell teammates before force pushing and consider git push --force-with-lease instead of plain force

Summary and final warning

git reset --hard is a blunt and useful tool for moving a branch to a chosen commit and restoring the working tree to that commit. Check your working tree with git status stash anything important find the right commit with git log run git reset --hard update the remote if required and use git reflog to recover if you make a mistake. Use it responsibly and your repo will live another day. Use it recklessly and you will be eating instant noodles while apologizing to your team.

"}

{ "new_title": "Fix SonarQube jvm.dll errors by pointing to 64 bit Java", "new_heading": "Troubleshoot SonarQube JVM loading problems on Windows and Linux hosts", "new_body": "

Quick reality check

If SonarQube croaks with a jvm.dll missing or server JVM error you probably have a Java mismatch, or a PATH playing matchmaker with the wrong runtime. This guide walks through the usual suspects and how to stop SonarQube from trying to load a 32 bit jvm into a 64 bit process and other classic Windows and Linux pratfalls.

Symptoms to look for

  • Startup log shows failure to load jvm.dll or a server JVM error
  • java -version reports a different runtime than JAVA_HOME
  • Windows machines use a stray JRE instead of the JDK

Step by step fixes

  1. Install a matching 64 bit JDK

    SonarQube expects a 64 bit Java JDK for server mode. If you installed a 32 bit runtime that will trigger the missing jvm.dll error because the wrapper cannot load a 32 bit DLL into a 64 bit process. Grab a supported JDK from OpenJDK, Oracle, or a trusted build and install the 64 bit variant.

  2. Set JAVA_HOME to the JDK root

    Point JAVA_HOME at the JDK root not a JRE. On Windows use the System Environment Variables dialog to create a system variable named JAVA_HOME and set it to the JDK folder. On Linux export JAVA_HOME before starting SonarQube for example

    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-11-openjdk-amd64

    Then verify with

    echo %JAVA_HOME% for Windows or echo $JAVA_HOME for Linux

  3. Point SonarQube to the right Java binary

    Edit the startup scripts so SonarQube uses the JDK you just declared. On Windows check bin/windows-x86-64/StartSonar.bat. On all platforms check conf/wrapper.conf for any hard coded Java paths and replace references to a bundled or system JRE with the JDK bin folder. The wrapper and scripts prefer JAVA_HOME so make sure that path is correct.

  4. Fix PATH and remove stray JRE entries

    Make sure the JDK bin appears ahead of any older Java installations in PATH. Remove stray JRE entries that might supply a 32 bit jvm.dll. Helpful checks

    • where java on Windows
    • which java on Linux
    • java -version to confirm the binary that will run

  5. Restart SonarQube and read the logs

    After making changes restart the SonarQube service or run the startup script from the SonarQube folder so new environment variables are picked up. Watch the logs for a successful JVM load message and any remaining path mismatches.

Troubleshooting tricks that actually help

  • If the wrapper still fails check that JAVA_HOME points to a JDK root and not a JRE. The wrapper looks for the JDK in a very literal way.
  • Make sure you did not accidentally install a 32 bit JDK or JRE on a 64 bit OS. That is the most common cause of jvm.dll issues.
  • If you use a packaged OS JDK double check distribution support for SonarQube versions. Not every combo is happy together.
  • If changes do not take effect run the startup script from the same shell that has the environment variables set. Services do not always pick up user level changes.

Parting advice

Think of SonarQube and Java as picky roommates. If you do not point them at the same places you will get a passive aggressive log file. Match the JDK architecture to SonarQube, set JAVA_HOME to the JDK root, fix PATH order, and edit startup scripts if they hard code a bad runtime. Do that and the jvm.dll drama should exit stage left.

" }

{ "new_title": "Maven and Jenkins best practices for Java CI and builds", "new_heading": "Use Maven for reproducible Java builds and Jenkins for scalable CI pipelines", "new_body": "

Quick primer that does not bore you to tears

Put it this way. Maven is the polite librarian who keeps your Java project organized and tells everyone where the artifacts belong. Jenkins is the caffeine addicted stage manager that runs the jobs when code lands, on a schedule, or when a developer hits merge like they just solved world hunger.

What Maven actually does

Maven manages the build lifecycle and dependencies through a pom.xml file. It enforces a standard layout and lifecycle so teams stop arguing about where compiled classes belong. Typical commands you will type into the terminal when pretending you know what you are doing are

mvn clean install
mvn test

Maven also offers a plugin ecosystem that hands off testing, packaging, and publishing chores if you would rather not script every little thing.

What Jenkins actually does

Jenkins runs the automation. It triggers builds on commits, on a timer, or when someone hits a button with dramatic flair. Jenkins coordinates agents across machines, captures console output, test reports, and artifacts, and stores pipeline logic in a Jenkinsfile so your CI is reproducible and versioned along with the code.

When to use each one

  • Maven for declaring dependencies, compiling sources, running tests, and producing artifacts that make sense across machines.
  • Jenkins for running those Maven goals automatically, orchestrating environments, scheduling builds, and giving humans a dashboard to blame when pipelines fail.

Want to make them play nicely

People who like order will want Jenkins to call Maven. Do that inside a container or an agent so builds are reproducible. A minimal declarative pipeline looks like this

pipeline {
  agent any
  stages {
    stage('Build') {
      steps {
        sh 'mvn -B clean install'
      }
    }
  }
}

Practical integration tips that actually save time

  • Cache the Maven local repository on build agents at ~/.m2/repository to avoid repeated downloads and network grief.
  • Run Maven inside a consistent container image so developers and CI share the same environment.
  • Attach test and coverage reports to Jenkins using the JUnit and JaCoCo publishers for fast feedback.
  • Archive important artifacts and publish them to your artifact repository as part of the pipeline.
  • Use parallel stages for unit tests and integration tests when your test suite likes to linger.

Common gotchas and how to avoid them

Bad configuration choices will make your pipeline flaky and slow. Common mistakes include not pinning plugin versions in Maven, not caching dependencies, and running heavy integration tests on the main build agent. Also avoid storing large build artifacts in Git instead of a proper artifact store unless you enjoy dealing with bloated repositories and regret.

Conclusion with minimal preaching

Maven makes builds reproducible and handles dependency resolution. Jenkins runs those builds automatically and scales them across machines. Use Maven to define how a Java project is built and tested. Use Jenkins to schedule run and report on those builds so your team can move fast and break things less often. Together they are boringly effective and will save you time and stress when set up right.

Final survival tip Keep your pom.xml tidy cache the Maven repo and put your pipeline as code in the repo so you and future you can stop fighting fires and start fixing features instead.

" }

{ "new_title": "Set up Nexus OSS for Maven repositories fast and reliably", "new_heading": "Host and proxy Maven artifacts with Nexus OSS for CI and dev teams", "new_body": "

Quick overview

If your team treats the public Maven Central like a sketchy buffet then you need a repository manager. Nexus OSS is the no-nonsense repository manager that hosts your private Maven artifacts and proxies remote Maven repositories for CI and local development. This guide walks through a pragmatic setup so you can stop wrestling with dependency hell and start blaming cache policies instead.

Before you start

  • Java installed and working. Run java -version and try not to cry if the JVM is ancient.
  • Download the Nexus OSS archive from Sonatype or a trusted mirror.
  • A non root user for running Nexus, because running services as root is a great way to write horror stories.

Install and start Nexus Repository Manager

Unpack the distribution into the directory you intend to run Nexus from and set ownership so the Nexus user can actually read and write files.

tar xvf sonatype-nexus-oss-2.x.y-bundle.tar.gz
sudo chown -R nexus:nexus sonatype-nexus-oss-2.x.y

Start the server with the bundled script and tail the log to watch startup messages.

sudo -u nexus ./bin/nexus start
tail -f sonatype-work/nexus/logs/nexus.log

The default HTTP port is 8081 unless you or that ancient sysadmin changed it. Note the port so Maven and CI can reach Nexus.

Access the web UI and secure the admin account

Open the Nexus web console in your browser at the host and port from the previous step. Log in with the default admin credentials documented for your Nexus version and immediately change the password. The web UI is where you create repositories, manage users, and break fewer things than you would via config files alone.

Create hosted, proxy and group Maven repositories

Minimal setup for a typical Maven workflow includes:

  • A hosted repository for internal artifacts and CI deployments
  • A proxy repository that points at Maven Central, typically using the URL https://repo1.maven.org/maven2
  • An optional group repository to present a single endpoint to Maven clients

Give repo names that humans and scripts can live with long term. Avoid whimsical names unless you enjoy painful rename migrations later.

Repository tips

  • Use semantic naming like maven-releases and maven-snapshots
  • Limit anonymous access unless you want the whole internet to see your artifact hoard
  • Set proxy cache timeouts according to your network and build reliability needs

Configure Maven to use Nexus

Edit your Maven settings.xml to add credentials for deploys and a mirror so normal Maven requests go to your Nexus endpoint. Update your projects to point distributionManagement at the hosted repo when you publish artifacts.

Example snippet to add to ~/.m2/settings.xml:

<settings>
  <servers>
    <server>
      <id>nexus-repo</id>
      <username>deploy_user</username>
      <password>password_here</password>
    </server>
  </servers>
  <mirrors>
    <mirror>
      <id>nexus-mirror</id>
      <mirrorOf>central

If your security policy is picky then use Maven's password encryption with the settings security file. That's the grown up way to avoid the stickynote on the monitor approach.

Deploy and verify artifacts

Update your POM with the distributionManagement coordinates for the hosted repository and run the usual Maven choreography to publish.

mvn deploy
mvn dependency:get -Dartifact=groupId:artifactId:version

Use mvn dependency:get for quick checks that Nexus is serving the artifact you just pushed. CI pipelines should be configured to authenticate to Nexus for deploy steps and to use the group repo for resolving dependencies.

Housekeeping and artifact management

Snapshots pile up like bad decisions. Configure snapshot cleanup policies and retention rules in Nexus so your disk does not become a shrine to old builds. Set retention rules for both snapshots and releases according to your release cadence and storage budget.

  • Automate cleanup of old snapshots
  • Enable content validation to avoid corrupted artifacts spreading to builds
  • Monitor cache hit ratios to tune proxy settings and save bandwidth

Wrapping up

Setting up Nexus OSS as your Maven repository manager gives DevOps teams a controlled artifact management solution for local development and CI. You get hosting, proxying and grouping of Maven repositories along with access controls and retention policies. It is not magic but it is reliable. Document your repo names credentials and policies so future you does not open a ticket that tries to explain this to past you.

If you run into trouble check the Nexus logs, consult Sonatype documentation for your specific Nexus OSS version, and remember that most problems are either permissions or typos. Prefer the former to avoid blaming typos forever.

" }

{"new_title":"Build a Bottom Up SOAP Web Service in Eclipse and Tomcat","new_heading":"Step by step guide to JAX WS Bottom Up SOAP services in Eclipse","new_body":"

Ready to build a Bottom Up SOAP service in Eclipse

If you ever wanted to turn a plain Java class into a SOAP endpoint and watch WSDL appear like magic you are in the right place. This guide covers building a Bottom Up SOAP web service with JAX WS annotations inside Eclipse deploying a WAR to Tomcat and testing with SOAP UI or a generated client. It keeps things practical and avoids holy rituals that only senior developers pretend to enjoy.

Step 1 Create the project and service class

Create a Dynamic Web Project or a Maven web project in Eclipse. Add a plain Java POJO and mark it as a web service with JAX WS annotations. Typically you annotate the class with @WebService and mark public entry points with @WebMethod. That POJO becomes the source of truth for WSDL generation in a Bottom Up approach.

Step 2 Dependencies and packaging

Pick a JAX WS runtime and add its libraries to your project or declare them as Maven dependencies. If you rely on your servlet container runtime be careful not to ship conflicting JAX WS implementations inside the WAR. Package the build as a WAR file for deployment to Tomcat or your favorite servlet engine.

Step 3 Publishing and WSDL generation

Deploy the WAR and let the JAX WS runtime publish the endpoint. The runtime will generate WSDL from the annotated class automatically. Use the Eclipse server console or the Tomcat log to confirm the endpoint address and that the WSDL endpoint is exposed. Verify namespace and service name match what your clients expect to avoid awkward surprises later.

Step 4 Test the service

  • Import the generated WSDL into SOAP UI for ad hoc calls and quick verification.
  • Or run wsimport to generate a Java client and exercise typed calls against your endpoint.
  • Send sample SOAP requests and check that responses reflect the Java method logic.

If you see a fault check parameter types namespace values and method signatures. A mismatch in element names or target namespace is the usual culprit when the runtime and the client speak different dialects of XML.

Common pitfalls and how to survive them

  • Classpath collisions between container JAX WS jars and your project jars. Keep the runtime single and decisive.
  • Implicit namespace values that differ from client expectations. Prefer explicit namespace attributes on annotations to avoid surprise mismatches.
  • Missing web.xml or servlet mapping confusion. You can rely on servlet 3 annotations in most cases but check your container version first.

Quick checklist before you call it done

  • POJO annotated with @WebService and public methods annotated with @WebMethod where needed
  • Proper JAX WS runtime dependencies declared and no duplicate implementations on the classpath
  • WAR deployed to Tomcat and WSDL accessible from the endpoint URL reported in the server log
  • Successful test runs in SOAP UI or a wsimport generated client

Follow these steps and you will have a Bottom Up SOAP web service that behaves predictably and can be shared with clients without drama. If things go wrong compare the generated WSDL with what your consumers expect and set explicit annotation values for names and namespaces. That little bit of explicitness buys a lot of sanity when SOAP and XML decide to be awkward.

"}

{"new_title":"Easy JFrog Artifactory setup and JAR deployment for Java","new_heading":"Local Maven repositories with JFrog Artifactory for CI and DevOps teams","new_body":"

If you want a place to store your Java babies and stop emailing JARs to colleagues like it is 2003 this guide walks you through downloading, running and using JFrog Artifactory to host a local Maven repository. It covers installing with Docker or a service package, creating a repository, configuring Maven and actually pushing a JAR so your CI pipeline will stop crying.

Download Artifactory

You can grab the Artifactory distribution from the vendor site or use the official Docker image for a fast lab. Docker is the little black belt move here because it avoids system dependency drama and makes cleanup pleasant when you inevitably try a new idea that fails spectacularly.

Install and start Artifactory

For a quick local test run the Docker image. A minimal example looks like this.

docker pull jfrog/artifactory-oss:latest
docker run -d --name artifactory -p 8081:8081 jfrog/artifactory-oss:latest

If you installed the service package follow the installer prompts, start the service and open the web console at http://localhost:8081. Create an admin user and do the basic health check. No, the wizard will not judge your commit history.

Create a local Maven repository

In the web console create a new repository of type Maven local. Pick a sensible name like my-maven-local. Naming things is 90 percent of good DevOps so do not name it "repo1" unless you enjoy chaos.

Configure Maven to talk to Artifactory

Edit your ~/.m2/settings.xml to add server credentials for a dedicated deploy user. Then point your project POM distribution management to the new repo. Example snippets.

<settings>
  <servers>
    <server>
      <id>artifactory-repo</id>
      <username>deploy-user</username>
      <password>REPLACE_ME</password>
    </server>
  </servers>
</settings>
<distributionManagement>
  <repository>
    <id>artifactory-repo</id>
    <url>http://localhost:8081/artifactory/my-maven-local</url>
  </repository>
</distributionManagement>

Use a dedicated deploy user so your CI jobs do not run with admin permissions. That is how accidents become incidents.

Deploy a JAR

Two main options. For automated pipelines use the Maven deploy goal. For manual testing use the web UI upload.

  • Automated deploy from a project build agent run mvn clean deploy after making sure the POM distribution management id matches the server id in settings.xml.
  • Manual upload open the Artifactory UI, navigate to your repository and use the Deploy artifact button. It is delightfully low tech for emergency use.

Verify the deployed artifact

Check the UI to confirm the JAR and its metadata are present. If you prefer REST calls use the Artifactory storage API to inspect the item and verify checksums. Example with curl.

curl -u deploy-user:REPLACE_ME \
  "http://localhost:8081/artifactory/api/storage/my-maven-local/com/example/my-artifact/1.0/my-artifact-1.0.jar"

The response contains file info and checksums so you can script verification in CI or just flex your newfound power.

CI integration tips

  • Store credentials in your CI secret store and avoid putting passwords in plain text. This is not optional.
  • Use a non admin deploy user for pipeline jobs to reduce blast radius if a token leaks.
  • Consider using Artifactory as a proxy for Maven Central to improve build stability and performance.

Recap and final snark

We covered downloading and running Artifactory, creating a Maven local repository, updating Maven to use that repository and deploying a JAR either by Maven or manual upload. You now have a basic artifact management workflow suitable for local testing or small CI pipelines.

Pro tip use the Docker image for local labs because you will probably tear it down and rebuild it several times while pretending you knew what you were doing all along.

Why Artifactory chokes on the object heap

Artifactory is a polite beast until Java runs out of object heap space and then it throws a tantrum called OutOfMemoryError. The log will often spell out the culprit with a reference to a 2097152KB object heap requirement. In plain human terms this means the JVM was not given enough heap to stomach the repository metadata and blobs you threw at it.

Quick checklist to confirm the problem

  • Check the logs under $ARTIFACTORY_HOME/var/log or use journalctl -u artifactory.service for systemd installs
  • Search for the phrases object heap or OutOfMemoryError to confirm the 2097152KB requirement
  • See the running JVM options with ps aux | grep java so you know what the current limits are

Fix it in four boring steps

  1. Open the startup config

    For RPM and DEB based installs edit /etc/opt/jfrog/artifactory/default. For manual installs edit $ARTIFACTORY_HOME/bin/artifactory.default. Look for JAVA_OPTIONS or ARTIFACTORY_JAVA_OPTIONS and stop blaming the UI.

  2. Increase the heap sizes

    Raise the maximum heap so it comfortably exceeds 2097152KB. A practical change is to set Xmx to 3G or 4G depending on the host. Also set a sensible Min heap and direct memory if needed. Example export to drop into the default file or environment is below.

    export ARTIFACTORY_JAVA_OPTIONS="-Xms512m -Xmx3072m -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=512m"

    Pick values based on available RAM. If your server has 8GB, 3G for Xmx is reasonable. If it is starving for RAM, increase the host memory or move to a bigger VM before making the JVM greedy.

  3. Make sure the startup user can allocate the memory

    System limits and cgroups can block memory allocation. Check ulimits and any container or cloud provider memory caps. If the JVM cannot reserve the memory it will still fail at startup.

  4. Restart and verify

    Restart using the normal command for your platform. For systemd use

    systemctl restart artifactory.service

    Then watch the console log and the JVM options that the process reports to confirm the new heap values are in effect.

    tail -f $ARTIFACTORY_HOME/var/log/console.log

What to look for after restart

  • Confirm the object heap error no longer appears in the logs
  • Verify the JVM started with the expected Xmx value using ps aux | grep java
  • Monitor memory usage for the first few hours to catch any runaway growth

Troubleshooting notes and practical tips

  • Give a buffer above 2097152KB rather than matching it exactly. Computers are not fans of edge cases.
  • If Artifactory still fails, check for contradictory settings in multiple startup files. Some installs have both an OS level file and a bin file that fight like siblings over the remote control.
  • Use monitoring tools to keep an eye on heap and resident memory. If usage grows over time you may need to investigate leaks or tune caches.

Quick summary

In short, find the OutOfMemory message in the logs, edit the appropriate startup file to raise Xmx and related JVM options, restart the service and confirm the JVM is running with the new values. Do this and you will save yourself from angry console watching and whispered curses at midnight.

{ "new_title": "Confident GitHub Interview Answers That Actually Save Your Day", "new_heading": "Quick confident answers for GitHub version control and pull requests", "new_body": "

Quick primer for the interview stage

If you want to sound like you actually know what you are doing without looking like a robot, this guide covers the common GitHub interview topics with short direct answers and a dash of human sarcasm. You will get the facts on Git, GitHub, branching, pull requests, merge and rebase, plus notes on CI with GitHub Actions and open source etiquette.

Git vs GitHub

Git is the tool that lives on your machine. It tracks commits, branches, merges, and the occasional moment of existential dread when a rebase goes sideways. GitHub is a web platform that hosts repositories and adds collaboration features like issue tracking, pull requests, code review, and CI integrations.

Short answer for interviews say this and mean it. Git is the version control system. GitHub is a place to collaborate and automate work around Git.

Branching vs forking

Branching creates a parallel line of development inside the same repository. Forking copies the whole repository into another account so you can work independently and send patches back with pull requests. Use branches for team workflows and forks for external contributors or when you want to work in your own sandbox.

Pull request workflow

Keep it simple and repeatable. A typical workflow looks like this

  • Create a branch for a single concern
  • Make your changes and write focused commits
  • Push the branch and open a pull request with a clear description
  • Request reviews and respond to feedback
  • Run CI checks and address failures
  • Merge according to project rules and tidy up the branch

Remember that reviews are not an opinion contest. They are quality gates and an audit trail for future you who will be very grateful.

Merge vs rebase

Merge keeps the true history and adds a merge commit. Rebase rewrites commits onto a new base so the history looks linear and neat. Use merge when you want to preserve topology and context. Use rebase when you want a tidy linear history and you are working on local or private branches. Never rebase shared public commits without warning everyone.

Resolving conflicts like an adult

Conflicts occur when two changes touch the same lines. The process is mundane and fixable

  • Fetch the latest and bring the target branch into your work
  • Open the diffs and decide which change makes sense
  • Run tests or the app to be sure nothing broke
  • Commit the resolution with a clear message and push

Pro tip give the commit a message that explains why you chose one change over the other. Future you will send cake.

Protected branches and required reviews

Enable branch protection to require reviews, passing checks, and to prevent force pushes. This reduces accidental breakage and makes it harder for chaos to sneak into main. Configure required reviewers and checks to fit the team size and risk profile.

Authentication options

SSH keys give secure key based access from your machine. Personal access tokens have replaced passwords for API and command line operations. For automation use fine grained tokens or GitHub Apps and apply least privilege. Treat secrets like molten metal and never commit them to source.

GitHub Actions basics

Actions automate builds, tests, and deployments on events like push or pull_request. Start with a simple workflow that runs tests on each push. Expand with reusable actions and environment secrets for deployments. Keep workflows fast and focused so CI is not a sleeping giant that ruins developer morale.

Security best practices

  • Scan dependencies with Dependabot or similar tools
  • Do not commit secrets and rotate tokens regularly
  • Apply least privilege to teams, tokens, and apps
  • Protect branches and require passing checks

Open source etiquette

Read contribution guidelines and follow the code of conduct. Write helpful PR descriptions, link issues to changes, and respond to feedback politely even when you disagree. Give credit and be thankful when someone points out a smarter way to do things.

How to practice answers

Practice talking out loud. Be ready to explain a brief live demo on a test repo such as creating a branch, making a small change, opening a pull request, and resolving a conflict. Keep answers concise and include why you chose a workflow. That shows judgement not just memorization.

In short be accurate, keep workflows predictable, automate the boring stuff, and never ever push a secret to public main. Say that in your interview and you will sound smart and mildly terrifying in a good way.

{"new_title":"Master Jenkins Interviews with Practical Pipeline Answers","new_heading":"Real world Jenkins pipeline tips for CI CD and DevOps interviews","new_body":"

What Jenkins actually does and why you should care

If you are prepping for a Jenkins interview this guide will get you from nodding politely to sounding like you own the CI CD pipeline. Jenkins is an open source automation server used to build test and deliver software. It ties together commits to builds to tests to deploys and lets teams automate repetitive tasks so humans can worry about more dramatic failures.

Master and agents explained

Think of the master as the traffic cop and agents as the worker bees. The master schedules jobs, stores configuration and serves the UI. Agents run the actual build steps on separate machines or containers. Use agents when you want isolation, different OS images, or to scale horizontally without turning your master into a stressed out paperweight.

Freestyle jobs versus pipeline jobs

Freestyle jobs are GUI friendly and fine for tiny tasks or legacy setups. Pipelines are code driven workflows that live in a Jenkinsfile next to your source. Pipelines travel with the repo and handle complex logic, parallel stages and retries much more cleanly.

Why Jenkinsfile matters

A Jenkinsfile gives you pipeline as code. It makes builds reproducible, reviewable and versioned. Interviewers will love that you can show a real Jenkinsfile and explain it step by step instead of reciting vague platitudes.

pipeline { 
  agent any 
  stages { 
    stage('Build') { 
      steps { echo 'Building' } 
    } 
    stage('Test') { 
      steps { echo 'Testing' } 
    } 
    stage('Deploy') { 
      steps { echo 'Deploying' } 
    } 
  } 
}

Declarative versus scripted pipelines

Declarative pipelines give structure and sensible defaults, making them easier to read and maintain. Scripted pipelines use Groovy and give you full control when you need it. Bring examples for both if you can, but prefer declarative for most interview answers unless the role requires heavy Groovy customization.

Handling credentials like a responsible human

Store secrets in the Jenkins Credentials store and reference them by id in your pipeline steps. Never echo secrets into console output. If you must use an external vault mention how you would integrate it and why it reduces blast radius for secrets.

Plugins you should at least be able to name and explain

  • Pipeline plugin for pipeline as code
  • Credentials plugin for secret management
  • Git plugin for source pulls
  • Blue Ocean for a nicer UI experience
  • Kubernetes plugin for container based agents

For each plugin say what problem it solves and one limitation to show you actually tested it instead of reading a marketing blurb.

Scaling and reliability basics

Use distributed agents, run builds in containers, and keep pipeline as code so you can spin up new builders fast. Back up JENKINS_HOME regularly and use role based access control to reduce the chance someone accidentally nukes production with a misplaced shell step.

Where logs live and how to troubleshoot failed stages

Build logs are stored per job under the Jenkins home directory and you can view them in the UI. The system log is usually available on the server at a path or in the service logs for your OS. When a stage fails check the console output, look for exit codes, rerun with extra verbosity and isolate steps locally if possible. Mentioning how you would reproduce a flaky test outside Jenkins will score points.

Security and good interview talking points

  • Never print secrets to logs
  • Use least privilege for service accounts
  • Prefer ephemeral agents to reduce persistent attack surface
  • Keep plugins up to date and audit them for risky permissions

Practical prep tips for your interview

Bring a small Jenkinsfile for a build and test flow that you can walk through. Be ready to explain how a commit travels through CI to CD and where failures would be investigated. Practice reading a Jenkinsfile out loud and describing what each stage does. If you can show a brief debugging story where logs and retries fixed the problem you will turn theory into credibility.

Final thought for the brave

Jenkins interviews look for practical experience more than buzzword fluency. Show you can explain masters and agents, choose the right job type, protect secrets and keep pipelines maintainable. Do that and you will sound calm, competent and annoyingly employable."}
